There will be a bit more passing, and more vertical downfield shots in the new system.

Dampier returns after earning Big 12 Newcomer and improving on turnovers and passing accuracy even despite the upgrade in competition from the Mountain West to the Big 12. Dampier is the most elusive pocket scrambler in America, threw 24 touchdowns with just 5 picks, and did so while battling injuries. His backup Byrd Ficklin was lightning-in-a-bottle and he rushed for 10 touchdowns (8.4 per carry). Look for Ficklin to get some packages again this year and these two don’t mind sharing.

Wayshawn Parker vowed to be a thousand-yard back and he got to 981 with a high 6.6 per-carry average that ranked second in Power 4 (min. 100 carries) only behind Heisman runner-up Jeremiyah Love. Parker returns as the workhorse back, and the staff added short-yardage bulldozer Steve Chavez-Soto (San Jose State).

Utah’s top three pass-catchers are gone: Big 12 honorable mention receiver Ryan Davis, plus tight ends Dallen Bentley and JJ Buchanan (Michigan). Even still, Scalley called this 2026 unit “the best wide receiver crew we’ve ever had at Utah.” The program hasn’t had a 1,000-yarder in 13 years, but they signed two transfers who got close last year. Braden Pegan (Utah State) and Kyri Shoels (San Jose State) were both All-Mountain West, combined for 1,700 yards last year, and both were graded as four-star transfers. Other returners could be poised for breakout seasons like Larry Simmons, Ricky Johnson, and Creed Whittemore in the slot. Hunter Andrews returns at tight end after his 2025 injury.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Scalley led the Utah defense for a decade with his “RSNB” culture: Relentless, Smart, Nasty, Ballhawks. That last one, ballhawks, is a perfect description for their nation-best 24 straight seasons taking back a Pick Six.

Scalley delegated the coordinator role and play-calling duties to Colton Swan who has coached the linebackers here since 2019.

Nine starters are gone, including all four defensive linemen, their sack leader, two veteran backers, and their top corner.

John Henry Daley led Power 4 in sacks/game but he and starting tackle Jonah Lea’ea both followed Whittingham to Michigan. So did All-Big 12 corner Smith Snowden.

On the inside Pupu Sepulona and Karson Kaufusi both got 130+ snaps last year, and at the end spots Kash Dillon and Lance Holtzclaw move up into starting roles. The staff signed North Texas starter Ethan Day to join the end rotation. Last year, the Utah defense was unusually weak against the run and had some breakdowns in November like when Kansas State rolled up 472 yards on the ground.

Tackle leader Johnathan Hall returns at linebacker though they will miss Lander Barton and Levani Damuni. Trey Reynolds moves up the depth chart, and the staff must feel confident as they did not sign any transfers here.

The safety room is a strength, and simply put, Jackson Bennee is a play-maker. He had four interceptions, always seems to be near the ball, and should get All-Big 12 hype. Original starter Rabbit Evans and sixth-year veteran Nate Ritchie are both back from 2025 injuries.

Five defensive backs transferred out to Power 4 rosters, including their star Snowden, but the staff backfilled with three- star transfers from the non-AQ and JUCO levels. Scooby Davis is the lone returner at corner, former JUCO Rock Caldwell could start at nickel, and Elijah Reed and James Chenault (USF) will battle at the other corner.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
2025 was a total disappointment. With nine eventual NFL Draft picks, and the most veteran lineup in the league, they fell to their worst season since 2010.

Swinney doubled down on his anti-transfer plan, added zero offensive linemen or quarterbacks, but Clemson’s high school recruiting still keeps them in ACC contention. They are no longer on the Dynasty Tier but should remain a Top 25 team with a roster packed with former four-star recruits.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
The transfer portal has exploded since 2020 and changed how programs build their rosters. Thousands of players shift schools every offseason in what has become the biggest Musical Chairs in sports. While every other program doubled down and tripled down on the transfer market, Clemson and head coach Dabo Swinney remained committed to traditional recruiting with an anti-transfer stance.

Without the steady influx of proven college talent to patch up roster holes or cover for recruiting/scouting misses, the Dabo model meant the strength of the team would be cyclical year to year: developmental years with younger rosters, but then eventually the proven, veteran roster to cash in for championship runs.

With 17 starters returning from an ACC title team, Clemson was set to cash in. This was it – the year of vindication for Dabo’s model. They entered 2025 as unanimous ACC favorites to repeat, and started with a high #4 preseason ranking.

Far from a title run, the whole thing collapsed in September.

Clemson lost the opener to LSU, needed a 16-point comeback to survive against Troy, and then lost ACC games to Georgia Tech and Syracuse. The offense was unproductive, the defense couldn’t get the ACC offenses off the field, and they hit their first 1-3 start to a season since 2004.

Another wave of losses dropped Clemson to its worst season in 15 years. “I feel like I’m in 2010 all over again,” Swinney said.

Though they did take back the rivalry crown from South Carolina, Swinney’s “greatest turnaround team in Clemson history” praise rings hollow.

Clemson remained committed to the old strategy and signed the ACC’s second-fewest transfers this cycle and notably did not sign a quarterback or a single offensive lineman. Multi-year starter Cade Klubnik graduated, the entire starting line is gone, but they kept the reload in-house.

That strategy, along with Swinney’s change at offensive coordinator, will define the 2026 season.
pick_six_2026.offense:
It does feel like 2010 with the hire at offensive coordinator. Clemson brought back Chad Morris, whose so-called “Smashmouth Spread” offense helped end the school’s ACC title drought in 2011 and eventually his successors kept the scheme through the dynasty years.

Morris said he wants a two-back offense, a commitment to a physical rushing attack, and vertical shots downfield in the pass game.

That was all missing last year, as Clemson fell to #105 in rushing yards/game – Swinney’s lowest – and below average marks in Offensive Line Run Push and Explosive Passing. And that was with the most veteran offense in America.

It’s a full transition heading into 2026 with just three returning starters. Multi-year starter Klubnik graduated and Clemson doubled down on their quarterback room. Chris Vizzina was the #6 ranked quarterback in the 2023 recruiting class, and the former Top100 prospect spent three years as a backup. Vizzina started the SMU game and went 29/42 for 317 yards and three touchdowns but is otherwise an unknown. Against Furman, dual-threat Chris Denson posted Clemson’s first 100-yard quarterback rushing game since Trevor Lawrence. But after spring, Swinney said the fall camp battle will be between Vezzina and incoming freshman three-star Tait Reynolds.

The other surprise was Clemson signing zero linemen from the portal to help fuel a reload as all five starters depart. Blake Miller earned first-team All-ACC honors after 50+ career starts while three others joined him with all-league honors. Despite the individual accolades, the unit struggled to get a run push and fell by 60 spots in all key stat categories.

Aside from Harris Sewell and Collin Sadler getting bowl game starts, this is a completely fresh starting five. Four of them are former Top200 four-star recruits but they collectively lack game experience.

All-ACC Adam Randall graduates and the staff signed SMU co-starter Chris Johnson who brings explosiveness, speed, and a high 7.1 yard/carry average. 2025 Top100 Gideon Davidson got some carries as a true freshman and gets a bigger role this year.

Clemson was able to retain two all-league stars in outside receivers Bryant Wesco and TJ Moore. Wesco had a season-ending injury but at full strength he is a potential All-American. They do lose Antonio Williams in the slot, but Tyler Brown returns there, and they signed near-five-star Naeem Burroughs.

Both tight ends return, and it sounds like Morris will be using both much more this season. Christian Bentancur and Olsen Patt-Henry combined for 36 catches last year but should get more this fall with one at end and one in an H-back role.
pick_six_2026.defense:
From 2014-2023 Clemson posted 10 straight Top 10 defenses in my opponent-adjusted rankings – a full decade of elite defense. The 2024 and 2025 units ranked #43 and #39 of 68 Power 4.

Tom Allen took over as coordinator last year and helped boost the rush defense into the Top 25. The second-year coach bonus may be muted due to the loss of star power with six All-ACC defenders leaving.

TJ Parker and defensive tackles Peter Woods and Demonte Capehart all depart, but the productive Will Heldt is back at end after a 15.5 tackle-for-loss, 7.5 sack season. Jahiem Lawson moves up into the other end spot and the staff signed All-Freshman London Merritt (Colorado) who was second on his team in tackles-for-loss.

Both tackle spots are open but could remain a strength again with Oklahoma transfer Markus Strong and five-star Amare Adams in his second season.

First-team All-ACC Sammy Brown returns at linebacker as the star of the defense. Brown finished second in the ACC with 106 tackles and should push for All-America consideration. His co-star Wade Woodaz graduated, and Clemson lost a late transfer battle for Cal’s Luke Ferrelli, so Kobe McCloud will battle former five-star Jeremiah Alexander for the starting role.

Three more all-league stars are gone from the secondary as Avieon Terrell graduated and safeties Ricardo Jones (Vanderbilt) and Khalil Barnes (Georgia) transferred out. The staff used the transfer portal here and signed three projected starters in three-stars Corey Myrick (Southern Miss), Jerome Carter (Old Dominion), and Elliot Washington (Penn State). Myrick and All-Sun Belt Carter will be the safety pair, while Washington drew huge Dabo praise: “by far the best guy in camp.”

Ashton Hampton takes over as the new #1 corner, Corian Gipson is back at nickel, and Donovan Starr (Auburn) and Branden Strozier add talent to the room.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Few programs have built up a track record like Ferentz and Parker at Iowa. Even with another round of draft picks departing, you know what to expect: a powerful offensive line, elite tight end room, workhorse running back, a swarming defense, and nation-best special teams.

While this is a younger two-deep than usual, and low on transfer additions, Iowa will remain in the Big Ten upper half until proven otherwise.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Not counting the shortened 2020 pandemic season, Iowa notched its tenth straight eight-win season to join very elite company: Alabama, Georgia, Ohio State. That’s it.

“Eight wins doesn’t make headlines… it’s hard to win, it’s hard to win in college… I’m proud of the consistency,” said head coach Kirk Ferentz who in September became the Big Ten’s all-time winningest coach with 206 career wins.

Two things stood out about this 2025 eight-win regular season. Iowa thoroughly destroyed their old Big Ten West rivals, but came up just short against their ranked opponents.

Wisconsin dominated the division during the 2010s, but it is clear that Iowa has now taken the throne. They swept their border state rivals Minnesota, Nebraska, and Wisconsin by a combined score of 118-19 and extended their recent series dominance: 10 of the last 11 over Nebraska, 10 of the last 11 over Minnesota, and now four straight over Wisconsin.

They were also painfully close to knocking off their ranked opponents. Iowa was tied or held leads in the final two minutes in three losses, blew a 14-point lead in the fourth one, gave eventual national champion Indiana its closest battle, and had semifinalist Oregon on the ropes.

Four ranked opponents, four losses by a combined 15 points. Though there are no moral victories, from a metrics perspective my Game Grader formula was impressed and ranked Iowa #16 – a five-year high for the program.

In the bowl game, Iowa was given one last ranked shot and beat #14 Vanderbilt, along with Heisman finalist Diego Pavia, to finally snap the 13-game losing streak against ranked teams.
pick_six_2026.offense:
They did it the Iowa way: defense, special teams and a power run game.

Mark Gronowski was an upgrade at quarterback. The FCS national champion missed preseason due to injuries, which slowed his passing progression early on, but he ended up breaking the school records for quarterback rushing yards (545) and touchdowns (16). Gronowski tied Michigan’s Denard Robinson for the most rushing scores by a Big Ten quarterback in the past 30 years.

Gronowski’s mobility helped on third downs and in the red zone, and his 67-yard run made the difference in the Penn State win. Two fourth-down conversions on the final drive gave Iowa a late lead over Oregon.

They lose his veteran presence as coordinator Tim Lester decided to stay in-house for the 2026 quarterback battle. Hank Brown was the original backup but struggled in September spots and Jeremy Hecklinski passed him on the depth chart midseason. Hecklinski showed off a variety of throws and arm angles, has pocket mobility, and Lester called him a “gunslinger.”

After finishing 2024 as semifinalists, the 2025 offensive line won the Joe Moore Award. All five starters, plus the blocking tight end, earned Big Ten honors with center Logan Jones winning the Rimington Award as a unanimous All-American. The line was packed with veterans, and three multi-year starters depart for the pros: Jones, guard Beau Stephens, and tackle Gennings Dunker. That trio alone accounted for 110 career starts.

Trevor Lauck and Kade Pieper are returning starters and both should be All-America candidates for 2026. Leighton Jones is a lock at guard, while the other three candidates for starting jobs are former three-star prospects.

Kamari Moulton returns after a workhorse season. He got the bulk of carries with 170 for 878 yards (5.2 average) to earn All-Big Ten honorable mention. Xavier Williams (5.8 per carry) returns, and the staff signed an explosive FCS back in LJ Phillips (South Dakota) who rushed for 1,921 yards with 55 10+ yard carries.

Iowa loses their blocking tight end Hayden Large but they return a talented trio. DJ Vonnahme led the entire team in receiving yards and touchdowns as a freshman, had a breakout performance in the bowl game, and looks to continue Iowa’s “Tight End U” lineage. Addison Ostrenga and Zach Ortwerth round out a top-notch room.

Three of the top four receivers are gone including consistent two-year starter Jacob Gill, do-it-all Kaden Wetjen, and Sam Phillips. Wetjen leaves as one of the best return specialists in college football history and was the first to win consecutive Jet Awards. He was a weapon on special teams but also got carries on reverses and end-arounds.

Reece Vander Zee returns and has the size and athleticism to be the #1 target. Iowa signed a pair of FCS Freshman All-Americans in Evan James (Furman) and Tony Diaz (UTRGV). They combined for 1,677 yards and 18 touchdowns last year and both add a vertical, explosive element to the pass game.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Legendary coordinator Phil Parker delivered yet another Top 10 defense. Iowa finished #7 of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted ranking – Top 10 for the sixth time in eight years.

The pass defense was elite again and ranked #1 in my opponent-adjusted number, holding top passing attacks like Indiana, Oregon, and USC all well below their season averages.

There is a significant rebuilding project on this side of the ball heading into 2026. Iowa had eight defenders earn All-Big Ten honors, but seven are gone. 11 of the top 14 tacklers depart, two transferred out to Power 4 programs, but the staff went FCS-heavy with as many as three new starters coming from the lower level.

Six of the top eight defensive linemen are gone including all-league stars Aaron Graves, Jonah Pace, and Max Llewellyn. Bryce Hawthorne and end Kenneth Merrieweather return from the rotation, and two FCS transfers will compete for starting jobs. Brice Stevenson (Holy Cross) was a three- year starter as an interior space-eater, while Kahmari Brown (Elon) had 12 sacks last year off the edge. Five-star Iose Epenesa may be poised for a breakthrough in his second season.

The starting linebacker trio Karson Sharar, Jaden Harrell, and Jaxon Rexroth departs, though Jayden Montgomery actually took over Harrell’s job late in the season. A pair of former four-stars – Cam Buffington and Derek Weisskopf -- are drawing huge praise and could jump up into starting jobs.

The top-rated secondary lost three All-Big Ten starters as corner TJ Hall and safety Xavier Nwankpa went pro and Koen Entringer transferred out to Louisville. Zach Lutmer is the star of the defense at the “CASH” position as a nickel/slot corner. Deshaun Lee returns at corner, but the staff went transfer-heavy to fill out the safety room. Tyler Brown (James Madison) was All-Sun Belt on JMU’s playoff defense and the hard-hitter should start at strong safety. Anthony Hawkins (Villanova) was an FCS Freshman All-American and has the cover skills to start at free safety.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
The Big 12 has a crowded top-half of the league and each team has strengths and uncertainties. TCU is tied with Texas Tech for the #1 five-year recruiting average and Dykes’ plan has been recruit & retain, rather than enter the transfer market.

TCU was in the Big 12’s top six in all three opponent-adjusted metrics – Game Grader, Offense, and Defense – and is strong on both lines of scrimmage. The wildcard is at quarterback with Craig, an FCS star with NFL buzz, who is stepping up from the Ivy League to the Big 12. TCU is my pick for fourth in the league.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
In 2024 TCU went 9-4 with a pair of league losses by a combined four points that could have vaulted them back to Dallas for a title shot.

With their gunslinger quarterback surrounded by a veteran roster, that remained the target for 2025.

They certainly looked the part in the season opener, a Labor Day national spotlight game with all the coverage focused on Bill Belichick’s UNC program. TCU flattened them. The 48 points were the most ever allowed by a Belichick defense.

TCU knocked off both rivals, too. Eric McAlister posted 254 yards and three touchdowns on eight catches as TCU won the final scheduled Iron Skillet over SMU. Then the defense picked off the nation’s passing leader Sawyer Robertson three times in the 42-36 win over Baylor.

A knock on the 2024 team was their schedule strength and lack of a ranked win. TCU ended the drought by beating #23 Houston and then #16 USC in the Alamo Bowl. But like 2024, two close losses leave behind a mixed legacy for the season. TCU blew a 17-0 lead, and then later a 24-17 fourth-quarter lead to defending league champs Arizona State. Then after dominating the stat sheet, a crazy rambling punt return touchdown in the final minutes flipped the Iowa State

game to a loss.

Another year, the same 9-4 record, and two winnable games that blocked potential runs to the league title game.

Turnovers were a constant theme in the losses, with Josh Hoover tossing eight picks in the four losses, with a 4-8 touchdown-to-pick ratio in losses compared to the 25-5 split in wins. Hoover holds the TCU single-season passing record and was eligible to return for a fourth season as the starter, but he shockingly transferred out to Indiana. When asked about it, head coach Sonny Dykes noted “Josh started 31 games here, and turned the ball over 42 times.”

Hoover’s departure was shocking, but otherwise TCU excelled in player retention this offseason cycle. In fact he appears to be the only guy from the two-deep to transfer away.

It was a smaller transfer haul, but TCU placed #1, #2, and #1 in Big 12 high school recruiting 2023- 2025 and doubled-down on retaining and developing that talent.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Offensive coordinator Kendal Briles left for South Carolina after some mixed results here: strong passing attack, but an ineffective run game. Dykes hired UConn’s coordinator Gordon Sammis who posted #15 and #35 scoring offenses in his two years at the helm there. Sammis will implement a pro-style offense with more tight end usage and more under-center snaps – a move away from Briles’ spread, Air Raid, veer- and-shoot scheme.

With Hoover leaving for Indiana, the staff pulled their next starter from the FCS level. Jaden Craig was a three-year starter for Harvard, holds their career touchdowns record, and took care of the ball with a 52- 12 TD-INT ratio. Craig is a 6’3, 230-pounder who brings mobility to the position and showed off straight- line speed on scrambles. In spring, Craig impressed with big arm strength, looks to improve on accuracy in fall camp, but is the unquestioned starter heading into the season. Craig was ranked as the #22 transfer quarterback this cycle, and is a rare FCS to Power 4 starter.

Adam Schobel was a Top200 prospect in the 2025 class and is the heir apparent for 2027.

Original starter Kevorian Barnes was injured halfway into the season and Jeremy Payne thrived with the opportunity. Payne surged in the final few games – 174 yards vs. Cincinnati, 103 vs. Houston – and then scored the overtime game-winner by breaking four USC tackles. He ended with 623 rushing yards (5.7 per carry) and should hit 1,000 with Sammis’ tilting the play selection more towards the run.

Eric McAlister was a dominant force all season. He finished with 1,190 receiving yards, 10 touchdowns, and was named a third-team All-American and Biletnikoff semifinalist. He and starting slot receiver Joseph Manjack are both gone, but TCU did retain Jordan Dwyer (730 yards and 7 touchdowns) who takes over as the new #1 target. TCU has recruited well here with three former four-stars batting for starting spots: slot Ed Small, 6’4 spring hero Terry Shelton, and former Notre Dame transfer Braylon James. The staff also signed South Alabama starter Jeremy Scott.

Both tight ends DJ Rogers and Chase Curtis graduated, but a potential All-Big 12 star is emerging. Former Top100 recruit, 6’6 Ka’Morreun Pimpton exploded in spring and looks like a third-down favorite for Craig. Kari Ashley was ranked the #2 JUCO tight end.

The offensive line has been disappointing in the run game the past two years, ranking #103 and #97 in my OL Run Push metric. This is Sammis’ area of expertise, and the room looks poised for improvement with three returning starters joined by a pair of impact transfers. Ben Taylor-Whitfield enters his third season as the starting tackle and was named the most impressive spring lineman. Cade Bennett is back at guard for a seventh college season after winning an appeal, and original starter Ryan Hughes is back from an injury. The staff signed Oklahoma State starter Noah McKinney who barely missed a four-star transfer rank, and Jaheim Buchanon (FIU) who was All-CUSA and allowed just two sacks over 1,600 snaps.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Andy Avalos didn’t get a second-year coordinator bonus, as TCU regressed 11 spots in my opponent- adjusted defense rank from #23 to #34 of 68 Power 4. The pass defense fell further – below average in the Big 12 – despite two all-league safeties and two of the top five fastest linebackers at the NFL Combine.

Those backers will be missed. Kaleb Elarms-Orr earned first-team All-Big 12 honors with 130 tackles (#4 in Power 4), Namdi Obiazor added 88, and the pair combined for 15 tackles for loss. Last year’s third backer Max Carroll steps up into the lead role and Virginia Tech transfer Michael Short battles a bunch of three-stars for the other spot.

Bud Clark has been a program icon all the way back to his Pick Six against Michigan in the 2022 Playoffs. Clark took another one back in the UNC win and became a three-time All-Big 12 pick. Clark, nickel Austin Jordan, and corner Channing Canada are all gone but the secondary has a star to build around with second-team All-Big 12 safety Jamel Johnson back. Johnson was heavily involved in the run game with 96 tackles and also grabbed five picks. Kylin Jackson moves up to the starting nickel spot and C-USA Defensive Player of the Year Jacob Fields (Louisiana Tech) is projected at safety.

TCU needs improvement from the corners, and while they brought in two starters – Teon Parks (Colorado) and Kalen Carroll (Central Michigan) – it appears Gil Jackson surged in spring alongside returning starter Vernon Glover.

The defensive line loses a big one in defensive end Devean Deal, but has plenty of star power as the strength of the 2026 defense. Nose tackle Markis Deal is poised for a breakout, Ansel Din-Mbuh is a returning starter at tackle, Paul Oyewale is a rotational veteran at end, and Zach Chapman ranked in the Big 12’s top ten in QB Pressures after an All-Freshman campaign in 2024.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Auburn was better than their record showed the past two years – especially defensively. Golesh kept defensive coordinator Durkin, who was able to keep five starters off their Top 20 defense.

Then to fix the other side of the ball, Golesh swapped in ten players from his Top 5 USF offense including dynamic dual-threat Byrum Brown. Auburn should return to bowl season and may even post their first Top 25 offense in a decade.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
In 2013, Auburn pulled off their “Miracle at Jordan-Hare” and then the “Kick Six” within a three-week span. It’s almost as if they used up a decade’s worth of good fortune and are still paying off the debt.

Attempting to snap a five-year streak of losing seasons, the 2025 team appeared to be cursed.

Week after week they were on the short end of tight, one-score SEC losses. Oklahoma pulled off a controversial trick play and sacked Auburn nine times in a 24-17 finish. Auburn went 0/12 on third downs and lost by six at Texas A&M. Another controversial call at the goal-line ended up flipping the Georgia game, and then they lost in double-overtime to Missouri.

After that unlucky stretch, a 10-3 loss to Kentucky was the final straw for head coach Hugh Freeze who finished under .500 at 15-19 overall – 6-16 vs. the SEC – and was just the third Auburn coach in 75 years to post a losing record at Jordan-Hare.

It wasn’t just the losses. Freeze was picked as the offensive guru type hire, but his offense was still completely broken in his third year. And that was with a stockpile of five-star receivers and one of the SEC’s best offensive lines on paper.

The program is ready to put their 2025 campaign, and the six one-score losses, in the rear-view mirror and move forward with one of the sport’s most productive offensive coaches.

Auburn emerged from the most crowded coaching carousel in history with South Florida head coach Alex Golesh, and the offensive innovator is bringing most of his Top 5 offense with him.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Many coaches call their offense “spread” but Golesh truly means it. He stretches the defense from sideline to sideline, with the receivers as wide as possible. He also operates at a hyper- fast tempo and his scheme has produced Top 5 offenses at UCF, Tennessee, and South Florida. The 2022 Tennessee offense led the entire nation with 46.1 points/game.

Alongside Josh Heupel and then again on his own at South Florida, Golesh has led offensive turnarounds at each stop. They certainly need a fix here, as Auburn hasn’t had a Top 25 offense since 2014.

“Quarterback play is so much about putting a system together that fits the quarterback,” said Golesh at his opening presser. No need to worry about system fit this year – he’s bringing his star with him.

Byrum Brown (USF) was the only quarterback in FBS to post 3,000 passing yards and 1,000 rushing yards. It’s such a rare feat that he became the 12th all-time. Auburn’s three starters Jackson Arnold, Ashton Daniels, and Deuce Knight all transferred out and Brown was ranked the #9 transfer quarterback after earning All-AAC honors last year.

In addition to Brown, Golesh brought five receivers, two offensive linemen, a tight end and a running back off his #5 ranked USF offense. The transition at receiver is most striking, as Auburn’s entire stockpile of five-star weapons all transferred out: Cam Coleman (Texas), Eric Singleton (Florida), Malcolm Simmons (Texas Tech), Horatio Fields (Ole Miss), and Perry Thompson (Minnesota).

Like a hockey line-change, Golesh reloaded the room with his USF starting rotation. Keshaun Singleton led USF in all stat categories, Jeremiah Koger was second and earned a four-star transfer grade, Christian Neptune impressed as a freshman, and Chas Nimrod is now the fastest player in the Auburn program. Those four combined for 149 catches, 2,275 yards, and 20 touchdowns last year, in this scheme, from this quarterback.

Tight end Jonathan Echols (USF) added three more scores and forms a solid duo with Power 4 veteran Jake Johnson (North Carolina).

It’s another complete rebuild in the trenches with all five starting offensive linemen gone. This unit was stacked on paper, and Connor Lew and Jeremiah Wright were drafted, but as a unit they collapsed in pass protection allowing a sack on 12% of attempts (#132). 17 new linemen joined the program this offseason and several spots are up for grabs heading into fall camp. Cole Best (USF) was All-AAC, Jo Simmons (James Madison) was All-Sun Belt, and tackle Stanton Ramil (Michigan State) was a Big Ten starter.

Finally a familiar face. Jeremiah Cobb is the lone returning starter on offense and earned third- team All-SEC after nearly hitting 1,000 yards. The staff packed the room with two starters who earned four-star transfer grades: Nykahi Davenport (USF) and the physical Bryson Washington (Baylor). Many overlook the run game in this up-tempo, spread scheme, but Golesh wants a downhill run game. USF ranked in the Top 20 in all rushing stat categories last year.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Golesh retained defensive coordinator DJ Durkin, rewarding his work building a Top 20 defense per my opponent-adjusted rankings. They were #4 against the run, and as a unit they certainly held up their end of the bargain in SEC play but had no help from the offense.

Keeping Durkin here helped them retain five starters – none bigger than linebacker Xavier Atkins who becomes the first returning All-American defender here since Takeo Spikes in 1997. Atkins was also first-team SEC, a Bednarik semifinalist, and led the SEC with 17 tackles for loss. His co- star Robert Woodyard left for Missouri, but Elijah Melendez returns after earning SEC All- Freshman. Former Top100 Demarcus Riddick is back healthy after flashing as a true freshman in 2024.

The safety room is the next strongest position with returning starters Kaleb Harris and Eric Winters joined by two-year USF starter Fred Gaskin. AnQuon Fegans is another Top100 who could push for a starting role at nickelback.

Auburn lost their strong starting cornerback pair to the portal, as Jay Crawford (Ole Miss) and Kayin Lee (Tennessee) both went to other SEC programs. But Rayshawn Pleasant is back and he made the game-winning Pick Six in Auburn’s only SEC win last year. Andre Jordan (UCLA) is projected at the other corner after earning All-Big Ten honors, while Top100 Blake Woodby is the third corner.

Like the offensive line, this side is a total rebuild as three were drafted and two more transferred out with high grades. Keldric Faulk and Keyron Crawford will especially be missed off the edges. The staff landed some four- star transfers of their own with tackles Cody Sigler (Arkansas State) and Walter Mathis (LSU) and end Da’Shawn Womack (Ole Miss) who got huge spring praise. Durkin was able to retain two of their prized 2025 signees with tackles Malik Autry and Jourdin Crawford both back. Dallas Walker is back at nose tackle and edge Chris Murray got a bonus year of eligibility.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Drinkwitz has elevated the recruiting profile and the program’s floor, but there is too much change to call for 2026 to be their breakthrough season. It’s a full rebuild on defense with all 11 starters gone.

Their power run game is enough to get them back to bowl season, but Drinkwitz is still 0-16 against teams with SEC winning records and they draw five of the top six this fall.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
“Good, not great” was how head coach Eli Drinkwitz summed up the 2025 season. Simple, but accurate.

Missouri’s eight wins came against teams that finished with losing records. Against winning teams, they went 0-5. It was the same split based off their opponent’s ranking – 0-5 vs. ranked, 8-0 vs. unranked.

Good, not great. It’s an extension of Drinkwitz’s six-year career here with a 26-24 record against the SEC, but a league-worst 0-16 mark against SEC teams that finished with winning league records.

Even with the struggles against the elite tier, Drinkwitz has certainly raised the floor of the program as they notched three-straight eight-win seasons for the first time since 2009-11.

Missouri beat Kansas 42-31 in the first “Border War” played in over a decade, Beau Pribula led a fourth-quarter win over South Carolina, then an overtime win over Auburn. Ahmad Hardy was the engine of the offense and won the Power 4 rushing title with 1,649 yards.

opponent-adjusted ranking, as well as top ten marks in several other national stat categories.

Corey Batoon’s defense reloaded and posted a Top 10 finish in my

But ultimately their lack of a serious passing threat was a limitation against their ranked opponents. Missouri ranked #131 (third-worst in Power 4) in QB Rating against teams with winning records.

Missouri heads into 2026 focused on rebuilding their passing attack – with a new quarterback, coordinator, and quarterbacks coach – and reloading nearly the entire starting lineup.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Only four starters return to the entire team, but their best one returns in the backfield. Hardy earned consensus All-America honors after posting a school-record rushing season. He pinballed off tacklers all season and actually rushed for over 1,000 yards after contact.

His running mate Jamal Roberts also returns to form one of the best running back pairs in America. Last year Hardy (1,649) and Roberts (753) were one of just four Power 4 duos to run for 750+ yards joining Indiana, Michigan, and Texas Tech.

Missouri went run-heavy last year, especially when Pribula missed time with injuries. It wasn’t just quantity, but quality on a per-play basis. Missouri had the biggest difference in passing/rushing rankings per my opponent-adjusted stats: #8 Rushing, #65 Passing of 68 Power 4.

Kirby Moore left to become the head coach at Washington State, and Drinkwitz hired journeyman Chip Lindsey to take over the offense. This will be Lindsey’s eighth school in the past 12 seasons and his stat impact has been mixed. The most recent two stops – UNC and Michigan – produced below average passing offenses despite featuring Drake Maye and #1 overall recruit Bryce Underwood.

Drinkwitz also hired Garrett Riley who helped lead TCU to the national title game in 2022, but also underwhelmed the past few seasons at Clemson.

Pribula added a dynamic layer to the run game, broke Chase Daniel’s school record with 21 straight completions, but also struggled with turnovers. Pribula transferred out to Virginia, backup Matt Zollers returned after starting a few games as a freshman (53% completion, 4 touchdowns, 2 picks), but their announced starter is incoming transfer Austin Simmons (Ole Miss). The lefty was the original starter for the first two games (60%, 4 TD, 5 INT) before being unseated by DII phenom Trinidad Chambliss. Simmons has a strong arm, enough mobility to create plays, and earned a four-star transfer grade as the #10 quarterback this cycle.

Missouri lost three of their top four receivers when Kevin Coleman went pro and Marquis Johnson and Joshua Manning left for other Power 4 programs. Donovan Olugbode was a Top100 super-recruit and played like it right away, posting 30 catches for 401 yards as a true freshman. The staff signed two other starters from the portal, with four-star transfer Cayden Lee (Ole Miss) and Caleb Goodie (Cincinnati). Lee will start in the slot, has experience with Simmons at Ole Miss, and put up 106 catches for 1,623 yards in his three seasons there. Goodie is a vertical threat on the outside, and speedy four-star Shaun Terry is next in the rotation.

Brett Norfleet returns for a fourth season as the starting tight end.

The offensive line made a major improvement in my OL Run Push stat boosting all the way up to #22, but pass protection fell to #103 though some of that blame was shared by the inexperienced quarterbacks. Keagen Trost and Cayden Green earned All-SEC honors, but Trost and 48-game starting center Connor Tollison are gone. Three starters are back, with Green as the anchor at left tackle, and Curtis Peagler and Dom Giudice on the interior. Tristan Wilson is next in line at center, Logan Reichert is a former four- star, and Johnnie Jones was a Top100 signee this class. The staff signed three Power 4 starters from the portal in Josh Atkins (Arizona State), and a pair from Mississippi State: Luke Work and Zach Owens. All were graded as three-star transfers.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Batoon has done an excellent job continuing the success of Blake Baker and the 2025 unit was their best yet at #8 in my opponent-adjusted stat.

2026 will be his toughest test yet as all 11 starters are gone.

That includes three elite stars from the front seven. Defensive end Damon Wilson transferred out to Miami as a Top 10 overall transfer, end Zion Young and linebacker Josiah Trotter went pro, and that’s a trio of All-SEC talent gone.

Young and Wilson were both in the SEC’s top three of QB Pressures, and departing starting tackles Chris McClellan and Sterling Webb combined for 68 tackles, 11.5 for loss, and 8 sacks. Missouri also lost their prized Top50 2025 recruit Javion Hilson who left for Virginia Tech.

Darris Smith returns at end and for a third rusher he posted a productive 5.5 tackles for loss and four sacks. Former DII Langden Kitchen, Top200 Daeden Hopkins, and four-star transfer Kamauryn Morgan (Baylor) round out the two-deep. In the middle, Jalen Marshall and Marquis Gracial rise to the starting spots.

Three of the four-man linebacker rotation are gone. Nicholas Rodriguez is the lone returner and he started a few games in 2025. To replace the impact of Trotter, the staff signed an All-SEC backer in Robert Woodyard (Auburn). They have recruited this position well and have three former four-stars loaded in the two-deep: Dante McClellan, Jeremiah Beasley, and Brian Huff.

All five starters are gone from the secondary with four graduations plus a transfer shocker by Marvin Burks (Wisconsin). Batoon has plenty of former blue-chippers to pick from in this reload. At corner, Chris Graves (Ole Miss) started nine games last year for the Rebels, Jahlil Florence (Oregon) is a former Top200 and Sione Laulea (Oregon) was the #1 JUCO corner back in 2024. Santana Banner got partial starter reps at safety, Trajen Greco and Kensley Louidor-Faustin (Auburn) are both former Top200 recruits. Elijah Dotson (Michigan) is another Top100 guy who earned a four-star transfer grade and is projected at the “star” position.

pick_six_2026.outlook: After finishing 14th in the SEC in Game Grader, South Carolina made a solid offensive coordinator hire and landed enough transfer talent to bounce back to the SEC’s mid-tier. They also draw four of the bottom five teams in the league.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
South Carolina has had worse seasons on paper than their 2025 4-8 campaign. But paired with their all-time high preseason expectations, AP Top 15 ranking, and Playoff hype… this was certainly their most disappointing season ever.

It started with old-fashion “Beamer Ball” with Vicari Swain returning three punts for touchdowns over the first two games, including an 80- yarder against Virginia Tech to help Shane Beamer beat the program where his dad became a legend.

Beamer’s special teams didn’t get enough help from the offense and the offensive line rated as a bottom five unit in sacks allowed and tackles-for-loss. South Carolina got blown out by Vanderbilt to end their 16-game series streak, lost close decisions to Missouri and LSU, and blew a lead in the final two minutes against Alabama.

A lost season had one last glimmer of hope as South Carolina surged to a 30-3 lead at #3 Texas A&M. Beamer said “we’re not surprised, we beat this team by 24 points last year” before celebrating towards the South Carolina section as he ran into the tunnel. A&M responded with a 28-0 second half. Since 2004, teams were 286-0 in SEC play when leading by 27+ points, but South Carolina made it 286-1.

The loss to Clemson’s worst team in over a decade was one last sting.

This completes a three-year boomerang for South Carolina: #54 of 68 Power 4 in Game Grader, then up to #12 in 2024, and then back down to #44 for the third-largest year-over-year decline.

Beamer made quick work this offseason. He fired his offensive line coach in October, fired offensive coordinator Mike Shula in November, then hired a proven offensive mind in Kendal Briles to take over the unit. South Carolina lost six starters to the transfer portal, but they punched back by signing six Power 4 starters of their own in their #19 ranked class.

Most importantly, they retained dual-threat phenom quarterback LaNorris Sellers, and beefed up their offensive line by adding veteran, multi-year starters.
pick_six_2026.offense:
With Shula at coordinator, South Carolina averaged just 15 offensive points per game and ranked in the bottom ten of my opponent-adjusted offense ranking. There was a clear uptick in the games after he was fired – 29 offensive points per game and a top ten rank in the same metric.

Maybe there was more raw talent bottled up than what was shown on the stat sheet.

Briles has made improvements almost everywhere he’s been and showed he can adapt his scheme to fit the personnel on hand. At Arkansas he went run-heavy with his 6’6 quarterback KJ Jefferson, and went pass-heavy at TCU to play to the strengths of pocket-passer Josh Hoover.

At his best, Briles operates the offense at hyper-tempo with wide spread formations, and a heavy dose of RPO and quarterback-run. His best units featured dual-threats like Robert Griffin III, D’Eriq King, and Jefferson.

Sellers certainly fits that skillset. The third-year starter looks to bounce back after falling in every stat category, most importantly placing 10th in QB Rating in the SEC after a 3rd place finish in 2024. The offense was one-dimensional and it limited his rushing production from his 674-yard (4.1 average) 2024 season down to just 270 yards (1.8 average) last year. Late-game moments hurt too, with multiple wide-open passes overthrown late in the Missouri loss, as well as a costly fumble in the Alabama loss.

A bright spot was their explosiveness in the pass game (#29 nationally) and the vertical threat is back on the outside. Nyck Harbor was a former five-star athlete and last year he was tracked as the fastest player in FBS. Harbor led with 618 yards and six touchdowns, plus an SEC-best 20.6 per- catch average. #2 receiver Vandrevius Jacobs transferred out to Miami with four-star grades, Brian Rowe left for UCLA, but Jayden Sellers is back in the slot. The staff signed former Top100 Nitro

Tuggle who is a big-play threat and started for Purdue. They also added a wildcard in Top200 Jayden Gibson (Oklahoma) who had a solid 2023 but has battled injuries since. 6’5 tight end Brady Hunt enters his third season here and should have an expanded role.

Rahsul Faison and Oscar Adaway graduated, Matt Fuller returns after rushing for 260 yards as a freshman, and the staff added a pair of former four-stars in Christian Clark (Texas) and Jabree Coleman (Penn State). Clark rushed for 105 yards and a score in Texas’ bowl win, and Coleman followed running backs coach Stan Drayton.

The offensive line has been a limiting factor for several seasons here and 2025 was no different. They joined Stanford as the only Power 4 lines ranked in the bottom ten in both OL Run Push and Pass Protection, and allowed a sack on 13% of pass attempts. And that was with the elusive Sellers behind them. It’s a total restart here after the midseason coach firing and the addition of eight transfer linemen. Beamer wanted a more veteran line and he got it.

Shed Sarratt is the only returning starter after stepping up as a true freshman last fall. Josiah Thompson is also back but will miss the 2026 season with an injury. Two starters left for Power 4 programs but the staff signed plenty of starters themselves. Jacarrius Peak (NC State) is a five-star transfer, the #2 lineman in the entire portal, and earned All-ACC honors after starting 32 straight games. Similarly, four-star transfer Emmanuel Poku (East Carolina) was All-AAC, started 26 straight, and allowed zero sacks over 977 snaps. Carter Miller (UCF) and Hank Purvis (Purdue) combined to start 15 games last year.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Clayton White’s defense fell in every stat category from 2024 to 2025 but still remained above average.

Their clear MVP Dylan Stewart missed some time with injuries but still earned a second-team All- SEC honor after his All-Freshman 2024 season. Stewart is a legit All-American candidate and first- round projection off the edge. Their next two edges and two starting tackles are all gone, but they

leveraged the portal for a reload. Tomiwa Durojaiye (Illinois) earned a four-star grade after starting in the Big Ten last year, Kelby Collins (Alabama) has been a rotational tackle in the SEC for three years, and they will join former five-star Gabriel Brownlow-Dindy on the interior. Caleb Herring (Tennessee) is projected at the end spot opposite of Stewart.

Three linebackers share the two spots in the 4-2-5 base, and all three are back for 2026: Justin Okoronkwo, Fred Johnson, and Shawn Murphy.

South Carolina lost three stars in the secondary with All-SEC Jalon Kilgore, second-round draft pick Brandon Cisse, and DQ Smith all departing. Judge Collier and punt return weapon Vicari Swain are back at corner, Peyton Williams returns at safety, and the staff signed Kentucky’s starter Quay’Sheed Scott to take the nickel spot. Gerald Kilgore will battle Top100 J’Zavien Currence (South Pointe, SC) for the other safety job.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
To Florida fans skeptical of hiring another Non-AQ winner like Napier, Sumrall noted that Urban Meyer and Curt Cignetti followed similar paths: “judge me for who I am, I’m a winner, we’re going to win.”

With that said, there are some concerns with the transition season. Usually a coaching hire brings a highly- touted transfer haul but Florida is still ranked dead last in the SEC in the two-year transfer average. The lines of scrimmage lost several starters and need to be strengthened before Florida can return to SEC contention. Bowl season would be a win here with four swing games all on the road: Auburn, Missouri, Kentucky, and Florida
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
When Billy Napier was hired here in 2021 he stressed patience, and how he wanted an “army of staffers” to expand their recruiting operations and build the program from the high school ranks.

Napier became Florida’s first head coach with back-to-back losing seasons since 1979, and then his third season 2024 was off to another poor start. Athletic director Scott Strickland issued a public vote of confidence to quell the hot seat pressure, and Florida surged with a 4- 0 finish to get to 8-5.

After all the patience, 2025 was the year to cash in. Napier’s roster was veteran, with handpicked players that he and his staff had recruited and developed, and they had a five-star quarterback entering his second season.

it was an even worse collapse. Instead of a breakthrough, Questionable play-calling, poor time management, lack of discipline – it was a comedy of errors and Florida lost to USF 18-16. That loss was bad enough, but then DJ Lagway threw five interceptions in the loss to LSU, Miami held Florida to 0/13 on third downs and their lowest yardage since 1999, and then Texas A&M made it 0-14 for Napier in road ranked games.

Patience had run out and there was no sign of improvement. Florida fired Napier, their first head coach since the 1940s with a career losing record.

After getting caught up in the Lane Kiffin Sweepstakes, they found a winner in Tulane’s Jon Sumrall.

Sumrall took his team to the conference title game in his first four seasons -- twice with Troy, and twice with Tulane – the only FBS coach to do so with different schools. He brings a 42-12 record, a Playoff bid, and urgency to win right away.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Napier was the play-caller and continued to double-down on his role, ignoring the boosters’ guidance to delegate. His offense collapsed last year, ranking outside the Top 100 in both

explosive rushing and passing, and scored just 18.5 points/game against FBS opponents.

Sumrall is a defensive-minded coach, but in his opening presser he said his offense will be “aggressive, explosive, with mixed tempos.” Back to Florida’s roots.

He hired Georgia Tech’s Buster Faulkner who won FootballScoop’s 2025 Coordinator of the Year for helping build Tech’s power run offense around Heisman nominee Haynes King. Faulkner improved Tech 100 spots in scoring offense. His Tech offenses were run-heavy to highlight their personnel strengths but he showed he can design potent passing attacks at prior stops and even comes from the epicenter of the Air Raid Valdosta State.

Lagway was the former #1 overall recruit but regressed in his second season, tossing an SEC-worst 14 picks. He left for Baylor, and Faulkner brought his Tech backup Aaron Philo with him. Philo was rated a four-star transfer and the #12 QB this cycle, and in high school he broke Trevor Lawrence’s GA state record for passing yards (13,922). Philo has shown pocket poise, and can be a physical runner if needed. Former Top250 Tramell Jones was Lagway’s backup last year and will make it a fall camp battle.

Jadan Baugh closed 2025 with an exclamation point. His 266-yard game to beat Florida State was the second-most in UF history and put him over the thousand-mark as UF’s tenth all-time. Baugh decided to return for 2026 and is one of Sumrall’s “Fab Five” retentions. The staff also added East Carolina starter London Montgomery and two-year Cincinnati vet Evan Pryor.

The receiver room was stocked enough to withstand some departures and remain a top unit. Florida has a pair of five-stars in Vernell Brown and Dallas Wilson. Brown was the top receiver and earned SEC All-Freshman as a WR, all-purpose, and return specialist, while Wilson’s year was cut short by an injury but he shined in the Texas upset win. Eric Singleton (Auburn) was ranked the #9 transfer

receiver this cycle, is rumored to have 4.2 40 speed, and put up two 700-yard seasons in Faulkner’s offense at Georgia Tech. That is an elite starting trio, plus they signed near-five-star Davian Groce (Frisco, TX) who posted an insane high school stat line of 3,300 receiving yards and 2,400 rushing yards. Micah Mays (Wake Forest) and speedy Jaylen Lloyd (Oklahoma State) add more Power 4 depth.

Florida lost both starting tight ends and backfilled from the portal with Georgia Tech starter Luke Harpring and James Madison starter Lacota Dippre.

The offensive line loses three starters, most notably All-American center Jake Slaughter and NFL draft pick left tackle Austin Barber. Two starters return – Knijeah Harris and Caden Jones – but the other three will be fall camp battles decided by ace line coach Phil Trautwein. Three transfers have starting experience with Harrison Moore (Georgia Tech), TJ Shanahan (Penn State) and Emeka Ugorji (Stanford). Former Top100 Jason Zandamela will challenge Moore at center, and Eagan Boyer (Penn State) is a contender at tackle. This unit remains an uncertainty given the loss of star power.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Sumrall hired Kentucky defensive coordinator Brad White who built consistently above-average defenses there with three Top 25 units in seven years, and just one ranked outside the Top 40.

Two more stars were drafted from the defensive line – Caleb Banks and end George Gumbs – and starting nose tackle Michai Boireau transferred out to Ole Miss. The new-look starting line is packed with potential, with SEC All-Freshman Jayden Woods off the edge and former five-star LJ McCray back from injury at defensive tackle. Kamran James tied for the team lead in sacks and he’s joined by first-team All-CUSA Emmanuel Oyebadejo (Jacksonville State) at end. Brendan Bett moves up into the starting spot at nose tackle.

The secondary is also down several starters with top corner Devin Moore going pro, and Jordan Castell (Kentucky) and Sharif Denson (Ole Miss) both landing on other SEC rosters. Former five- star Cormani McClain finally had a breakout season last year and returns at corner, while original starter Dijon Johnson is back from injury. Bryce Thornton returns at strong safety, and the staff added Power 4 starters in DJ Coleman (Baylor) and Cam Dooley (Kentucky). Two Top100’s stack the two-deep: safety Lagonza Hayward and corner CJ Bronaugh.

There are no questions at linebacker and this is the strength of Sumrall’s transition-year defense.

Myles Graham led the team with 76 tackles, Jaden Robinson and Aaron Chiles both had 50+, and the trio is a top unit. Ty Jackson is another Top100 prospect in the room.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Fritz has done an excellent job identifying under-the-radar transfer talent and coaching them up into all- leaguers. To continue the momentum from last year’s breakthrough season, this next round of transfers has to hit again.

The formula is similar as they targeted experienced, veteran, all-conference players from the lower tiers. Despite losing 13 starters, they reloaded their experience level and Houston still ranks in the national top ten of career snaps.

Houston will continue to improve each year into their Power 4 transition, and even signed a five-star superstar for the future. But they were #7 in the Big 12 in my Game Grader last year -- #12 in the opponent-adjusted yardage margin – which both signal they were not as strong as their record. Their 6-1 performance in one-score games is unlikely to be repeated, and they remain outside the Big 12 title game projection.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
After a 4-8 transition season, Willie Fritz knew the importance of the upcoming talent acquisition cycle. With a funding disadvantage compared to some of their conference peers, Houston had to go with the “moneyball” approach of finding under-recruited gems and as Fritz put it simply “we have to be right.”

Houston was right. With an emphasis on college experience and career starts/snaps, Houston’s transfer haul ended up producing 13 starters on the 2025 team and eight of them earned All-Big 12 honors.

They also led the school’s first 10-win season in a Power conference since 1990.

Houston ended up in seven one-score games and thanks to three game- winners by kicker Ethan Sanchez, and gutsy performances by quarterback Conner Weigman, they went 6-1 in those toss-ups.

After he was hired, Fritz called Houston a “sleeping giant” due to their location in talent-rich Texas, their academic profile, and now their Power conference patch on their uniforms. The 2025 season was a breakthrough with six Big 12 wins – more than their first two seasons combined post- transition.

The 2026 transfer haul may not be as highly-touted on paper, but Houston only lost two starters to the portal, signed two Power 4 starters of their own, and added another round of all- conference performers from the non-AQ level. Fritz is doubling down on what worked last cycle.

They also landed a potential program-changer on the high school recruiting trail by signing five-star super-recruit Keisean Henderson (Spring, TX), the #1 overall prospect in the nation.
pick_six_2026.offense:
While Henderson is certainly the future of the program, he will learn from returning starter Weigman who is back after passing for 2,711 yards, 25 touchdowns and a #5 finish in QB Rating in the Big 12. A former five-star himself, Weigman was impressed with Henderson’s strong arm in spring ball: “the talent is off the charts, he can throw a football with the best of them.”

Fritz did not rule out the possibility of getting Henderson extended game reps in 2026 and depending on fall camp progress, defenses may have to scheme for both guys.

In addition to the passing production and leadership, Weigman also shouldered a heavy workload in the run game with 13 carries/game for 700 yards and 11 rushing touchdowns.

Dean Connors was one of the toughest runners in the nation last year and got All-Big 12 honorable mention after finishing just shy of 1,000 yards. He graduated and leaves behind a three-man committee at running back. DJ Butler rushed for 300 yards last year, Re’Shaun Sanford was the 2024 leading rusher and is back from his ACL injury, and then Fritz signed a familiar face in Makhi Hughes (Oregon). Before getting stuck in a crowded NFL backfield at Oregon, Hughes rushed for 1,378 yards for Fritz’s Tulane team in 2023, and then another 1,401 in 2024. Over 1,000 of that yardage was after contact, and if he can get back to 2024 form, Houston has a star to rely on.

Houston focused their targets on just two pass-catchers with Amare Thomas and tight end Tanner Koziol getting 141 receptions – all other receivers combined for just 45. Both guys earned first- team All-Big 12 honors, but Koziol went pro after an FBS TE-high 74 catches.

Thomas returns in the slot after his 966-yard, 12-touchdown explosion last year. Koby Young started eight games and returns on the outside, and the staff signed two-year Oregon State lead receiver Trent Walker who put up 1,714 yards the past two seasons. The staff added two more three- star transfers from Power 4 rosters in Tyson Turner (Texas Tech) and Muizz Tounkara (Florida) and then signed four-star Jeremiah Bushnell from the high school ranks.

Patrick Overmyer (UTSA) was one of the most productive tight ends in the AAC last year and he’ll take over Koziol’s starting role.

The offensive line struggled with a #106 rank in my OL Run Push metric and now must replace three starters Dalton Merryman, Jason Brooks, and center Demetrius Hunter who left for Colorado. Alvin Ebosele and McKenzie Agnello are returning starters and then the staff pulled in three all- league linemen from the Non-AQ level to round out the new starting five. Anthony Boswell (Toledo) and Drew Terrill (Miami, OH) were both All-MAC, Shadre Hurst (Tulane) was first-team All-AAC at guard, but they all earned three-star transfer grades.

Fritz’s coordinator hire Slade Nagle led the offensive improvement from bottom five in 2024 up to #35 of 68 Power 4 in 2025. Now Houston gets a second-year bonus at coordinator and quarterback, coupled with the boost of several proven Non-AQ stars.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Last offseason, coordinator Shiel Wood left for Texas Tech and then Houston slid from #24 to #52 of 68 Power 4.

Six defenders earned All-Big 12 honors and five are gone. The defensive line loses their best run stopper Carlos Allen and sack leader Eddie Walls. Khalil Laufau is back at defensive tackle along with both edge hybrids Brandon Mack and Latreveon McCutchin. The staff signed former four-star Ashton Porter (Oregon), All-Ivy Ejiro Egodogbare (Yale), and former Vanderbilt starter De’Marion Thomas.

Two starting linebackers are gone after Jalen Garner graduated and Corey Platt transferred out to Texas Tech. The staff signed a Power 4 starter of their own with Jaden Yates (Ole Miss) who started nine games last year. Yates posted 115 tackles the year prior at Marshall and earned his “100-Yard Landlord” nickname. Starting middle backer Sione Fotu is back and Chance Bryant and Carmycah Glass move up the depth chart.

Three starters return to the secondary but Houston loses two All-Big 12 stars in Latrell McCutchin and Wrook Brown. Will James is an all-leaguer at cornerback, Kentrell Webb and Jordan Allen are both veteran returning starters at the safety spots, and the staff signed two high-three star transfers.

Javion White (Tulane) was All-AAC last year and will start at nickel, while Jalen Mayo (Stephen F. Austin) was an FCS standout corner who played well against Houston in the 2025 opener. Incoming four-star Paris Melvin may play early after the two-deep was thinned out by three backups graduating.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
The talent drain on defense hurts, but Kansas State leveraged the portal well to backfill with experienced Power 4 starters at end and defensive back. The offense is clearer with Klein reunited with his quarterback, plus a workhorse back, and an elite tight end pair.

Kansas State moves a few spots up the Big 12 ladder due to the best schedule draw as they avoid the league’s top three.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Kansas State entered 2026 as the Big 12 media’s pick to win the league. That expectation was quickly grounded with a loss to Iowa State in the week zero Ireland kickoff game, losses to Army and Arizona, and a near- loss to FCS North Dakota.

Twice more Kansas State lost games with in-game win probabilities over 95%. They led Baylor by 14 in the fourth quarter, but quarterback Avery Johnson threw a Pick Six and their last-second field goal was blocked. Then, despite rushing for a school-record 472 yards, KSU blew a 12-point lead in the final minutes at Utah.

Though it wasn’t the full reason, the wild, emotional, 51-48 loss to Utah apparently weighed on seventh-year head coach Chris Klieman. “I’ve given my life for this place for seven years, I’ve given everything,” he said after the loss. A few days later he told athletic director Gene Taylor he was ready to retire. And a day after their season-ending win over Colorado capped the 6-6 regular season, Klieman publicly retired.

Klieman hired former Kansas State star quarterback Collin Klein as his offensive coordinator back in 2022 and the move helped spark a title run. They beat eventual national runner-up TCU with a goal-line stand in overtime to earn KSU’s third Big 12 title in school history. That 10-win season was followed by a pair of nine-win campaigns and Klieman leaves Manhattan as their second-winningest coach.

Now four years later, Kansas State brought Klein back – this time as head coach.

Klein was a Big 12 champion quarterback here, a Heisman runner-up, and now has stacked four successful years as a playcaller. His Kansas State and Texas A&M offenses have an average rank of #24 in my opponent-adjusted metric, and the final one led A&M’s Playoff run last year.

Klein mentioned the impacts of all three head coach mentors. From Bill Snyder he learned how to build a culture and foundation, Klieman’s defensive expertise helped grow his football knowledge from the other side of the ball, and Mike Elko helped on the recruiting trail.
pick_six_2026.offense:
As a runner himself, Klein’s offenses are built around mobile quarterbacks and in his transition season he gets to coach a familiar face. Klein originally recruited Avery Johnson to KSU, coached

him in 2023 as Johnson got his first starts, and now re-unites with the dual-threat.

Johnson enters 2026 tied with Will Howard for the school’s passing touchdown record (48) and is 2,500 yards off Josh Freeman’s career yardage record. It has been boom-or-bust for Johnson. He has flashed breakaway straight-line speed, and streaky passing, but has been inconsistent over his career. His rushing skillset needs improvement and he struggles to power for the final extra yard when needed.

He has ranked #9 and #11 in the Big 12 in QB Rating, but he should make some statistical gains here in his final season with Klein’s impact. The KS native originally picked KSU over national powerhouses because he wanted to play in Klein’s offense.

The staff has mentioned a focus on a downhill, power run game. They certainly have the running back room for it, though the offensive line needs improvement.

In the opener, former five-star Dylan Edwards was injured on his first touch and was out most of the season and has since transferred over to Kansas. Joe Jackson took the opportunity as the new lead back and surged in November with a school-record 293 yards vs. Utah and then another 142 in the Colorado win. Jackson rushed for 900 but it snapped KSU’s 1,000-yard back streak since 2020. Jackson is joined by Rodney Fields, who was a rare bright spot for Oklahoma State last year. He rushed for 614 yards (5 per carry), added 276 in the pass game, and was arguably their best player.

The uncertainty is in the trenches after a statistical decline last year from #5 to #93 in OL Run Push and the loss of two-time All-Big 12 lineman Sam Hecht. John Pastore returns as a sound pass-blocker and Gus Hawkins and former Ohio State transfer George Fitzpatrick are both back after injury-shortened seasons.

On the interior, the staff added three guys who could push for starting spots with Keiton Jones (Missouri), Delvin Morris (Akron) and Tanner Morley (Colorado State). All three had three-star transfer grades.

Kansas State has one of the best tight end pairs in the Big 12 with the return of school-record holder Garrett Oakley and former five-star Linkon Cure.

Jayce Brown had 1,500+ receiving yards over the past two seasons and was considered one of the top players in the program but transferred out to LSU. Jerand Bradley graduated, so Jaron Tibbs is the lone returning starter at receiver. The staff added three transfers with Hawaii starter Brandon White and a pair of former four-stars Josh Manning (Missouri) and Izaiah Williams (Texas A&M). The staff nearly signed Manning out of high school, and he has a connection with Johnson – this could be the surprise breakout player they need.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Klieman originally ran a 4-2-5 here, joined the Big 12’s 3-3-5 craze, and now the program is back to a 4- 2-5 base scheme with Klein’s defensive coordinator pick Jordan Peterson. He was a co-coordinator for Texas A&M’s playoff team last year, and before that he had a successful stint at Kansas landing four guys on the All-Big 12 teams.

It is a total reload here with nine starters gone.

Six of them earned All-Big 12 honors including all four defensive linemen. Cody Stufflebean and Damian Ilalio graduated but then the star duo of edge rushers Tobi Osunsanmi and Chiddi Obiazor both transferred out to Indiana.

The staff landed two proven playmakers of their own in Wendell Gregory (Oklahoma State) and Elijah Hill (Kennesaw State). Gregory earned a high four-star transfer grade and was the best Oklahoma State defender last year, while Hill led the entire C-USA with nine sacks as a freshman.

The incoming tackle duo has limited game experience but both are in from Power 4 programs: Kamari Burns (Cincinnati) and Austin Ramsey (Kentucky).

Both linebackers are gone with tackle-leader Desmond Purnell graduating and two-time All-Big 12 Austin Romaine transferring to Texas Tech. Kansas State added All-CUSA Mekhi Mason (Louisiana Tech) and rising sophomore Darien Whitaker has drawn big reviews.

The two returning starters are the two corners: Donovan McIntosh and all-league Zashon Rich. VJ Payne graduated and two more starters left for Power 4 programs with nickel Daniel Cobbs (Baylor) and Qua Moss (Tennessee). Kansas State landed some starters of their own with nickel Ja’Son Prevard (Virginia) and Kaleb Patterson (Illinois). Adrian Maddox (Georgia) was a spring hero that could earn a starting safety spot.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Arizona State loses 18 starters and the core of their two-year run. Dillingham reloaded at quarterback and landed one of the nation’s best transfer hauls at receiver.

There are too many uncertainties with this transition roster – the offensive line and 10 new starters on defense -- to call for a Big 12 title run, but Arizona State remains in the crowded mid-tier of the league.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Heading into 2024, Arizona State was picked dead last by Big 12 media but Kenny Dillingham’s upstart roster surged to a surprise Big 12 title and Playoff appearance. With virtually the entire starting lineup back – minus the hardnosed running back Cam Skattebo – ASU entered with an AP Top 15 ranking as Big 12 contenders.

Arizona State opened up Big 12 play with consecutive 27-24 wins over Baylor and TCU. Both games featured last-minute drives led by quarterback Sam Leavitt and eventual first-rounder Jordyn Tyson. Leavitt showed off pocket elusiveness, scramble touchdown runs, and even a jump pass.

Leavitt again led a game-winning touchdown drive in the final minute against #6 Texas Tech, fans stormed the field, and Tech head coach Joey McGuire praised him: “that quarterback changes everything – he’s a difference maker.”

Unfortunately Arizona State learned the hard way, because with Leavitt knocked out of the lineup, his absence did change everything. Utah dealt a 42-10 beatdown, ASU lost another to Houston, and then gave away five turnovers in a 23-7 Territorial Cup loss to Arizona.

While the 8-5 season appears to be a disappointment, it should be viewed together with the 2024 title run, within the context of a two-year window. With essentially the same cast of characters, and despite injuries to Leavitt and Tyson, Arizona State won 19 games – the best two-year span since 2013-14 and third best here since the 1970’s.

As he promised two years ago, Dillingham did in fact Activate the Valley.

18 starters are gone, and Arizona State flips from the most veteran roster to a new-look transition lineup.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Dillingham boosted the transition with an impressive transfer haul that ranked third-best in the Big 12 and #15 nationally. While just one starter returns on offense, Arizona State added five other Power 4 starters.

Leavitt transferred out to LSU as the top-rated transfer this cycle, but ASU added back a starter of their own in 6’5 Cutter Boley (Kentucky). The former four-star started ten games as a freshman last year, ranked #12 in the SEC in QB Rating and #6 among all Power 4 freshmen.

Boley completed a high 65% of passes, and showed off a big arm with impressive touch and enough pocket presence and mobility to extend plays. He did toss 12 interceptions, though offensive coordinator Marcus Arroyo claims that many were in end-of-game desperation heaves downfield.

The staff also signed veteran Mikey Keene (Michigan) who started 34 games at UCF and Fresno State, but it was Top100 true freshman Jake Fette who stole the show in spring and could eventually win the backup job in fall camp.

Tyson was picked #8 overall in the NFL Draft and Malik McClain graduated, leaving All-Big 12 honorable mention Derek Eusebio as the lone returning starter on offense. But Arizona State dominated the portal here with one of the nation’s best receiver hauls. They signed three starters off Power 4 rosters headlined by All-Big 12 Omarion Miller, who was Colorado’s MVP and ranked as the #3 transfer receiver. Reed Harris (Boston College) also earned four-star transfer hype as a vertical threat and Raiden Vines-Bright (Washington) broke into the rotation as a true freshman. Jalen Moss also returns in the slot, and this is the clear strength of the team.

Raleek Brown rushed for 1,141 yards and a high 6.1 per carry in the workhorse role but he transferred out to Texas with four-star grades. Jason Brown rushed for 134 in the Sun Bowl, Kyson Brown is the returning veteran after injuries limited him in 2025, and a pair of FCS backs will compete for carries. Marquis Gillis (Del State) was a Top 10 FCS back (1,200 yards, 6.5 per) and David Avit (Villanova) is the short-yardage hammer.

Chamon Metayer graduated with Big 12 honors, and now Arizona State turns to a pair of former four-stars Khamari Anderson and AJ Ia.

The offensive line is a total rebuild with all five starters gone and anchor left tackle Max Iheanachor heading to the pros as a first-round pick. At least the center spot is set, as the staff stole Georgia Tech’s starter Tana Alo-Tupuola off a top-rated line. Luke Baklenko was a two-year starter at Stanford, a backup at Oklahoma, and should win the right tackle spot here. Another likely starter is incoming left tackle Jarmaine Mitchell, the nation’s #1 overall JUCO prospect and Georgia flip. Maki Stewart earned some starts late in the season at guard, but given the overall transition here a third-straight Top 40 finish in OL Run Push is in question.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Brian Ward has stacked consecutive Top 25 defenses per my opponent-adjusted metrics and Arizona State and BYU were the only in the league to do so.

To make it three straight, they must pull off a total reset to the two-deep. Ten opening day starters are gone including six who earned All-Big 12 nominations.

The lone returner is CJ Fite, the star defensive tackle who returned to Tempe after considering an early NFL bid. Prince Dorbah, Justin Wodtly, and Elijah O’Neal are all gone, but ASU got a break when 2024 starting defensive end Clayton Smith won an eligibility appeal for a final bonus year in 2026. The staff signed a pair of Power 4 starters at defensive end with Jalen Thompson (Michigan State) and Emar’rion Winston (Baylor). Four-star signee Julian Hugo was a spring hero per practice reports. Another wildcard is 6’5, 260-pound JUCO transfer Kirt Vakalahi.

Jordan Crook and Keyshaun Elliott both landed on the All-Big 12 second-team after combining for 199 tackles – first and second on the team – but both graduated. Martell Hughes got partial-starter playing time with 400 snaps and now rises to the starting lineup. Then the staff signed the nation’s tackle leader Owen Long (Colorado State) who was first-team All-Mountain West and earned four-star transfer grades. Long was flying all over the field in spring ball and should make this position a “reload” instead of a rebuild.

All five original starting defensive backs are gone, though safety Adrian Wilson stepped up after Xavion Alford was injured, and Montana Warren surged at nickel. ASU will miss the cornerback duo of NFL-bound Keith Abney and Wisconsin-bound Javan Robinson, though the staff added Ashton Stamps (LSU) who was once an SEC starter before falling out of the lineup last year. Rodney Bimage moved up into the other starting job opposite of Stamps, and safety Lyrik Rawls (Kansas) had 73 tackles last year.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
A nine-win team that returns an all-conference quarterback would normally be projected higher but there are some forces against Arizona in 2026. It was actually the defense that was the reason for their breakthrough, specifically their elite secondary, but all four defensive backs were drafted.

They are #8 in the Big 12 in five-year recruiting, and second-worst from the portal with just one four-star transfer the past two cycles combined.

Lastly, they drew the toughest schedule in the conference, as the only Big 12 contender to draw six of the top seven.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
The morale was low when head coach Jedd Fisch left for Washington, took several star players with him, and spoiled a potential dream season scenario for 2024.

Instead, Arizona struggled through the conference transition and finished 4-8 with a 49-7 loss to rival Arizona State as the final dagger.

Entering his second year, head coach Brent Brennan went with a double coordinator switch and both moves were home runs. Seth Doege’s offense added a full two touchdowns per game, and Arizona had a first-team all-league quarterback for the first time in 50 years.

The other side of the ball was even stronger. Danny Gonzales’ 3-3-5 defense puzzled opposing coordinators, and the star-studded secondary posted the nation’s #1 pass defense in opposing QB Rating.

Arizona started 4-3 with a pair of losses on the final play – a double- overtime loss to BYU and a walk-off field goal by Houston – but rallied over the back half of the season. Noah Fifita found another gear, the defense held Baylor’s top passing attack 200 yards under average, and

then the close games flipped to wins.

Arizona posted a nine-win season for just the eighth time in school history.

How’s that for a second-year coach bonus?

Brennan completed the three-year boomerang, from Top 20 in Fisch’s final year, to bottom ten, back to the Top 20 with a #18 finish in Game Grader.
pick_six_2026.offense:
In an era devoid of loyalty, Brennan claims Fifita “is the best story in college football… he’s chosen to stay, not take the money and run.” Fifita remained after the Fisch coaching change, again after his best friend Tetairoa McMillan went pro, and now again after All-Big 12 honors that certainly would have placed him atop the transfer portal wish list.

Fifita passed for 3,228 yards, 29 touchdowns and only tossed two picks over the final seven games. He even added a new facet to his game, with 220 rushing yards on designed runs. And now finally he gets coordinator stability, with another year in Doege’s scheme. He’s already got the career passing touchdown record (73) and needs 600 yards to pass Nick Foles for the yardage record.

Earlier in the season Javin Whatley was his top target, then Kris Hutson emerged with several 100+ yard games. Both top receivers are gone, but the 2026 room looks like an upgrade. 6’4 Tre Spivey returns after earning All-Big 12 honorable mention with 8 touchdowns on just 25 touches. Chris Hunter moves up into the starting rotation, Gio Richardson had 299 yards as a freshman, and Isaiah Mizell is the program’s fastest player. The staff added a pair of former blue-chippers with West Virginia starter Rodney Gallagher and Top100 DJ Jordan (USC).

The top two tight ends graduated but original starter Tyler Powell is back after his season ended on the first play from scrimmage. Cole Rusk started for Illinois and they signed a four-star Henry Gabalis.

It was a trio of backs last year and the rushing leader Ismail Mahdi graduated after leading with 859 yards. Quincy Craig had the game-winner to beat Kansas, Kedrick Reescano punched in nine touchdowns including the Cincinnati winner, and these two form a thunder-lightning pair for 2026.

The offensive line had to use seven different lineups in 2024 but finally got some stability last year and it paid off statistically with a 50+ spot jump in my OL Run Push from #90 to #40. Three starters are gone including their lone all-league honoree left tackle Ty Buchanan. The right side returns with guard Alexander Doost and tackle Tristan Bounds getting awarded a sixth year of eligibility. Due to injuries last year, Matthew Lado and Rhino Tapa’atoutai were forced into action with mixed results. Both now move up into the projected starting lineup, and in the middle the staff signed Zach Henning (Washington) who also got some starting experience due to injuries ahead of him.
pick_six_2026.defense:
