Gonzales led the biggest defensive turnaround in FBS last year. Arizona improved by 50+ spots in all 17 of my stat categories, jumped all the way up to #11 in my opponent-adjusted defense ranking, and the pass defense ranked #1 in Opponent QB Rating.

He says they are now “losing the best secondary in the nation” and before you dismiss that as coach- speak, Arizona had four defensive backs drafted this April to tie an NFL Draft record. And a fifth one was signed as a free agent.

Arizona ranked second nationally with 22 interceptions, led with 2.5 takeaways/game, and it seemed like every ten minutes they were stuffing another football on their Turnover Sword. They held eight straight opponents under 200 passing yards – a Big 12 best since 2004 Missouri.

Treydan Stukes and Dalton Johnson both earned first-team All-Big 12 and Genesis Smith got third- team recognition. Their big three are gone along with three other corners and it reminds me of when Illinois built the nation’s #1 pass defense in 2022, sent three guys to the Top 66 draft picks, and then fell all the way to #70 the following year.

In this example though, the mastermind coordinator returns. All-Big 12 corner Jay’vion Cole had four interceptions and is the lone returning starter. And they also packed the room with eight transfers to jump start the reload. Nebraska starter Malcolm Hartzog can play every position, Cam Chapa (Northern Colorado) was first-team All-Big Sky at the FCS level, and Tyrese Boss (Wyoming) was All-Mountain West. Some less experienced signees have bigger recruiting profiles like the pair of former Top100’s Daylen Austin (Oregon) and Matai Tagoa’i (USC) who the staff moved from backer to safety.

There is relatively more continuity in the front six, as they return six of their top ten. Original starter and team captain Tre Smith is back after a season-ending injury last year. He’s posted 60 tackles, 8.5 for loss, and 4.5 sacks over his two seasons. Leroy Palu is back in the middle, alongside

Mays Pese who made an instant impact and was named Big 12 All-Freshman.

Gonzales was creative with his linebackers and lined them up all over the field. He even rolled out a Red Rover package where the backers all held hands pre-snap and then dart in different directions after the snap. It worked right away as Jabari Mann took back a Pick Six the first time the tactic was unveiled. Taye Brown is a third-year starter, Chase Kennedy returns as a backer/edge hybrid, and Mann and Myron Robinson also return.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Virginia Tech hit a home run with the Franklin hire and he brought 12 Penn Staters and 11 more flipped commits with him. Their roster talent is improved and in the blink of an eye, Virginia Tech seems poised for a program revival.

With so many other ACC teams losing stars to the transfer portal, Virginia Tech was an example that benefitted from it and they earn a spot in my ACC top five.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Virginia Tech lost the opener to Shane Beamer’s South Carolina program – with a dose of their old Beamerball – then collapsed in the second half against Vanderbilt. After halftime they were outscored 34-0, and then opened up the next game with a 28-0 halftime deficit.

That 62-0 run over four quarters brought a chorus of boos from the home crowd in Lane Stadium, the 0-3 start was the program’s worst since 1987, and the next day Brent Pry was fired.

Pry finished with a 16-24 overall record which was the worst here since the 1970s and third-worst all-time. Worse than the record, the two main strategic goals with the hire were totally missed: defensive excellence and a resurgence of in-state recruiting.

With an “elite coordinator, first-time head coach” hire, that side of the ball is expected to be strong enough on its own. Instead, Virginia Tech’s defense never placed in the Top 25 of my opponent-adjusted metrics and had a four-year average of just #39 of 68 Power 4.

In-state recruiting came up short, too. The state of Virginia produced 40 four-stars over Pry’s tenure. Penn State signed seven, UNC signed six, Clemson took four … and Virginia Tech got just three of them. In his final game, Pry’s starting 22 only featured three former Virginia high school prospects.

Young, inexperienced coordinator hires, broken offensive lines, and struggles in one-score games (1-12 record) were other consistent themes.

By moving early in what would become the most crowded coaching carousel of all-time, Virginia Tech ended up hiring one of the most proven head coaches in college football in Penn State’s James Franklin.

Franklin was fired at Penn State after a 3-3 start to what was seen as a “National Title or Bust” season for the program. That doesn’t discount his long-term success there – 104-45 (.697) record at Penn State – and his program turnaround at Vanderbilt before that.

Virginia Tech added a significant financial commitment of $229 million over four years to primarily boost football resources. The funds are a perfect match with Franklin’s strong track record recruiting VA and the surrounding region.

Franklin went on ESPN’s College Gameday and declared he would win a national title at his next school. Whether or not that goal comes to fruition, this home run hire signals Virginia Tech is serious about returning to their winning ways from the Beamer Era.
pick_six_2026.offense:
In an attempt to continue what was working for him, there are Penn State connections all over the place. Franklin brought his co-offensive coordinator Ty Howle, quarterbacks coach Danny O’Brien, 12 transfers off the Penn State roster, and he flipped 11 former Penn State commits to sign with Virginia Tech.

The most important transfer of all is at quarterback with former Top100 four-star Ethan Grunkemeyer taking over after starting the last seven games for Penn State. He was rated the #7 quarterback of the 2024 recruiting class and the #13 transfer quarterback this cycle.

Grunkemeyer was thrown into action as a redshirt freshman once Drew Allar was lost for the season, and the pocket passer completed a high 69% of passes. Even after accounting for screens and short passes, he was sharp as a first-time starter and should get a second-year bonus here. They also signed dual-threat Bryce Baker (UNC) who was also a Top100 four-star from the 2025 class.

Virginia Tech didn’t use the tight ends enough in the pass game last year but that will change given Howle’s success with the position at Penn State. Co-starter Benji Gosnell returns, but the staff brought two Penn State tight ends with them. Luke Reynolds was ranked a five-star as the #1 tight end in the entire 2024 recruiting class, and again was named the #1 top transfer at the position.

Marcellous Hawkins returns after leading the team in rushing with 749 yards and his explosive 6.4 per- carry average is the highest among returning ACC backs with 100+ carries. Jeff Overton flashed as a freshman, and 5’9 250-pound bowling ball Bill Davis (UL-Lafayette) earned All-Sun Belt honors.

Ayden Greene is back at outside receiver and the staff added four more to the room. Que’Sean Brown (Duke) earned four-star transfer grades and will start in the slot after catching 107 balls (just two drops) the past two seasons. Tyseer Denmark and Jeff Exinor are both Penn State transfers who will join the rotation, and backup slot Takye Heath returns.

The offensive line is the biggest rebuilding project on offense and needs to improve on pass protection after finishing #114 in sack rate – and that was with mobile Kyron Drones at quarterback. Center Kyle Altuner and guard Layth Ghannam are returning starters, Montavious Cunningham started four games at guard, and Brody Meadows is back from injury. The tackle spots are wide open with an influx of three- star transfers from Power 4 rosters: Logan Howland (Oklahoma), Michael Troutman (Penn State), Justin Terry (Ohio State), Justin Bell (Michigan State).
pick_six_2026.defense:
In a rare twist, Pry was actually re-hired by Virginia Tech three months after being fired. Franklin picked him as his defensive coordinator with hopes of recreating what worked together at Penn State when all six of his defenses finished in the Top 25 from 2016 to 2021.

The staff pumped the defensive line with transfers to jumpstart the transition. They signed four former four-star defensive ends and a fifth Samuel Okunlola who had productive starting experience at Colorado and Pittsburgh. Former Top100 prospect Javion Hilson (Missouri) is the headliner and is projected to start opposite of returner Aycen Stevens. Cortez Harris, Mylachi Williams, and Daniel Jennings are all redshirt freshmen who followed the staff from Penn State.

The defensive tackle starters both return with Elhadj Fall moving back inside and Kemari Copeland poised for All-ACC consideration.

Leading tackler Kaleb Spencer returns at inside backer, and although Caleb Woodson and Jaden Keller both depart, Noah Chambers impressed as a freshman and should earn a starting spot. He’ll be challenged by Penn State transfer Keon Wylie.

Entering 2025, the secondary had to replace their elite duo of Mansoor Delane and Dorian Strong and then Dante Lovett entered the portal after four games. As expected, the pass defense took a statistical hit and dropped 75 spots in Opponent QB Rating down to #116, and #114 in yards/attempt.

Tyson Flowers, Jordan Bass, and original starter Quentin Reddish are all back at safety but this position needs to improve on tackling. The corners also return with Thomas Williams and Isaiah Brown-Murray and they will be pushed by two-year UConn starter Cam Chadwick and All-Sun Belt Jaquez White (Troy).

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Though Virginia loses plenty of starters, they stayed with their veteran-transfer strategy and reloaded both sides -- their 2026 roster is #1 nationally in career snaps.

The Cardiac Cavs used up a lot of magic last season so while a return to Charlotte is unlikely, Elliott has elevated the program’s floor and they remain a top-half ACC team.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Rather than start over with a coaching change, Virginia doubled down on head coach Tony Elliott and they rallied up enough financial commitment to sign a Top 25 transfer class.

Their strategy was to target transfers with significant game experience – no matter the level – over former top recruits who hadn’t gotten onto the field yet.

Elliott won 11 games in his first three seasons combined from 2022 to 2024. But with 50+ new players, the 2025 team doubled that total, clinched the school’s first 11-win season and reinvigorated the UVA fan base. They earned the nickname “Cardiac Cavs” after a wild string of close wins to keep their ACC title hopes alive.

Reminiscent of their major upset wins in 1995 and 2005, Virginia hosted #8 Florida State and won the 46-38 overtime shootout. As the final pass hit the turf, UVA fans swarmed the field faster than I’ve ever seen.

Then they did it with defense. Virginia had two defensive scores in an overtime win over Louisville, got a game-winning safety in the final minute to beat Washington State 22-20, and then stuffed UNC at the goal-line on a game- deciding two-point attempt. Then, Kam Robinson grabbed a Pick Six in the final thirty seconds to hold off California’s comeback attempt.

Five games – three overtime wins, and all five decided in the final minute. This run got them to an 8- 1 start, their first Top 15 ranking since 2004, and their longest winning streak since 2007.

In front of 58,800 fans they dominated Virginia Tech 27-7 to win the Commonwealth Cup for just the second time in 21 years. After years of fan apathy, Scott Stadium came alive. Even better, the win punched their ticket to Charlotte for the ACC title game with a Playoff berth on the line.

Even though they dominated Duke a few weeks earlier, the rematch wasn’t a repeat. In fact Duke beat them with their own formula: ball control, clutch overtime moments, and a game-ending defensive turnover. The Gator Bowl win over Missouri got UVA to their 11-win milestone and this goes down as an all-time season for the school.

Though not even the most optimistic Virginia fan could have predicted 11 wins, the expectations shifted so quickly that there will be a feel of missed opportunity mixed in. A 7-5 opponent they already beat by 17 was the only barrier to their first ACC outright title and first Playoff appearance.
pick_six_2026.offense:
After a taste of postseason football, can Elliott make it two-in-a-row? On offense, it is a complete rebuild as they have to replace their quarterback, top two running backs, top three receivers, All-ACC tight end, and two linemen.

When a program ascends to an all-time season, the hope is that an influx of talent would follow. Instead, Virginia finished the 2026 talent acquisition cycle as the only Power 4 program to not sign a single four- star recruit or four-star transfer.

Rankings aside, I’d say they did well reloading at quarterback. Chandler Morris threw for 3,000 yards and powered their fast start but was denied an extra year of eligibility. The staff signed two former Power 4 starters in Beau Pribula (Missouri) and Eli Holstein (Pittsburgh). Pribula was Drew Allar’s backup at Penn State then won the starting job at Missouri and posted a 2,000-yard, 11 touchdown (9 picks) season, and added 10 carries/game. Holstein won the Pitt job in 2024 and got them off to a 7-0 start before cooling off and then eventually getting benched four games into 2025.

Pribula brings a dual-threat skillset and is the projected starter, though Holstein has more game experience, a higher QB Rating, and big stat line: 3,306 yards & 29 touchdowns over the 1.5 seasons.

Virginia finally established a traditional run game and J’Mari Taylor took a 200-carry workload and earned first-team All-ACC honors. Taylor and #2 back Harrison Waylee are both gone, and Elliott mentioned he wants to return to more of a “committee” approach. Peyton Lewis (Tennessee) is a former Top200 prospect and a Top 10 running back from the 2024 class. Jekail Middlebrook (Middle Tennessee) earned All-CUSA honors after his 750-yard season and can help in the pass game with 40 catches last year. Veteran Xavier Brown is also back from injury to round out the trio.

The receiver core needs to be fully rebuilt with the top three departing: Jahmal Edrine and a pair of All- ACC stars Trell Harris and Cam Ross. Kam Courtney is the leading returning receiver and should start in the slot. Isaiah Robinson got action in the bowl game and will battle incoming transfers Jacquon Gibson (UMass) and Rico Flores (UCLA). Gibson ranked 11th nationally with 6.3 catches/game, while Flores was a starter most of the season for UCLA.

The offensive line’s improvement was a key factor in the 11-win season. They gave up 47 sacks in 2024 but cut that to 18 in 2025 for a jump from #127 all the way up to #11 in Sack Rate. The line helped establish the run, and they rushed for 200+ in three straight games for the first time since 2004. Virginia loses its headliner in second-team All-ACC center Brady Wilson, but gets two more all-league linemen back with tackle McKale Boley and guard Noah Josey. Drake Metcalf shifts over to center, and the two openings should be filled by 2025 highly-rated transfers Monroe Mills and Makilan Thomas who were both injured in fall camp last year.
pick_six_2026.defense:
The offense led the fast start to the season, but once it slowed down, the defense rose to the occasion. This is a strange twist on “complementary football,” per my opponent-adjusted metrics:

- UVA Offense, first seven games: #30 of 68 Power 4 then #60 final seven - UVA Defense, first seven games: #45 of 68 Power 4 then #5 final seven

It starts with do-it-all linebacker Kam Robinson who was trending as a candidate for ACC Defensive Player of the Year before an ACL tear cut his season short. He became the only FBS player in the past 20 years with a Pick Six, blocked punt, and fumble touchdown. Throw in a game-winning safety to beat Washington State and this was arguably the most impactful defender in the league.

Robinson’s rehab timeline may keep him out of a few early games, but Virginia returns the whole room. Maddox Marcellus returns and Landon Danley is back after filling in well for Robinson.

Virginia loses a pair of All-ACC defensive linemen with tackle Jahmeer Carter and end Mitchell Melton both graduating. While five of the eight two-deep linemen are gone, they rotated this group more than most, so they do return three with high experience. Fisher Camac had 6.5 tackles for loss and 4.5 sacks and could push for All-ACC consideration off the edge, and the tackle pair of Anthony Britton and Jason Hammond returns. The staff added veteran Matthew Fobbs-White (Baylor) and former four-star Devon Baxter (Michigan) to the end rotation.

There’s plenty of shuffling in the secondary with two corners transferring out with high grades – Ja’Son Prevard (Kansas State) and Emmanuel Karnley (Washington) – plus All-ACC safety Devin Neal heading pro. Ethan Minter and nickel Corey Costner are returning starters, and the staff added 130 career starts (10,000+ career snaps) of experience via the portal. Brandyn Hillman (Michigan) and Jacobie Henderson (Rutgers) both graded as high three-star transfers and are projected to earn starting spots.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Quarterback injuries have handcuffed the offense the past three seasons. Fickell signed a proven, all-league dual-threat in Joseph whose skillset will elevate the other position groups. The quarterback fix – from meltdown to proven asset – plus a schedule boost will have Wisconsin returning to bowl season.

After facing one of the hardest schedules, Wisconsin wins the schedule lottery by drawing six of the bottom seven and
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Not even the biggest doubters could have envisioned a 5-7 year in Luke Fickell’s second season here. Even fewer would have seen a 4-8 third year.

The losing season in 2024 snapped their FBS-best 22-year bowl streak, and last year’s collapse marked Wisconsin’s first consecutive losing seasons since 1991-92. That was before Barry Alvarez built Wisconsin into Offensive Line U and the eventual Big Ten West bullies.

Considered by most as the top hire of the post-2022 coaching carousel, Fickell now ranks dead last of the 10 Power 4 hires, when comparing the three-year output to the four-year sample size before the hire for program context.

Sitting at 2-6 in mid-November, and despite fans in Camp Randall Stadium chanting “Fire Fickell,” athletic director Chris McIntosh issued a vote of confidence in his head coach and confirmed they would retain him for 2026.

Two days later, Wisconsin upset #23 Washington, snapped Fickell’s 0-10 record against ranked opponents, and fans stormed onto the field to celebrate. Same thing two weeks later, with another field storming after Wisconsin knocked off #21 Illinois.

The ranked wins could help spark some momentum into Fickell’s fourth year, but the returns from his first three are hard to ignore. It’s the second straight year in which their rivalry trophy case is empty. He’s 17-21 overall – 10-17 vs. the Big Ten – with a drop in the win column each year.

Any momentum from the ranked wins did not translate into the Talent Acquisition game. Wisconsin signed 33 transfers – zero four-stars – to rank 49th nationally and 13th in the Big Ten. Worse, they were unable to retain several veteran multi-year starters.

Wisconsin’s best decades were built on continuity and player development. So far without their old formula, they have not been able to adapt to the NIL/Portal era.
pick_six_2026.offense:
On the third play of the season, starting quarterback Billy Edwards was injured and essentially knocked out for the year. Backup Danny O’Neil threw as many picks as touchdowns and was injured in the fourth game. The collapse of the quarterback room was the catalyst for a broken offense that averaged just 12 points/game -- the worst in Power 4.

It was déjà vu for Wisconsin. 2025 made it three straight years of transfer starting quarterbacks getting injured early in the season. Without a passing threat, this time around they couldn’t even muster up their reliable rushing attack that defined the program for 20+ years. Wisconsin averaged just 3.3 yards/carry (#128), got no run push from the line (#129), and it took until the 11th game to finally get a 100-yard rusher.

Fickell hopes the fourth time is the charm, and they signed Colton Joseph (Old Dominion) who earned second-team All-Sun Belt honors last year. Joseph is a true dual-threat, and adds a mobile element that the program has been missing. He rushed for over 1,000 yards last year, including a pair of 75-yard touchdown runs against Indiana, and is a threat in read option and quarterback-designed runs.

In two years, Joseph amassed 4,200 passing yards, 1,600 rushing yards, 56 total touchdowns and was ranked the #21 transfer quarterback this cycle. O’Neil should be back in time for fall camp, and Carter Smith also returns after stepping up as a true freshman last November.

The top two running backs missed seven games due to injury and combined for just 663 yards. Dilin Jones transferred out to LSU, but lead rusher Darrion Dupree returns. The staff signed veteran Abu Sama (Iowa State) who has accumulated 1,933 rushing yards in his three seasons. He went for 270 yards in the infamous 2024 “Snowmageddon” game.

Receivers and tight ends actually got 48 carries for 260 yards last year but the staff mentioned they want a running back rotation for 2026. With Dupree and Sama, plus USC transfer Bryan Jackson, there are plenty of options.

Vinny Anthony and Trech Kekahuna got the vast majority of snaps and catches last year but both are gone. Backup Chris Brooks moves up the depth chart, the staff kept four-star Eugene Hilton away from

the portal, and Tyrell Henry drew high praise in spring. They signed Oklahoma State starter Shamar Rigby as a playmaker in the slot, and then took lottery tickets on a pair of former Top100 recruits Malachi Coleman (Minnesota) and Zion Kearney (Oklahoma).

Tight end Lance Mason led the team with 398 receiving yards, but he and two other tight ends are gone. Grant Stec flashed as a freshman before his injury, and Jacob Harris (Bowling Green) caught five touchdowns last year.

Wisconsin hired Eric Mateos to take over the offensive line. Mateos and coordinator Jeff Grimes were together at Baylor with his “RVO” Reliably Violent Offense. Last year at Arkansas, Mateos’ line helped them land the #1 rushing offense in my opponent-adjusted ranking.

Two starters return in Colin Cubberly and Emerson Mandell, but they lost two others to the portal with Joe Brunner going to Indiana with a high four-star grade and Jake Renfro going to Illinois. Kevin Heywood was originally a projected 2025 starter but tore his ACL last preseason. He is back at left tackle, and the staff added three Power 4 transfers: Blake Cherry (Arkansas), PJ Wilkins (Ole Miss) and Oklahoma State starting center Austin Kawecki.
pick_six_2026.defense:
The defense held the explosive offenses of Washington and Illinois to just 10 points apiece, and finished ranked #26 in my opponent-adjusted ranking -- #10 against the run. They just didn’t have any help at all from the offense.

“You start to feel like a touchdown is the end-all, be-all” said outside backer Mason Reiger. One touchdown is an insane bar that they were forced to hit.

Just three starters return and it starts in the middle with last year’s freshmen phenoms Mason Posa and Cooper Catalano. The inside backers finished first and second in tackles (117 and 6 sacks combined) with Posa earning All-Big Ten honors. Both return, along with incoming Jon Jon Kamara (Kansas) but two veterans transferred out to Power 4 programs: Christian Alliegro (Ohio State) and Tackett Curtis (UCF).

Their top four defensive linemen, top four outside backers, and five of the top six defensive backs are all gone. In the interior, All-MAC Junior Poyser (Buffalo) and Charles Perkins are the projected starters. There is more proven experience on the ends with Tyreese Fearbry and Sebastian Cheeks who was second on the team in QB pressures last year. The staff signed a roulette chip with Liam Danitz, a DIII transfer with All-America track speed.

The secondary should be transfer-heavy with as many as four starting spots going to newcomers. Javan Robinson (Arizona State) is a certainty, having started the past two years in the Big 12. Eric Fletcher (Oklahoma State) and a pair of former four-stars Cai Bates (Florida State) and Bryce West (Ohio State) will battle at corner and nickel. Marvin Burks (Missouri) brings SEC game experience at safety, and Matthew Jung returns after filling in well last season.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Nebraska hopes that Colandrea’s scrambling skillset can help elevate the other positions groups around him. The offensive line’s breakthrough still hasn’t materialized, and now the defense has a coordinator/scheme change.

Nebraska was #10 in the Big Ten in Game Grader, #11 in my opponent-adjusted yardage margin, and now the schedule heats up as they draw the Playoff trio and six of the league’s top ten.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Matt Rhule was hired to improve Nebraska’s player development, their physicality on the lines of scrimmage, and then cash in with his usual third-year breakthrough.

2025 was Rhule’s third season, but there was no breakthrough. Far from it.

Nebraska entered 2025 on a 10-35 run in one-score games, and they were able to notch a few close wins like the 20-17 opener over Cincinnati, a roller-coaster 34-31 win over Maryland, and touchdown decisions over UCLA and Northwestern. It was enough to punch a ticket to bowl season.

But Nebraska has been waiting for a signature, ranked win on the national stage. They had two opportunities last season, both in Lincoln, but lost to Michigan and USC by a combined seven points. They have now lost 30 straight against ranked teams – second-worst behind Rutgers’ drought – and while the run started before Rhule, he has personally lost 20 straight including his Baylor tenure.

There was no breakthrough in the trenches. Michigan sacked quarterback Dylan Raiola seven times, Minnesota set a school-record with nine sacks, and the defensive line finished #114 against the run.

Player development? Nebraska is second-worst in the Big Ten with just three NFL draft picks (2024- 2026) despite signing Top 25 recruiting classes most years.

Rhule’s November record fell to 2-10 after consecutive blowout losses at Penn State 37-10 and then a 40-16 loss to Iowa for the 10th time in 11 years. In the bowl game, they were outgained by 200 yards and lost to Utah 44-22.

Part of the Rhule era breakthrough was supposed to be five-star Raiola, but he shocked Husker Nation and transferred out to Oregon. There were other factors at play – weather, their March Madness run – but it was still shocking to see Memorial Stadium empty for their annual Red-White spring game. Was it a Rhule Referendum? HuskerOnline’s Steven Sipple noticed it: “Nebraska needs a boost to fan enthusiasm now more than I can ever remember, and I’ve been covering this since 1995.”
pick_six_2026.offense:
Raiola was injured in the ninth game and freshman TJ Lateef led the UCLA win before the season-ending three-game losing streak. With Raiola gone to Oregon, the staff got a commitment from four-star Notre Dame backup Kenny Minchey but 24 hours later he flipped to Kentucky. Finally, they signed Mountain West Player of the Year, Anthony Colandrea (UNLV).

At UNLV, Colandrea dazzled with 23 passing touchdowns, 10 more rushing scores, and cut down on his 26-20 touchdown-to-pick ratio from his time at Virginia. If there was ever a fit for the term “gunslinger” Colandrea is the definition – he will produce highlight-reel scrambles and off-balance throws but will also turn it over (29 picks and 17 fumbles over three seasons).

Offensive coordinator Dana Holgorsen is intrigued by Colandrea’s pocket elusiveness and creativity when the play breaks down. They studied Diego Pavia film of off-script plays, and Colandrea’s mobility adds an element missing from Raiola’s skillset. Theoretically this will help cut down on the pass protection woes, and even create more downfield explosive plays with the extra few seconds outside the pocket.

Lateef also returns but Colandrea is the focal point of the offense heading into fall camp.

As the pass game began to struggle last season, the staff doubled down on what was working in the run game. Emmett Johnson was the engine of the offense with a 251-carry workload, and he surged for 1,451 yards and earned first-team All-Big Ten. Johnson went pro and leaves behind a wide-open running back room which Rhule decided not to supplement from the transfer portal. It looks like a trio for 2026 with Mekhi Nelson, four-star Isaiah Mozee, and true freshman Jamal Rule who had huge offseason reviews from the staff and scored on a 75-yarder in the spring game.

Dane Key departs but the other two starters Jacory Barney and yardage-leader Nyziah Hunter return to the receiver room. Hunter made game-changing plays in three of their wins and could push for All-Big

Ten this season. The staff signed UCLA starter Kwazi Gilmer to replace Key, and the starting trio are experienced former four-stars. Starting tight end Luke Lindenmeyer also returns after a productive 29- catch, 312-yard season that earned him All-Big Ten honorable mention.

Nebraska has patiently waited for an offensive line breakthrough but last year it collapsed in pass protection -- #112 in Sack Rate – and stunted the pass game. Rhule made a coaching change and hired offensive line guru Geep Wade who just helped build Georgia Tech into one of the sport’s strongest lines.

They hit the transfer portal and brought in three experienced Power 4 starters that Wade was familiar with: Paul Mubenga (LSU), Brendan Black (Iowa State), and Tree Babalade (South Carolina). Black earned a four-star transfer grade and started 30 games at guard, Babalade was also a four-star with 15 starts, while Mubenga started 11 at LSU. Nebraska returns two impact starters with center Justin Evans and former five-star left tackle Elijah Pritchett who is developing into a pro prospect.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Rhule made another coaching change on defense after the Blackshirts were pushed around in the final three games and ultimately finished #41 of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted rankings -- #62 against the run.

He replaced John Butler with San Diego State’s Rob Aurich who helped lead a stat turnaround from #97 to #5 in scoring defense in his only season as their coordinator. Nebraska will shift away from their 3-3- 5 scheme to Aurich’s 4-2-5. But Rhule was more focused on non-scheme items: “I want player development, I want physicality, I want effort.”

The defensive line loses two full-time starters in end Elijah Jeudy and tackle Keona Davis who transferred out to Miami with high four-star grades. Two ends return in Cameron Lenhardt and former five-star Williams Nwaneri. At tackle, the staff added Boston College starter Owen Stoudmire and breakout freshman Jahsear Whittington (Pittsburgh) to join veteran Riley Van Poppel.

Three of the top four linebackers are gone, but Vincent Shavers returns after battling through injuries to post a productive 61-tackle (7.5 for loss) season. Aurich wanted a bigger set of linebackers and they added a pair of 6’3 transfers in Dexter Foster (Oregon State) and Owen Chambliss (San Diego State) who earned first-team All-Mountain West in this scheme.

The secondary played well last year, ranking #3 nationally in pass/yards game, and #28 in my opponent-adjusted passing number. Two All-Big Ten defensive backs are gone but they return one in corner Andrew Marshall. At the other corner spot Nebraska signed five-star Danny Odem (Orlando, FL) and he’ll battle spring game starter Jeremiah Charles. Aurich brought his starting safety Dwayne McDougle with him from San Diego State, Jamir Conn will start at the other safety spot, and Donovan Jones moves into the new nickel role. It’s worth noting true freshman Odem is the only blue-chipper on the secondary’s two-deep as they go through a scheme change.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
The graduation of a large, program-changing senior class leaves behind a younger and inexperienced two-deep for 2026. While the recruiting is surging in the right direction, it may need a few development seasons to translate onto the field.

Illinois also loses Altmyer, their cheat code in close games. While they fall down a few spots in the Big Ten projection in this transition-type season, Bielema has clearly elevated the program’s floor. If the JUCO wildcards hit, Illinois can get back to the upper-half of the league.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
In the Music City Bowl, quarterback Luke Altmyer led a game-winning drive that melted the final five minutes to knock off Tennessee. It was a fitting end to an all-time career.

For the past three seasons, Altmyer has been Illinois’ get-out-of-jail- free card, bailing them out of one-score games. His seven game- winning drives are the nation’s most over that span. Head coach Bret Bielema has grown accustomed to the late-game heroics: “I looked at Luke before our final drive, he gave me a head nod, that’s all I needed to see.”

Altmyer has been the leader and figurehead of the program’s best five- year run (37 wins) since 1905. The 10-win season in 2024 tied a program-high and they clinched back-to-back bowl bids for the first time in 15 years. Illinois stacked consecutive 9+ win seasons for the first time ever.

The wins led a fan resurgence too. Memorial Stadium posted four consecutive sell-outs last season for the first time since 2008.

Illinois demonstrated some staying power in the top half of the deep Big Ten, and as they attempt to ascend further, Bielema credits this senior class for building the foundation: “our 2026 recruiting class is one of the best I’ve ever assembled – these seniors have been a big part of that.”

Far from just coach-speak, the rankings back up that claim. At #21 nationally, the 2026 class became the highest-ranked class Illinois has ever signed in the modern recruiting era. In the ten years prior to Bielema, Illinois signed just three Top 50 classes. He’s five for five, and this Top 25 class raises the bar.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Altmyer ended his Illinois career with the second-most wins by a quarterback (23), the highest completion percentage (64%), highest QB Rating, and became the first 3,000-yard passer since Nathan Scheelhaase in 2013.

Illinois hit the transfer portal again and signed a former four-star Katin Houser who began at Michigan State but then posted two successful seasons at East Carolina. Last year he placed fourth in the AAC in QB Rating with an impressive two-year stat line: 5,306 yards, 37 touchdowns, and 17 picks.

Houser has a bigger frame, strong arm, but lacks the elusiveness of Altmyer. That could be an issue given the complete rebuild of the offensive line. Last year the veteran line was expected to become a strength with the ability to grind down opponents, Big Ten West style. Instead, they remained average in OL Run Push (#50), below-average in yards/carry (#98), and struggled in pass protection (#110) allowing a sack on 9% of attempts. And that was with a top-notch scrambler in Altmyer.

Four starters are gone, including first-team All-Big Ten JC Davis, with guard Brandon Henderson as the only returner. Nathan Knapik played well in the bowl game with Davis opted out, center Jake Renfro (Wisconsin) transferred in with Big Ten starting experience, and then the staff hit the junior- college ranks. They signed three of the top five JUCO linemen this cycle: Maika Matelau, TJ Taylor, and Alfred Washington.

Christian Abney moves up into a starting role after both tight ends – blocker Tanner Arkin and receiver Cole Rusk – departed. Rusk (Arizona) earned a four-star transfer grade and left after posting the most yards by a tight end here since Daniel Barker in 2020.

Illinois at least has stability at the other skill positions. Last year Kaden Feagin, Aidan Laughery, and Ca’Lil Valentine shared carries and the trio returns intact for 2026. The speedy, shifty Valentine led with 614 yards, Laughery may be the best of the bunch if he can avoid injuries, and big-back Feagin was getting reps at tight end this spring.

They do lose their top receiver in third-team All-Big Ten Hank Beatty who emerged as a reliable playmaker in the slot. He finished #2 in the Big Ten in yards-after-catch trailing only the Biletnikoff

winner Makai Lemon. Beatty, and red zone threat Justin Bowick (Oklahoma State) are gone, but their #2 and #3 receivers return. Collin Dixon and Hudson Clement combined for 1,002 yards and eight touchdowns. A pair of freshmen Brayden Trimble and four-star Nas Rankin could push into the rotation. Then the staff signed first-team All-CUSA 6’5 Alex Perry (FIU) and speedy Jayshon Platt (FAU) who together combined for 1,560 yards and 14 touchdowns at the non-AQ level.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Back in 2022, Bielema threw out the defensive playbook and together with Ryan Walters they designed a new scheme from scratch. It puzzled opposing coordinators and they posted the #1 scoring defense in America. Since then, Bielema claims two-thirds of the Big Ten has copied the scheme, and that it’s essentially been figured out by now. Illinois fell to #31 in 2024, #56 in 2025, and Bielema wanted another change this offseason.

He surprised by hiring longtime Montana head coach Bobby Hauck. Bielema said he was the “only person in mind and I offered only one man the job.” Hauck is from the Rocky Long tree, known for its aggressive, attacking 3-3-5 scheme.

The scheme change caused an exodus from the defensive line and four top linemen transferred out to Power 4 rosters: four-star Tomiwa Durojaiye (South Carolina), Angelo McCullom (Texas A&M), Eli Coenen (Michigan State), and Curt Neal (Purdue). That is quite the talent drain. Pat Farrell was in the rotation last year and moves into a starting role. The staff backfilled with rotational linemen from the non-AQ level in Connor Sullivan (Washington State) and Darrell Prater (Jacksonville State) and All-Ivy Carter Janki (Penn).

Top defender Gabe Jacas is off to the pros after earning first-team All-Big Ten honors and posting one of the program’s best pass rushing seasons. He led the league with 11 sacks, and two other outside backers Alec Bryant and Leon Lowery are also gone. Joe Barna played well in the bowl game, and Daniel Brown is a former JUCO All-American.

Starting middle backer Dylan Rosiek is gone, but four-star Grant Beerman impressed as a freshman and could become their next star. James Kreutz is back and Ismael Kante was ranked the #1 JUCO linebacker.

The clear strength of the defense, and the overall team, is in the secondary. Safeties Matthew Bailey and Xavier Scott both turned down the pros for a final season in Champaign. Juice Clarke is back at corner to make it three all-league stars in the defensive backfield. They added yet another JUCO star in #1 cornerback Jakwon Morris and this room is strong enough to lead them through the scheme change. They will miss three-year starter and two-time captain Miles Scott, but this will still be a top secondary in the Big Ten.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Heintschel’s 6-1 run against the ACC provides optimism for the program going forward, but three areas of uncertainty remain. The offensive line has struggled for several seasons now, in the transfer portal Pitt lost six proven star players yet signed zero four-star transfers (joining Boston College as the only Power 4 programs with zero), and now longtime ace defensive coordinator Randy Bates retired.

Pittsburgh is a solid ACC team but those issues hold them back from title contention.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Pat Narduzzi made a surprise move at quarterback and it ended up salvaging Pittsburgh’s 2025 season.

Eli Holstein, after going 7-2 as the starter last year, threw three picks in Pitt’s two September losses. They blew a 10-point lead in the Backyard Brawl overtime loss and then again wasted a 17-point lead against Louisville.

Riding a seven-game losing streak vs. Power 4 opponents, Narduzzi made the switch.

True freshman Mason Heintschel took over and lit up Boston College for 323 passing yards and four touchdowns in the 48-7 win. The 18-year-old played with poise and elevated the playmakers around him. Pitt rattled off six straight ACC wins – four 300+ passing games for Heintschel – and found themselves in the league title race in late November.

They aced the first test, upsetting Georgia Tech on the road. Pitt raced to a 28-0 lead, and Braylan Lovelace took back a 100-yard Pick Six that effectively shattered Haynes King’s Heisman campaign.

Playing for an ACC title bid on the final day of the regular season is certainly a win for the program, but the talent gap was too significant in the 38-7 loss to Miami. Pitt rushed for just 30 rushing yards here, and they were held under 100 rushing yards in their four regular season losses.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Heintschel finished with 16 touchdowns (eight picks), a 64% completion rate, and placed #2 in Power 4 in QB Rating among true freshmen. Beyond the stat sheet, he impressed with pocket elusiveness, continued to make highlight reel plays, and made everyone around him better.

From 2024 to 2025, Pitt’s passing yards/attempt and explosive passing both jumped up 50+ spots.

Look for a second-year bonus here as Heintschel now gets an entire offseason of starter reps. Holstein transferred out to Virginia which officially ends any quarterback battle here.

The offense was expected to rely on 2024 All-American Desmond Reid, the do-it-all playmaker, but he battled injuries and missed five games. Reid put up 200 yards and caught two touchdowns in the Florida State win, and now heads to the pros.

In Reid’s absence, another true freshman stepped up big time. Ja’Kyrian Turner rushed for 652 yards, 7 touchdowns, and showed off speed and shiftiness. He rushed for 201 yards in the Georgia Tech win and solidified his starting role for 2026. Backup Juelz Goff transferred to Boise State and the staff added a physical downhill runner in La’Vell Wright (Western Kentucky) who cashed in 10 touchdowns last year. Their top high school signee this cycle -- Top200 four-star Damon Ferguson -- could push for carries.

Heintschel will be throwing to a whole new group of pass-catchers as Pitt loses their top three tight ends and three of their top four receivers. Kenny Johnson emerged as the #1 receiver and also helped flip the Syracuse game with a 66-yard punt return touchdown, but he transferred out to Texas Tech. Raphael Williams and Deuce Spann both graduated, leaving Cataurus “Blue” Hicks as the leader for 2026. Hicks is a big-play speedster (17.6 yards/catch) and Censere Lee was in the rotation in 2024. The staff added another Western Carolina player from the Kade Bell pipeline in All-SOCON Malik Knight.

The tight end room had its most productive season here since 2021 but all three are gone. Carson Kent (Oklahoma) and Elijah Lagg (UAB) both transferred in with three-star grades, but Max Hunt was the surprise spring hero.

The offensive line struggled again, allowing the third-most sacks in FBS (44), and ranked outside the Top 100 in pass protection for the second straight season. The #73 rank in OL Run Push was slightly better but in the four regular season losses they were held under 100 yards each time.

Ryan Baer and BJ Williams both earned ACC honorable mention and return on the right side of the line with 69 combined career starts. The left side was hit with injuries but as a result it’s a more experienced unit in 2026. Keith Gouveia was the original starter at left guard, Ryan Carretta and Kendall Stanley each started seven games filling in for injuries, and the staff signed All-MAC Keylen Davis (Akron) and FCS All-America tackle Netinho Olivieri (Penn). Even with starting center Lyndon Cooper transferring out to Vanderbilt, this room is more veteran and should see statistical improvements this fall.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Death, Taxes, and a Top 10 Rushing Defense at Pitt.

Longtime defensive coordinator Randy Bates retired this offseason after building one of the most consistent defenses in the nation. No matter the player personnel, you knew what to expect from Pitt’s defense every year: aggressive, blitz-heavy playcalling and disruption.

Pitt leads the nation in sacks (299) since 2019, they lead the ACC in defensive touchdowns (21) since 2021, four defenders were named All-Americans since 2020, and seven of his eight defenses placed in the Top 25 of my opponent-adjusted rankings.

2025 was no different. Pitt allowed just 2.7 yards/carry, 95 rush yards/game, and forced a Negative Play on 11% of snaps – all Top 10 national ranks.

Cory Sanders is the next man up after serving the last eight seasons on staff coaching the safeties.

Pitt’s linebacker room, aka “The Sharks,” was once again a top national unit. The trio of Kyle Louis, Rasheem Biles, and Braylan Lovelace combined for 162 tackles, 31 for loss, 8.5 sacks, and 4 touchdowns. Former All-American Louis heads to the pros, Biles left for Texas, and Lovelace returns at middle backer after his All-ACC season. Cameron Lindsey started three games when Louis was injured, former Ohio State four-star Jayden Bonsu is back from injury, and they signed two FBS starters in Alex Sanford (Purdue) and DeMarco Ward (Memphis).

Like the offense, two impact starters were lost to the transfer portal. In addition to Biles, All-ACC defensive tackle Francis Brewu left for Notre Dame and was ranked the #8 defensive lineman this cycle. Pitt still returns a pair of strong vets in the interior with Sean FitzSimmons and Nick James.

Jimmy Scott is a third-year starter at defensive end and Isaiah Neal showed he can play both end and tackle after sliding outside last year.

Pitt loses four starters from the secondary with Tamon Lynum, Rashad Battle, Javon McIntyre, and Kavir Bains- Marquez all departing. They did find a young star in Shawn Lee who was named a Freshman All-American by On3 as a top cover corner. Former WPIAL star Raion Strader (Auburn) transferred home and should start opposite of Lee. Shadarian Harrison is another veteran corner, and hard-hitting safety Cruce Brookins earned All-ACC honorable mention.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
The losses of do-it-all King and coordinator Faulkner are major hits to the offense. Instead of the 10,000-yarder they will have a first-time starter. The defense collapsed in November and there was no apparent overnight fix.

Still, with Key’s offensive line and a top running back duo, Georgia Tech will have its signature power run game and should return to bowl season as a mid-tier ACC team.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Georgia Tech’s nine-win season was a total success for a program that is not far removed from nine wins over a three-year span. But the way the season started quickly shifted expectations onto the real prizes of an ACC Title and Playoff bid.

Game by game, Georgia Tech found a way. In the opener, Haynes King scrambled 45 yards for the winning touchdown in the final minute to beat Colorado. Then they upset #12 Clemson with a school-record 55-yard kick when the field goal team sprinted into formation in the final seconds. The ensuing field storming capped third-year head coach Brent Key’s signature win.

The defense did their part with an overtime two-point stand to beat Wake Forest, and then again when Omar Daniels took back a fumble 95 yards for an essential 14-point swing to beat Duke.

Georgia Tech entered November with a perfect 8-0 record – their best start since 1966 – and a #7 AP ranking. King was the national leader in total offense and even ESPN’s Pat McAfee put on a “Haynes for Heisman” shirt.

Then the defense collapsed. They allowed 583 yards to NC State, 537 to a one-win BC team, and 42 points to Pittsburgh. From 8-0 to 9-4, Tech lost four of its last five games with a finish that leaves the program and fan base with a bittersweet view. It was undoubtedly a successful season in totality, but after the 8-0 start it seems like a missed opportunity in the most wide-open ACC title race in over a decade.

Key’s slogan is “JUMP” as in, the program continuing to make a jump each season. To jump higher than 9-4 in 2026, Tech must replace a program legend quarterback, the receiver trio, seven defensive starters, and will do so with a double coordinator switch.
pick_six_2026.offense:
King led all Power 4 quarterbacks with 953 rushing yards, was second in rushing touchdowns, and his productive season earned him the ACC Offensive Player of the Year and placed him 10th on the Heisman leaderboard. King leaves The Flats with the school record for completions and joined Joe Hamilton as the second player with 10,000+ total yards.

The transition at quarterback was already going to be significant, but then offensive coordinator

Buster Faulkner left for Florida – and brought quarterback Aaron Philo with him.

Philo had started a handful of games and was the clear projected starter until the transfer out. The staff hit the portal and signed Indiana backup Alberto Mendoza, brother of Heisman winner Fernando, to challenge incumbent Graham Knowles. Mendoza got 100 snaps during Indiana’s national title run and was graded the #31 transfer quarterback this cycle, while Knowles’ only snap was an 84-yard touchdown pass in the Gardner-Webb game.

Former Tech quarterback George Godsey takes over as coordinator after two decades coaching in the pros. Given the retention of excellent quarterbacks coach Chris Weinke, plus Key’s success building offensive lines, the offensive style should remain the same.

Key’s offensive line was one of the best in America last year and was one of just two lines to rank in the Top 10 of both my OL Run Push (#8) and Sack Rate (#3) stats. They lose their best one with first-team All-ACC guard Keylan Rutledge going pro, but return two starters – Malachi Carney and Ethan Mackenny – with ACC honors. Jameson Riggs and five-star Josh Petty are projected to start at guard, and three- star transfer Joseph Ionata (Alabama) rounds out the starting five at center.

Last year’s duo of Jamal Haynes and Malachi Hosley combined for 1,138 yards and 12 touchdowns with both backs averaging over 7 yards/carry. Former Penn transfer Hosley added explosiveness to the offense.

With Jamal graduating, the staff successfully reloaded their dynamic duo in the backfield by signing the #4 ranked running back transfer Justice Haynes (Michigan). He was a five-star recruit, played two years at Alabama, then was Michigan’s feature back (857 yards, 10 TD, 7.1 per carry) before an injury cut the season short. This is a top running back room again.

It’s a complete rebuild at receiver and tight end with the top three departing from both positions. Eric Rivers and Malik Rutherford graduated, then Isiah Canion transferred to Georgia with a high four-star transfer grade. Jordan Allen takes over the starting role in the slot, and a mix of incoming transfers are competing on the outsides. Isaiah Fuhrmann (Elon) put up 900 yards last year at the FCS level and was named first-team All-CAA, Jaiven Plummer (California) is a Power 4 veteran, and Jaylen Mbakwe (Alabama) is a true wild-card addition. Mbakwe was a five-star recruit in the 2024 class as the nation’s #2 cornerback, but wants to play both ways and could be a playmaker here in the receiver rotation.

Luke Harpring followed Faulkner to Florida, meaning all three tight end spots are newcomers. All three were graded as three-star transfers: Chris Corbo (Dartmouth), pass threat Gavin Harris (New Mexico State) and blocker Spencer Mermans (Yale).
pick_six_2026.defense:
King and the offense covered for a below-average defense over the 8-0 start, but then the unit collapsed in November per my opponent-adjusted metric:

- First 8 Games: #50 of 68 Power 4 - Final 5 Games: #67 of 68 Power 4

Jason Semore returns for his third stint at Georgia Tech and this time takes over as defensive coordinator. His coordinator experience has been successful, leading Valdosta State to a DII national title, and rebuilding defenses at Marshall and Southern Miss the past two seasons. Marshall played for a league title, and then his Southern Miss unit led the nation in interceptions last year.

Semore calls an aggressive defense focused on disruption and turnovers, and it’s backed up by the stats. Southern Miss ranked in the Top 25 in sacks, tackles for loss, third-down defense, and picks. Georgia Tech’s defense could use a boost in all four.

Four starters return, including the full two-deep at linebacker. Kyle Efford led the team in tackles, earned ACC honors, and returns with EJ Lightsey and Melvin Jordan. The trio looks for a bounce-back season to their 2024 standards.

Tech loses their top defender in first-team All-ACC Jordan van den Berg. They will miss his pass rush off the edge, but the staff signed three impact transfers in four-star Noah Carter (Alabama), Taje McCoy (Oklahoma State) and Rutgers starter Jordan Walker. Three more experienced ends return in Amontrae Bradford, Brayden Manley, and AJ Hoffler. Defensive tackle Christian Garrett is joined by two incoming transfers Tawfiq Thomas (Colorado) and Vincent Carroll- Jackson (UConn) who both have starting experience.

Five of the top six defensive backs are gone with backups Fenix Felton and Tae Harris moving up into starting roles. Jonas Duclona (USF) and Mbakwe are transfer additions, plus their two top-rated high school recruits this cycle are both corners Jaedyn Terry and Trae Stevenson.

pick_six_2026.outlook: Just like last offseason, NC State lost another round of program stars to the transfer portal and failed to add back any four-stars. They remain in the top-half of the conference thanks to do-it-all quarterback CJ Bailey and the league’s best schedule draw.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Head coach Dave Doeren did it again. Like clockwork, he finds ways to scrape out the most of his roster, overcome injury runs, and of course, beat UNC. NC State beat their rival for the fifth straight time, beat Florida State for the fourth straight time, ended #8 Georgia Tech’s undefeated season, and won four of their last five.

After a 4-4 start and midseason defensive collapse, Doeren got NC State to yet another 8-win season – their fifth in six years.

In the process, they found a star quarterback to build the program around. In his first full season as the starter, CJ Bailey threw 25 touchdowns, placed third in the ACC in QB Rating, and his 340-yard explosion led the upset win over Georgia Tech. They scored on 8 of 10 drives and got revenge on the 2002 game that ended Philip Rivers’ undefeated start.

The ensuing field-storming was the pinnacle of the season and sparked the strong finish.

The injury run on defense exposed some depth/recruiting limitations that NC State faces in the NIL era. It started back before the 2025 season when three established stars transferred out of the secondary: Devan Boykin, Bishop Fitzgerald, and Tamarcus Cooley. A roster strength turned into a question mark, and then an injury run destroyed the room in September. NC State finished #132 in passing defense.

And here again entering the 2026 season, NC State was hit with the same problem. Their All- ACC running back, top two receivers, and best offensive linemen all transferred out with high four-star grades – yet they didn’t sign any four-star transfers to offset the damage.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Bailey enters 2026 as an All-ACC candidate and the dual-threat gives NC State a puncher’s chance in every game. He posted the program’s first 3,000-yard passing season since Devin Leary in 2021 and really caught fire over the final six games with 13 total touchdowns and just two picks. His stat sheet may have looked even better but NC State found a cheat code in short- yardage situations with their bulldozer Will Wilson who powered in 10 rushing touchdowns. The staff will again use Wilson there and we may see more of a passing threat from him in the second year.

The offense ranked in the Top 25 of my three opponent-adjusted metrics – #25 overall, #23 passing, and #19 rushing – but aside from Bailey, program stars must be replaced from every position group.

Hollywood Smothers started fast with multiple 100+ yard games, and despite a lingering injury, he still led the ACC in rushing. He earned first-team All-ACC honors and became NC State’s first ACC lead rusher since 1997. Smothers transferred out to Texas as a high four-star and the #2 overall running back this cycle.

In his absence, Duke Scott impressed in his two starts – 196 yards against Georgia Tech and 108 in the bowl win. Scott moves into the top role, Jonathan Paylor is back from injury, and the staff added rotational back Davion Gause (UNC).

The top three wide receivers are all gone, too. Wesley Grimes graduated but two more left with high marks. Terrell Anderson led with 629 yards and transferred to USC as a Top 10 ranked transfer WR. Noah Rogers also got a four-star grade and left for Alabama.

The staff signed a pair of former high school blue-chips – Jojo Trader and Chance Robinson – who were teammates at Miami. Trader was originally a near five-star and was in the receiver rotation last year for the Hurricanes. They also signed first-team All-MAC Victor Snow (Buffalo) and a pair of incoming four-star true freshmen Amiri Acker and Tyreek Copper who posted a video-game senior season: 105 catches, 2,245 yards, 33 touchdown catches. Teddy Hoffmann is the lead returner after putting up 349 yards as a true freshman last year.

First-team All-ACC tight end Justin Joly set program records but now heads to the pros along with top blocking tight end Cody Hardy. The staff added two transfers here in former Top200 Vander Ploog (Oregon) and Top 10 transfer Hunter Provience (Montana State).

Jacarrius Peak seemed like an All-ACC candidate but instead transferred out to South Carolina with a four-star grade. They did retain a rising star in Freshman All-American Spike Sowells who was the school’s highest graded offensive line recruit of the past decade.

Teague Andersen returns at right tackle, and former four-star TK Whitset is drawing high praise. The staff added two key transfers in first-team All-AAC left tackle Jimarion McCrimon (East Carolina) and center Daniel Cruz (Texas).
pick_six_2026.defense:
Injuries and the talent drain in the secondary ended up catching up to the defense. NC State fell to 55th of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted metric and were plagued by missed tackles, lack of a pass rush, and poor third-down defense (#128).

The entire front six is gone, leaving behind a rebuilding project for defensive coordinator DJ Eliot.

All three line starters graduated and the trio of Brandon Cleveland, Travali Price, and Sabastian Harsh combined for 1,600+ snaps. Isaiah Shirley and Chase Bond move up from their backup roles, and the staff added third-team All-ACC Harvey Dyson (Tulane) at edge.

Caden Fordham returned from a 2024 injury to lead all of Power 4 in tackles (130) and earn first- team All-ACC honors. Fordham is gone along with original starter Sean Brown but the staff added two Power 4 transfers who project as starters this fall. Popo Aguirre was Miami’s third backer and will start in the middle, while former four-star Da’Karri Nelson (Penn State) is projected at outside backer. NC State also gets back Sterling Dixon, the former Alabama transfer who was injured for the 2025 season, at outside backer or edge.

Brian Nelson is back at one corner spot but they lose their top cover corner in Devon Marshall. Ondre Evans (Georgia) is a former Top100 recruit and should fill into Marshall’s spot.

The safety room was destroyed by the portal in the preseason, and then hit harder by injuries early in the season. This was the key reason why the defense fell apart and gave up five 300-yard passing games. The silver lining is that all those young guys thrown into action ahead-of-schedule are back, and that experience should pay dividends in 2026. Asaad Brown started ten games, Tristan Teasdell started the final five, and both freshmen are back. Original starter Ronnie Royal and nickelback Jackson Vick both return, they added Penn State starter King Mack, so look for fall camp competition and hopefully a second-year bonus for the room.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Game Grader loved Florida State last season compared to their losing record. The close losses and big yardage margins had FSU at #25 despite going 5-7.

Norvell’s cold streak has the program at pre-Bowden lows and the pressure is mounting. It’s the worst possible timing to snap his streak of top ten transfer hauls, and they appear downgraded at almost every position group.

Worst of all is the schedule draw. In addition to Alabama and Florida in the non-conference, Florida State draws seven of the ACC’s top nine and only one of the bottom eight.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
From 13-0 to Playoff Snub to 2-10, Florida State went through an extreme two-year rollercoaster.

Mike Norvell had shifted the emphasis from high school recruiting over to the transfer portal, and that reliance on one-year portal hits led to the boom-or-bust outcomes. 2023 was a hit, 2024 was an all- time miss.

Florida State signed another top-rated transfer haul and the thought was that 2025 would indicate which of the two prior extreme seasons was the exception and which was the rule going forward.

On opening Saturday, they stunned #8 Alabama 31-17 in Tuscaloosa and then proceeded to drop 143 points in their next two wins. They rolled up more rushing yards and touchdowns in the first three games than the entire previous season. It appeared the 2025 transfer round was a hit, and that 2024 was a fluke after all.

Then ACC play started. Florida State lost in double overtime and Virginia recreated their historic 1995 upset with the wildest field storming of the year. Then they lost again (Miami by six), and again

(Pittsburgh by 3), and again (Stanford by 7).

The hot start and Top 10 ranking quickly collapsed into a second-straight losing season. Penalties and a goal line stand cost them the Stanford game, two fumbled punts flipped the NC State loss, and their comeback bids fell short after trailing 18-0 to Clemson and 28-3 to Miami. Then, with bowl eligibility at stake, they lost to rival Florida with the interim-led Gators dropping 40 points and a 266-yard explosion by their back.

Florida State is now on a 4-17 run against Power 4 opponents – 3-13 vs. the ACC – and the 7- 17 overall record is the school’s worst two-year run in 50 seasons.

This latest transfer haul ranked #30 with just three four-stars and it snapped Norvell’s four- year streak of top ten transfer classes. Then shortly after Talent Acquisition season, offensive coordinator Gus Malzahn stepped down.
pick_six_2026.offense:
It may ring hollow to Florida State fans, but FSU was statistically better than their record showed last year. Even at 5-7 overall, they finished #25 in my opponent-adjusted Game Grader formula, up from second-worst 67th of 68 in 2024. They out-gained 10 of 12 opponents, had four one-score losses, and each win was by 14+ points.

Malzahn’s influence, plus transfer wins all across the offense, led to the nation’s #1 most improved offense from 2024 to 2025. Florida State was one of just five Power 4 offenses to average 200+ rushing and 200+ passing for an overall #10 finish in my opponent-adjusted stat.

Norvell is taking back the play-calling and promoted receivers coach Tim Harris to coordinator. They plan to tweak some pass concepts and formations, but they are both Malzahn disciples and the offense will not have drastic scheme changes.

Just two starters return. 6’6 Duce Robinson posted a 1,000-yard season and earned first-team All- ACC honors, track-speed Micahi Danzy averaged a Power 4-best 21 yards/catch, and both star receivers are back. Lawayne McCoy was another breakout star but he transferred to Louisville. Jayvan Boggs moves up into the starting slot role, and another round of young four-stars fills out the rotation with Tae’Shaun Gelsey and Top200 true freshmen Devin Carter and Jasen Lopez.

Quarterback Tommy Castellanos graduated and like the overall team, he had extreme highs and lows in 2025. He threw for 15 touchdowns, ran for nine more, but tossed nine picks. Florida State went back to the portal and signed the #30 ranked transfer QB Ashton Daniels who started three games at Auburn, including a 31/44 353-yard win against Vanderbilt. He was a two-year starter at Stanford before that, but finished dead last in the ACC in QB Rating both seasons. Norvell named him the starter after spring.

It was a strange rotation week-to-week at running back, but FSU signed a headliner in Texas starter Tre Wisner who rushed for 1,600 yards the past two years. Wisner and near-five-star Ousmane Kromah should get the bulk of carries.

Last year the staff signed a bunch of Power 4 starters to rebuild the offensive line and it worked, surging from bottom 10 to top 10 in OL Run Push. All five starters are gone, including All-ACC headliners Luke Petitbon and Richie Leonard. This cycle they reloaded with another round of starters, though just two are from the Power 4: four-star Xavier Chaplin (Auburn) and center Bradyn Joiner (Purdue). Paul Bowling (Troy) started all year as a true freshman, Nate Pabst (Bowling Green) started 38 games and earned All-MAC, and Chimdia Nwaiwu (FCS SFA) was All- Southland. Herb Hand is an elite offensive line coach and with this high experience level there shouldn’t be too much of a drop off.

Randy Pittman earned All-ACC honors but transferred out to SMU, former Top100 Landen Thomas steps up into the starting tight end spot along with Desirrio Riles (East Carolina).
pick_six_2026.defense:
Though not as drastic as the offense, the defense improved in all 17 stat categories under Tony White’s 3-3-5 scheme.

Seven starters are gone, and in total 12 defenders transferred out to other Power 4 programs. Yet they only signed four of their own, and just one four-star, for a net loss in the portal on this side of the ball.

Florida State loses both starting safeties Edwin Joseph (Ole Miss) and tackle-leader Earl Little (Ohio State) to the portal, and All-ACC corner Jerry Wilson graduated. They were able to pull back the other two starters from the portal – corner Ja’Bril Rawls and safety Ashlynd Barker – and then sign new starters of their own. Ma’Khi Jones (Duke) had a breakout freshman season, and Nehemiah Chandler (South Alabama) and Karson Hobbs (Notre Dame) had three-star transfer grades.

Of the five linebackers in the rotation, just two return in Blake Nichelson and Omar Graham. The staff signed the Sun Belt’s tackle leader Chris Jones (Southern Miss) and four-star Mikai Gbayor (UNC) who had his best season in White’s scheme at Nebraska in 2024.

Six defensive linemen transferred out to Power 4 rosters but they were able to retain the Desir twins. Mandrell Desir earned All-Freshman honors at defensive tackle with a team-high 6.5 sacks, while his brother Darryll returns at edge. Rylan Kennedy (Texas A&M) is projected at the other end spot, and Deante McCray and Daniel Lyons are the vets in the middle. While two-time all-league Darrell Jackson graduates, four-star nose tackle Kevin Wynn flashed high upside as a true freshman.

pick_six_2026.outlook: Mississippi State has some momentum heading into 2026 with a revamped defense, a proven coordinator who knows how to build a defense in Starkville, and solid player retention. Now it’s all about whether their home-grown, top-rated quarterback can rise to stardom and elevate the program back to bowl season.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
When Jeff Lebby was hired he vowed to bring an exciting, explosive brand of football to Starkville. In the second week of the season, he fulfilled his promise.

Trailing #11 Arizona State in the final thirty seconds, Blake Shapen heaved a bomb to Brenen Thompson who ran in for the game-winning score. Fans poured onto the field to celebrate the program’s first non-conference Top 15 win since 1991. “What an atmosphere, what an evening … that is Davis Wade Stadium at its finest,” Lebby said.

Mississippi State got to 4-0 for the first time since the Dak Prescott 2014 season, but when they hit SEC play they fumbled through multiple blown opportunities. MSU led Tennessee by seven with two minutes left but then lost in overtime, lost to Florida by two points with a controversial referee decision on a field goal, and then blew a 31-14 lead to Texas. Close but no cigar.

Finally some late-game magic broke their way, as Shapen led a final- minute drive to beat Arkansas 38-35 and snap the program’s 16-game SEC losing streak. The defense collapsed down the stretch allowing Georgia and Missouri to both rush for 300+ yards in blowout losses, Ole Miss won the Egg Bowl by 19, and then with a bonus bowl invitation despite the 5-7 record Wake Forest won 43-29.

Lebby is off to a 7-18 start – 1-15 in SEC play – and has been part of the program’s worst three-year stretch in decades. Entering his third season, Lebby remains optimistic: “we have great young players in our locker room who are excited to be here and continue to grow this thing the right way.”

Far from just coach-speak, the statement held true as Mississippi State did a nice job retaining their starters – only the offensive line had defections. They won the Player Retention portion of the offseason, found a dual-threat quarterback to build around, and brought back a familiar face to fix the defense.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Lebby’s offensive scheme was as-advertised. Mississippi State ranked #21 in my explosive passing category, #31 in yards per attempt, and #30 of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted passing stat.

Shapen bounced back from his 2024 injury and led the offense well with a 64% completion rate, 15 touchdowns (8 picks) and a #9 finish in SEC QB Rating. Entering the season finale, Lebby made the tough decision to bench Shapen in favor of true freshman Kamario Taylor, the highest-rated quarterback commit in school history.

The Noxubee County legend was used in some packages throughout the season, but in his first full start against Ole Miss, Taylor exploded for 173 rushing yards on 20 carries including a scramble and highlight- reel touchdown run. Taylor finished slightly ahead of Shapen in QB Rating and added in the rushing threat with 458 yards and eight touchdowns on the ground.

With Shapen graduated, Taylor is now the face of the program. The staff added former Vanderbilt and App State starter AJ Swann plus a wildcard in former Top100 Jaden Rashada (Sacramento State).

Fluff Bothwell was the lead back with 677 yards, 4.8 per carry, and returns as the clear #1 for 2026. Davon Booth graduated, so former four-star Xavier Gayten moves up to the #2 spot.

Thompson’s 58-yard game-winner against Arizona State was indicative of his entire season. He averaged a high 18.5 yards/catch which ranked second-best in the SEC, and his 1,054 yards broke Makai Polk’s single-season school record. Thompson graduated but the room remains a strength with the return of Anthony Evans -- 67 catches, 831 yards – and former Top100 Ayden Williams. Sanfrisco Magee was a spring hero and surged up into the top rotation. Plus, the staff signed Missouri’s #3 receiver Marquis Johnson who earned a four-star transfer grade, and speedy blue-chipper Zion Ragins (Oklahoma). Johnson will step into Thompson’s role as the downfield vertical threat.

Tight end Seydou Traore graduated and Mississippi State is now relying on four-star true freshman Zayion Cotton or Oregon State backup Riley Williams.

The offensive line struggled last year by allowing 40 sacks and ranking in the national bottom five in Pass Protection (#131). Their success in the run game was not much better, with a #106 rank in yards/carry and #59 mark in my OL Run Push. Taylor’s athleticism should help mitigate these issues but this remains an area of uncertainty.

It was also the only position group that got hit with transfer portal departures. Four linemen that started games last year transferred out and all landed on Power 4 rosters. Center Canon Boone is the only returning starter but they do get back right tackle Blake Steen who was an original starter injured in the first game. From there, it’s Pick Your Transfer as they added seven from Power 4 programs plus two top JUCO’s. LJ Prudhomme was projected as an Arkansas starting guard before the move, DJ Chester and Tyler Miller are both former Top200 LSU transfers, and Chester has 14 starts under his belt.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Lebby fired coordinator Coleman Hutzler and then made the shocking move to hire back his predecessor Zach Arnett. After the initial shock wore off, Arnett does fit the role well. Remember, he led three strong defenses here from 2020-22 that ranked #13, #36, and #14 in my opponent-adjusted numbers. His 2023 season as the head coach was a flop, but his three coordinator seasons before do the talking.

Arnett runs a 3-3-5 base scheme that is aggressive yet disciplined at the same time. In his three coordinator seasons, Mississippi State ranked in the SEC’s top five in both turnovers and limiting explosive plays.

That’s exactly what the doctor ordered after the 2025 unit failed in pass rush (#125 Negative Play Rate) with just 21 sacks, failed to stop the run (#117 yards/carry), and couldn’t contain explosive plays (#105).

Mississippi State brings back the bulk of their front six, with 10 of the top 14 linemen and linebackers returning. Will Whitson is back from an ACL injury and should be the top pass rusher along with former Top200 Amaree Williams edge (Florida State). Jaray Bledsoe and Trevion Williams are back at defensive tackle, Kalvin Dinkins and 6’5 350-pounder Diesel Moye return at nose tackle. The staff signed another Top200 tackle Dealyn Evans (Texas A&M) who should elevate the room.

Arnett’s linebackers led the SEC in tackles in consecutive seasons and he inherits another strong core here with middle backer Jalen Smith and weakside backer Zakari Tillman both returning. Tyler Lockhart was the top recruit of their 2025 signing class and lived up to the hype by earning SEC All-Freshman last year.

Isaac Smith was again the face of the defense and he returns for a third season. Smith led the SEC in tackles in 2024, starred again in 2025 as a backer/safety hybrid, and given the exodus of graduating senior safeties it appears Smith will stay in the backfield. The staff added a pair of SEC veterans Jardin Gilbert (LSU) and Kendel Dolby (Oklahoma) who combined for 31 starts. Kelley Jones earned third-team All-SEC at corner and was getting NFL Draft buzz but decided to return for a final season. Quentin Taylor (Iowa State) started six games there last year due to injuries ahead of him, and he’ll battle former Top200 Jamroc Grimsley (Florida) here.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Minnesota was an interesting case study for Game Grader. Their five close-margin Big Ten wins were against teams with a combined 9-46 league record, so yes Minnesota went 8-5 but placed down at 55th in Game Grader (13th in the Big Ten).

They return program stars in Lindsey, Taylor, and Smith but now the schedule reverses and they draw six of the Big Ten’s top nine. Statistically they were more like a six-win team last year, and that is where they are projected in 2026.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
In his ninth season, head coach PJ Fleck notched another eight-win season and winning record in Big Ten play for the fourth time in five years. That makes this the best extended run since the 1960s when Minnesota last won a national title.

They gave the fans in Huntingdon Bank Stadium plenty to cheer for. Minnesota went a perfect 7-0 at home for the first time since 1967 and did so with a disruptive defense and last-second resiliency.

The Minnesota defense set two school records by holding Northwestern State to just 42 total yards and then swarming Nebraska for nine sacks. Two-way sensation Koi Perich took back a game- winning Pick Six to beat Purdue, and redshirt freshman quarterback Drake Lindsey led late game-winning drives to beat Rutgers and Michigan State.

Stacking winning seasons is an achievement in such a deep league, but from a statistical standpoint, not all “8-5 seasons” are equal.

All five of Minnesota’s conference wins came against teams with losing Big Ten records (9-46 combined), they were outgained in four of them, and three were within a score. Their five losses were by an average margin of 24 points/game including blowouts against Iowa (41-3) and Playoff teams Ohio State (42-3) and Oregon (42-13).

This ended up as an interesting case-study for my opponent-adjusted Game Grader formula. Despite the 8-5 record, Minnesota finished just 55th of 68 Power 4 in Game Grader – their worst ranking in the entire Fleck era.

Then the program was stunned with the transfer departure of Perich -- the two-time All-Big Ten, homegrown face of the program – who took Oregon’s offer. There are thousands of FBS transfers each cycle, but this one was unbelievable.

The staff was able to rally a respectable transfer haul of their own, ranking 10th in the Big Ten, and are building around Lindsey for 2026 and beyond.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Like the pessimistic outlook from Game Grader, my opponent-adjusted offense stats dropped Minnesota all the way to second-worst in Power 4. It was one of the least explosive offenses in both long-yardage rushing (#128) and passing (#131). The run game finished #117 in yards/carry and averaged just over 100 per game (#128) and it was even worse in the handful of games when star running back Darius Taylor was injured.

They did find a bright spot at quarterback in Lindsey. The first-time starter exceeded expectations and took care of the ball with just six interceptions against 18 touchdowns. He showed off a strong arm, led several fourth-quarter scoring drives, and “took really good command of the offense,” per Fleck.

Lindsey returns and should get a second-year bonus. He noted pre-snap reads and audibles were points of emphasis for him this offseason, as well as pocket elusiveness. He finished 11th in the Big Ten in QB Rating – tied with fellow freshman Bryce Underwood (Michigan) – and that should improve in 2026.

Leading receiver Le’Meke Brockington graduated, and the entire second-tier of backups is gone. Last year’s second and third options Jalen Smith and Javon Tracy are both back after combining for 65 catches, 873 yards, and 10 touchdowns. The staff signed a big one in former five-star Perry Thompson (Auburn) who should have an instant impact in the slot. Zion Steptoe (Tulsa) could help with the explosiveness issue as the vertical threat led the AAC in average depth of target last year.

Taylor returns as the workhorse back. In 2024 he was just short of 1,000 yards, and when healthy last year he averaged just under 100 per game. Taylor closed with back-to-back 100-yard games against Wisconsin and New Mexico and the offense was noticeably different with him in the backfield.

He could use some help from the trenches. The offensive line ranked just #123 in my OL Run Push stat and will be rebuilding the right side of the line.
