Tackle Brendan Flakes and end Michael Kilbane slot in as veteran starters, and the staff added a trio of three-star transfers: Jamaal Johnson (UCF), Dominic Kirks (Ohio State) and tackle Glory Stephen-Wangboje (Sacred Heart).

Multi-year starter Mac Uihlein graduated after a 100-tackle, four-interception season. Braydon Brus had 81 tackles in his first starting season and returns at weakside backer. Kobie McKinzie (Oklahoma) earned a four- star transfer grade and should start in Uihlein’s spot.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Other programs signed flashier transfer portal hauls, but Maryland’s wins were on the high school recruiting trail, and more importantly, roster retention of emerging stars. Locksley retained all ten key players, and their pass rush should be elite.

Maryland draws both of the bottom Big Ten teams Rutgers and Purdue, and gets three mid-tier league teams at home in College Park (UCLA, Illinois, and Wisconsin). They are a step up from the bottom three, but have not
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
After a 4-8 season in 2024, and an exodus of players to the transfer portal, Maryland put their future in the hands of a core of highly- touted freshmen. New quarterback Malik Washington started fast and Maryland beat Florida Atlantic, Northern Illinois, and Towson to extend their nation-best nonconference win streak of 18 games. Washington’s 773 yards were the most by any Power 4 true freshman in his first three college games since 2018.

Then in the Big Ten opener Maryland beat Wisconsin 27-10 behind a pair of Washington touchdown passes and a 46-yard Pick Six from star safety Jalen Huskey.

From 4-8 to a 4-0 start – the expectations quickly shifted and Maryland was considered a surprise breakout team. They took a 20- 0 lead on Washington, but the Huskies rattled off 24 unanswered over the final quarter-plus.

Two more blown leads ensued in losses to Nebraska (34-31) and UCLA (20-17) and the losses piled up from there. When the dust settled, it

was another 4-8 season for head coach Mike Locksley.

“This year was not good enough, we did not meet expectations that any of us set,” said Locksley. There were many shortcomings – an ineffective run game, dropped passes, a weak run defense – but extreme roster youth was the overarching theme.

The focus on roster retention became clear right away. Maryland shifted most of its roster budget away from the transfer portal market and instead kept their best young prospects at home in College Park. Back in December, Inside Maryland Sports listed their top ten most important players, and Locksley was able to retain all ten – an incredible feat given the extreme player movement nowadays.

All the growing pains of 2025 are set to pay dividends in 2026. Thanks to their strong retention, Maryland now has the second highest amount of returning production in Power 4.
pick_six_2026.offense:
The next move was to fix the run game. Maryland averaged just 104 yards per game (#124), 4.1 per carry (#89), and they ranked #128 in my Offensive Line Run Push. Locksley re-assigned Pep Hamilton to an analyst role and hired Clint Trickett to take over at offensive coordinator. Last year Trickett led Jacksonville State to a nine-win season thanks to a ground game that produced the nation’s rushing champ.

Washington is back under center after starting all 12 games as a true freshman. The high four-star threw for 2,963 yards, 17 touchdowns, 9 picks, and his 459 yards against Michigan State placed second on the school’s all-time leaderboard. Efficiency-wise, he has room to grow from a 57% completion rate and a #16 finish in the Big Ten in QB Rating. Maryland is all-in on Washington as their franchise quarterback and he should get the usual second-year starter bonus in 2026.

Nolan Ray entered as the feature back but was passed by DeJuan Williams who finished as the lead rusher with 501 yards. Williams was heavily featured in the pass game and posted the most receiving yards by a Maryland running back (426) since 2001. Williams is back, Ray transferred out to Boston College, and the staff signed Harry Dalton (USC) who was a four-star recruit in the 2025 class.

Heading into 2025, Maryland had to replace a pair of NFL-bound stars in Tai Felton and Kaden Prather. They certainly missed them, as this was one of Maryland’s weakest receiver rooms in recent memory, plagued by dropped balls and a lack of separation. The three starters – Octavian Smith, Jalil Farooq, and Shaleak Knotts – all depart, leaving a wide-open room for 2026.

Two former four-star recruits, Kaleb Webb and Zymear Smith, will compete for starting jobs with the pair of incoming transfers. Chris Durr was Wyoming’s top receiver, Na’eem Abdul-Rahim Gladding (Old Dominion) earned All-Sun Belt, and the two combined for 96 catches, 1,136 yards,

and 10 scores last year. Dorian Fleming finished second among Big Ten tight ends with 40 catches and is joined by former Terp Preston Howard who transferred back from Auburn.

The offensive line has been a weakness here for most of the Locksley era, and the 2025 line remained an issue – at least in the run game. Aided by Washington’s quick release, Maryland actually finished #1 in pass protection and allowed a sack on just 2% of pass attempts.

Three starting linemen are gone: Isaiah Wright, Aliou Bah (LSU) and their best one All-Big Ten Alan Herron. Maryland has returning starters in tackle Rahtrel Perry and center Michael Hershey, plus Top100 Jaylen Gilchrist who is back from a season-ending injury and should become an all- league star. Maryland threw their hat into the Jordan Seaton sweepstakes, but the #1 transfer lineman picked LSU. The only incoming transfer they signed was three-star Tellek Lockette (Texas State).
pick_six_2026.defense:
The roster retention on defense was a major win for the program. Maryland kept a pair of Freshman All-Americans plus a pair of All-Big Ten honorable mention defenders.

Defensive end Sidney Stewart set the school record for tackles-for-loss by a freshman (10.5), and former Top100 Zahir Mathis was named a semifinalist for the Shaun Alexander Freshman of the Year Award. This was already one of the best young pass rush duos in America, but then Maryland landed their biggest recruiting prize in school history in local five-star Zion Elee (St Frances Academy). Elee was rated as the #1 defensive end, and #5 overall prospect, in the entire 2026 class. That’s some serious firepower off the edges.

The interior needs a boost after the run defense collapsed. Maryland allowed six straight 190+ yard rushing games, and veteran Dillan Fontus transferred out to Syracuse. The 350-pounder Bryce Jenkins was a four-star recruit and is a potential star, plus the staff added three more Power 4 linemen in Lavon Johnson (Texas), Derrick LeBlanc (UCF), and Armon Parker (Washington).

They retained Daniel Wingate who posted the school’s first 100-tackle season since Tre Watson in 2018. Wingate is joined by Trey Reddick and four-star sophomore CJ Smith who posted 64 tackles last year.

Maryland ranked just 53rd of 68 Power 4 defenses in my opponent-adjusted stat – 52nd in pass defense – but they led the nation with 19 interceptions. Both transfer additions last cycle ended up as Big Ten honorable mention cornerbacks, and both Jamare Glasker and Dontay Joyner return for 2026. The do-it-all safety Jalen Huskey heads to the pros, but Lavain Scruggs returns at strong safety, and former blue-chipper Messiah Delhomme is ready for a starting role.

pick_six_2026.outlook: The Petrino hire should spark a broken offense, but UNC lost too many starters to the transfer portal to call for a usual second-year coach bonus. In fact, the schedule heats up and UNC draws just two of the ACC’s bottom
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Last offseason North Carolina went all-in on football. They finally made the big-dollar financial commitment to being a serious player in college football – and perhaps to position themselves for a conference move in the next round of Realignment Musical Chairs.

They hired six-time Super Bowl winning head coach Bill Belichick, signed 70+ new players, and were one of the top national stories heading into the 2025 season. UNC got ESPN’s Labor Day national television treatment and they took the opening possession right down for a touchdown. Chapel Hill was the epicenter of the football world.

Then reality hit. As InsideCarolina said, it was like the moment at the top of a rollercoaster before the free fall.

TCU scored 41 straight points and spoiled Belichick’s debut and national moment. The 48 points were the most ever allowed by a Belichick defense.

After a pair of non-Power 4 wins, UNC got blown out by coaching- change UCF 34-9 and again by Clemson 38-10. Their nation-worst red zone turnovers showed up in close losses to California and

Virginia, but bowl eligibility was still in play in November.

For the first time in nearly 40 years, UNC lost to all three in-state rivals – Wake Forest, Duke, and NC State – all in the same season. Even worse, they did so in back-to-back-to-back weeks to close out a 4-8 season.

This was always set up to be an experiment, and while the first year was a failure, there is still a shot at overall success. Belichick made the necessary move to fire offensive coordinator Freddie Kitchings after failing to score 28+ against a single FBS opponent. He then hired one of the top offensive minds in football: Bobby Petrino.

That’s a way to get fan attention back. Then UNC signed a massive recruiting class of 40 prospects, a haul that ranked #19 nationally (#3 ACC) and is packed with 12 four-stars. The recruiting/transfer balance suggests they are going for a longer-term build rather than a quick fix, and the schedule heats up in 2026, but the Big Belichick Experiment is far from dead.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Petrino’s top mantra for his offensive scheme is FTS: Feed The Studs. He designs his offense to the personnel strengths and has had success for decades. He is an elite playcaller and is able to scheme up a few wide-open explosive passes per game.

Last year was no different. As the offensive coordinator of a 2-10 Arkansas team, his side of the ball did its job, ranking in the top 25 of almost every stat category including 7 yards/play (#7), 5.7 yards/carry (#4), and #1 in rushing explosiveness. As an overall unit, Arkansas was #2 in my opponent-adjusted offense rankings.

It’s quite the contrast to UNC’s output last year: #120 in scoring, #131 in total offense, and a bottom five mark in explosiveness.

Like last offseason, the roster turnover is extreme with just three starters returning on offense and rebuilds at every position aside from running back.

Three backs had 60+ carries and two of them return including their top rusher Demon June who led the pack with a 5.5 yards/carry average. Benjamin Hall returns and the staff added former four- star recruit Kaleb Jackson (LSU) to complete the new trio.

Gio Lopez was the staff’s handpicked quarterback last cycle and he failed to get the offense going. Lopez finished 14th of the 17 ACC starters in QB Rating, UNC was #121 in yards/attempt, #133 in explosive passing and rarely tried anything downfield. Lopez and backup veteran Max Johnson both transferred out, leaving behind a two-man battle between incoming transfers Billy Edwards (Wisconsin) and Miles O’Neill (Texas A&M).

Edwards put up 2,881 yards and 15 touchdowns as Maryland’s starter in 2024 before a season- ending injury cut his Wisconsin career short. He’s got the Power 4 experience, while O’Neill has the higher recruiting upside as a former four-star who Petrino personally recruited to A&M during his one season there.

UNC retained their top receiver Jordan Shipp but lost their next three wideouts and top two tight ends. Trech Kekahuna started eight games in the slot for Wisconsin and had all offseason developing chemistry with Edwards. Mason Humphrey (Lehigh) has a 6’4 frame and caught 80 passes for 1,237 yards the past two years at the FCS level. CJ Sadler should get reps immediately after a video-game 32-touchdown senior season earned him a Top200 four-star billing this cycle.

Tight ends Jake Johnson (Auburn) and Connor Cox (Virginia) transferred out but the staff pulled in a pair of former blue-chip recruits that were stuck on crowded rosters in Jelani Thurman (Ohio State) and Jordan Washington (Texas).

UNC loses 182 combined career starts from five veteran linemen. Original starting center Christo Kelly and starting guard Aidan Banfield are both back after their September injuries. Jordan Hall is back at left tackle as a projected starter. Petrino brought his starting right tackle Jacqawn McRoy (Arkansas) with him, and then the staff signed Andrew Threatt (Charleston Southern), a three-year starter from the FCS level.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Belichick’s defense posted average stats – 29th of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted stat – but got stronger as the season went on. In the same stat, UNC was 50th of 68 in the first half of the season, but was 12th over the final six games.

Eight starters depart and several of them transferred out with high rankings.

All three linebackers are gone with Khmori House (Arkansas) and Mikai Gbayor (Florida State) both grading as four-star transfers. The staff backfilled with a top FCS tackler Peyton Seelmann (Richmond) and a multi-year veteran in Derek McDonald (Syracuse) who missed most of 2025 with an injury. A pair of Top250 recruits could contend right away: DQ Forkpa and Calvin Thomas.

Three of the top defensive linemen transferred out – Tyler Thompson (Louisville), D’Antre Robinson (Oregon), and CJ Mims (Texas A&M) – and end Smith Vilbert graduated. At least this unit retained its top star with the ACC’s sack leader Melkart Abou Jaoude back and poised for an All-ACC run. Leroy Jackson and Isaiah Johnson both had 300+ snaps at the interior spots, Xavier Lewis flashed as a true freshman, and they signed two Power 4 ends Tarvorise Brown (Florida) and Jaylen Harvey (Penn State).

Four starters are gone from the secondary. Nickelback Kaleb Cost is the only full-time starter back, but Jaiden Patterson started half the year at corner after Thaddeus Dixon was injured. Cost and Patterson are joined by rotational backups Greg Smith and Coleman Bryson, a three-star transfer Ade Willie (Michigan State) and a Top100 2026 commit Kenton Dopson at corner.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
This is a textbook rebuilding year for Arkansas. Silverfield’s transfer strategy on offense centered on production from lower tiers, while the defense signed high-upside recruits who lack game experience.

Next recruiting and transfer cycle will be a key indicator for Arkansas moving forward, because in the NIL era they have struggled in both categories as well as player retention.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Trey Biddy’s “Walk & Talk” postgame reaction segments are well-known in the SEC footprint and his video following the season finale spoke volumes. He turned 360 degrees showing an empty, but state-of-the-art DWR Razorback Stadium – “look at this place, this is home to a two-win football team, two and ten, in this place.”

The frustration was palpable.

Not only was this Arkansas’ third 0-8 SEC season since 2018, this one had an extra layer of pain given their five one-score losses. They missed two field goals and lost to Ole Miss by six, fumbled the ball at the goal-line with a minute left when a field goal would have beaten Memphis, and lost another shootout against Texas A&M.

The offense posted Top 10 stats and moved the ball well but froze up in the red zone and in crunch time. Arkansas held fourth-quarter leads against Auburn and Mississippi State but lost them both. Against Auburn, the offense had turnovers on the final four drives. They actually went backwards, negative 15 total yards, on the final three drives against Mississippi State.

A day after suffering a 56-13 blowout by Notre Dame, Arkansas fired Sam Pittman. He delivered three winning seasons, a Top 25 nine-win season in 2021, an emotional win over Texas, but ended up below .500 with a 32-34 overall record (14-29 vs. SEC).

For all the good moments and lovable quotes, Pittman’s tenure extended the program’s decade-long drought without a winning season in SEC play. Player retention was a recurring issue. Each offseason, star players left for bigger deals which caused an over-reliance on reloading the roster via the transfer portal.

Bobby Petrino took over as the interim but they went 0-7 to close the season.

In the most crowded coaching carousel the sport has ever seen, Arkansas emerged with Memphis head coach Ryan Silverfield. In six years there, Silverfield went 50-25 overall – 29-9 in the last three years – with two bowl wins over Power 4 opponents. His Memphis squad even stole a last-minute win over Arkansas in September.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Hidden behind a 2-10 record, this was an extremely productive and explosive offense. In my opponent- adjusted rankings, Arkansas was the #2 offense in Power 4 and #1 in rushing. Petrino’s scheme opened up wide-open running lanes, dynamic Taylen Green ripped off explosive scrambles, and they found themselves in plenty of shootouts.

The problem was executing in crunch time. They blew four fourth-quarter leads, and went 0-6 in games decided in the final frame. Green accumulated 27 total touchdowns, 3,400+ total yards, but failed to deliver a single fourth-quarter win.

Green went pro, their 1,000-yard back Mike Washington graduated, and it will be a nearly full rebuild in Silverfield’s transition. On offense, four starters are back and he signed seven Non-AQ starters plus three more transfers who were former Top200 blue-chippers.

Arkansas’ first quarterback battle since 2019 will continue into the fall. KJ Jackson was Green’s backup last year and started the season-finale against Missouri. He apparently has a slight lead over AJ Hill, the 6’5 Top200 redshirt freshman who followed Silverfield from Memphis.

Braylen Russell rushed for 286 yards here last year and is joined by Memphis starter Sutton Smith and Top200 Jasper Parker (Michigan). Smith went for 669 yards (6.6 per carry) and brings elusiveness and home-run ability, like he flashed on his 64-yard touchdown to beat Arkansas.

Starting receivers O’Mega Blake and Raylen Sharpe graduated, Jalen Brown was thrown off the team in April, leaving CJ Brown as the lone 2025 returner. Ismael Cisse was poised to earn a starting job last spring before an injury knocked him out – look for a bounce-back season in 2026. Courtney Crutchfield was a Top100 super-recruit who still has potential for a breakout. The staff added three Non-AQ starters led by Chris Marshall (Boise State) who earned a four-star transfer grade after placing second in the Mountain West with an explosive 19.1 per-catch average.

All-SEC tight end Rohan Jones is gone but Jaden Platt surged late in the season. Matt Adcock (Memphis) caught three touchdowns last year, and Ty Lockwood (Boston College) still has untapped potential.

The offensive line was dominant in the run game, finishing #1 nationally in my OL Run Push metric. Petrino mixed gap and zone schemes, while Silverfield’s spread offense will be almost exclusively zone blocking. Their pass protection remained a liability, with consecutive finishes outside the Top 100 in Sack Rate. The left side of the line was the strength, with All-SEC tackle Fernando Carmona and guard Corey Robinson, but both graduated. E’Marion Harris also transferred out to Oklahoma with high transfer marks.

Caden Kitler and Kobe Branham are returning starters and the staff added five non-Power 4 linemen via the portal. Bryant Williams (Louisiana) is the headliner and was ranked a Top 10 tackle transfer this cycle and Malachi Breland (Memphis) was a starting guard for this staff last year. Recruiting rankings aren’t everything, but it’s worth noting that Arkansas has zero former four-star prospects on the line two-deep: 0/10.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Arkansas couldn’t stop anybody last year. The defense posted bottom ten marks in almost every stat category, most importantly in scoring (#129), QB Rating (#125), and both explosive rushing (#124) and passing (#131).

Silverfield hired Ron Roberts to install his 3-4 base scheme. Roberts has 17 years of coordinator experience – most recently at Florida (below average rankings), Auburn, and Baylor (Top 10 in 2021) – and is credited with innovations like the disguised blitzes and simulated pressures that have been so effective recently.

Just two starters return, and on this side of the ball the staff focused more on adding high-upside, though unproven, former blue-chip transfers.

The defensive line is packed with seven former Top200 prospects, including All-SEC Quincy Rhodes, Hunter Osborne (Virginia), Carlon Jones (USC), and Xadavien Sims (Oregon). Off the edge, three

transfers are all starter-caliber with Top100’s Jamonta Waller (Auburn) and Charlie Collins, plus Kentucky starter Steven Soles.

With Xavian Sorey and Stephen Dix gone, Bradley Shaw moves up to the starting middle linebacker role and incoming Ja’Quavion Smith (FCS Howard) was a spring hero.

Khmori House (North Carolina) earned All-ACC honorable mention as a linebacker but the staff moved him to their hybrid “star” role. Safety Miguel Mitchell is the only starter back in the secondary, and the staff added three Power 4 starters – Carter Stoutmire (Colorado), Christian Harrison (Cincinnati) and La’Khi Roland (Maryland) – plus a four- star transfer in All-AAC Jahiem Johnson (Tulane).

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Michigan State went with the “Hire the Opposite” approach and brought Pat Fitzgerald back to the Big Ten. They also flipped their transfer strategy to bring in experienced players from the non-AQ tier: college production over Signing Day hype.

The Megaphone Trophy returns with Notre Dame back on the schedule, but that means they need to find four league wins to earn a bowl bid. This is a program rebuilding year that should pay dividends in 2027.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
After hitting rock bottom in 2023, Michigan State hired Jonathan Smith to rebuild the program in the same way he turned his alma mater Oregon State from punching bag to the Top 25. The 5-7 transition year – with a signature win over Iowa -- was understandable, but the lack of progress in his second season quickly warmed up the hot seat.

Michigan State opened up with a 3-0 start, including a wild double- overtime shootout win over Boston College, but their Big Ten troubles returned. They lost eight straight league games, the first five by double-digits, and two others with blown leads in the final minutes. Looking back, the 38-13 loss to a 1-4 UCLA team was the point of no return for the Smith era.

In a classic “hire the opposite” move, Michigan State fired the calm, reserved former West Coast quarterback, and hired the fiery, passionate, Midwestern linebacker.

Pat Fitzgerald won two Big Ten division titles, posted nine winning seasons, and brought his alma mater Northwestern to four New Year’s Day bowls. He led their golden age of football, was fired in the aftermath of a hazing scandal, and was eventually vindicated with a wrongful termination lawsuit and settlement.

With his name cleared, Fitzgerald spent the past two seasons studying the modern era – NIL, transfer portal, roster retention, player analytics – and is fired up for the opportunity.

He certainly won the opening press conference, with countless one-liners including “toughness was born here in Michigan State football.”

Then the school received a massive $400 million commitment with most of it going towards the athletic department’s new “For Sparta” fundraising campaign. That financial boost may help with talent acquisition in future cycles, but it didn’t lead to a program-changing explosion in this transfer round.

Fitzgerald made it clear he wants college production over potential, and it became the first MSU transfer class with more players from the non-Power 4 levels than the Power 4. The strategy has merits, but their class ranked outside the national Top 50, 14th in the 18-team Big Ten: 27 transfers, zero four-stars.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Fitzgerald hired Nick Sheridan to lead the offense. Holding their scheme close to the vest, it’s been described as multiple formations, variable tempos, 11, 12, and 13 personnel. Sheridan was on the Alabama staff last year that resorted to a pass-heavy approach due to a lack of a run push. Before that he was with Curt Cignetti at Indiana. We won’t know what his 2026 scheme looks like until kickoff.

Aidan Chiles was Smith’s handpicked quarterback but midway through the year he was benched (and then injured) in favor of Alessio Milivojevic. Chiles transferred out to Northwestern, and Milivojevic is the face of the program now after a strong November as the starter. He completed 64% of passes for 1,267 yards, 10 touchdowns, and just three picks, and his QB Rating would have placed ninth in the Big Ten.

The staff added Cam Fancher, a veteran with 28 starts across three FBS schools, to backup Milivojevic.

Tackle Conner Moore is the only other returning starter, and the starting lineup and two-deep will be transfer-heavy. Three linemen graduated and a fourth, Stanton Ramil, transferred out to Auburn. It could be four incoming transfers rounding out the starting line with FCS All-American Trent Fraley (North Dakota State) at center, highly-touted Ben Murawski (UConn) at guard, and Nick Sharpe (South Carolina) and Robert Wright (Georgia Southern) joining Moore.

Leading rusher Makhi Frazier transferred to Ole Miss, but it remains a deep room with the return of short-yardage back Brandon Tullis and three impact transfers. Cam Edwards (UConn) has accumulated 3,000+ total yards and 31 touchdowns and is the likely starter. Marvis Parrish (Western Kentucky) was C-USA All-Freshman, and Jaziun Patterson (Iowa) is a Big Ten vet.

Their top three pass-catchers all earned Big Ten honors, but all three are gone. Nick Marsh went to Indiana as a Top 10 transfer receiver and Omari Kelly and tight end Jack Velling both graduated.

Chrishon McCray was the third receiver and steps up into the lead role. The staff added two high- potential players stuck in crowded rooms with KK Smith (Notre Dame) and Fredrick Moore (Michigan) both grading as three-star transfers. Top250 Samson Gash was the #1 receiver recruit in the state of Michigan and could earn playing time right away as a true freshman.

At Northwestern, Fitzgerald coined the term “Super Back” for the do-it-all tight end, H-back, fullback hybrids. Carson Gulker (Ferris State) fits the term perfectly after scoring 73 touchdowns – 50 rushing, 16 passing, and 7 receiving – in various roles on four national title teams.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Fitzgerald retained coordinator Joe Rossi, and then added a fan favorite in Max Bullough, the All- American who played on the peak Mark Dantonio MSU teams from 2011-2013.

This side of the ball needs help after a bottom ten finish in my opponent-adjusted ranking, but like the offense, it will be transfer-heavy.

The pass defense was torched all season -- #117 in opponent QB Rating – and their top six defensive backs are gone. That doesn’t count Nikai Martinez whose year was cut short with an injury, but is back as the top safety for 2026. Aveon Grose had the game-sealing pick in the Maryland win and is projected at the other safety spot. Corner Tre Bell transferred in after starting for Iowa State, and Charles Brantley returned to Michigan State where he earned All-Big Ten honors in 2024 before getting stuck in a deep Miami secondary in 2025. Michael Richard (Louisiana Tech) brings two years of starting experience to the room.

Jordan Hall led the team in tackles, earned All-Big Ten honors, and returns to lead the defense in 2026. The next three backers are gone, but the staff brought in two with heavy college experience in All-MAC Dion Crawford (Buffalo) and former Maryland starter Caleb Wheatland.

The line got hit hard with portal exits, with Jalen Thompson, Alex VanSumeren, and David Santiago all landing on Power 4 rosters. Isaac Smith is a returning starter at edge, Ben Roberts was playing well at defensive tackle before a midseason injury, and Derrick Simmons is a former Top250 four-star ready for a breakout. Eli Coenen (Illinois) will also contend for a starting spot in the interior.

Unlike most hires, Fitzgerald doesn’t have a legion of players following him from his former school. But even after several years, he was able to reconnect with Kenny Soares, who ended up as a starter at NC State and could move into an edge role here.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Cincinnati finished #11 in the Big 12 in my Game Grader last season, and now 17 starters are gone – including their dynamic star quarterback – but the next wave of starters are mostly from the lower tiers (non-AQ, FCS, DII). Cincinnati is also second-worst in five-year recruiting so their talent level keeps them out of title contention.

They draw the bottom two teams – Colorado and Iowa State – but also six of the top eight. Bowl eligibility may come down to their mid-October road trip to West Virginia, a Big East style swing game.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
In 2024 Cincinnati had five tries to clinch bowl eligibility but went 0-5 to close out a losing season.

Again in 2025 they started fast, riding their dual-threat quarterback and powerful offensive line to wins over Kansas, UCF, and a ranked Iowa State. This time, Scott Satterfield’s squad finished the job and clinched their ticket to bowl season and the locker room celebrated accordingly.

Cincinnati got to 7-1 with their longest win streak since their 2021 Playoff run and even cracked the AP Top 20.

But once the calendar flipped to November, it was a similar finish to their 2024 skid. Brendan Sorsby was held to just a 33% completion rate and the defense could not slow down Utah in the 45-14 loss. Then the turnovers continued in a close 30-24 loss to Arizona. Kicker Stephen Rusnak was perfect most of the year but missed three field goals in a 12- point loss to BYU.

Then the wheels fell off. TCU scored at-will in the 45-23 rout, and in the rain-soaked bowl game, Navy’s option attack dominated 35-13. Another

year, another five-game skid to close the season.

The offseason hit hard right away with Sorsby breaking his contract and transferring out to Texas Tech as the top-rated transfer of the entire cycle. Cincinnati sued him, and was embroiled in another off-field controversy and lost his college eligibility.

Sorsby is the headline departure, but in total Cincinnati loses 17 starters – eight from the offense, and nine from the defense -- and Satterfield is going with a double coordinator change to top it off.

Cincinnati has done well with scouting and turning non-AQ and FCS transfers into All-Big 12 stars and NFL draft picks. Their “Moneyball” approach will be put to the test again this cycle.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Cincinnati signed a pair of starting quarterbacks from the lower levels in JC French (Georgia Southern) and Liam O’Brien (Penn). French emerged as the leader after compiling 5,760 passing yards, 37 passing touchdowns, and another 554 rushing yards over the past two seasons. His dual-threat skillset fits the usual Satterfield offensive scheme, but French will need to improve on his passing efficiency after placing sixth in the Sun Belt in QB Rating last year, and ninth in 2024.

French says he was drawn to Cincinnati because of their heavy RPO and play-action usage. That scheme should remain the same even with the coordinator change as Satterfield hired from within and will retain the playcalling role himself like usual.

Tawee Walker and Evan Pryor combined for 1,231 yards with Walker earning All-Big 12 honors. Walker graduated, Pryor transferred out to Florida, and they have a new cast of backs for 2026. Zion Johnson got the bowl game start, surged in spring ball as the most explosive of the bunch, and Satterfield called him the starter. Three transfers will battle for carries: All-Sun Belt Zylan Perry (Louisiana), and Power 4 backups Gi’Bran Payne (Notre Dame) and Cole Tabb (Stanford).

The receiver room is another complete rebuild after the top three all departed. Cyrus Allen was second-team All-Big 12 after placing third nationally with 13 touchdown catches, Caleb Goodie transferred out to Missouri, and Jeff Caldwell posted one of the best NFL Combine performances of all-time.

JV Gibson (Oklahoma) emerged as the new #1 receiver in spring. Gibson was limited with injuries last year at Oklahoma but his breakout year was in 2024 with 70 catches at the FCS level. Cade Wolford (Kent State) averaged an insane 27 yards/catch last year to earn All-MAC honors and the staff may get him carries in the run game. Larenzo Fenner (South Dakota) had 15 touchdowns in the FCS, Malachi Henry (Central Arkansas) had 10, and DII Flynn Schiele (Colorado School of Mines) earned a four-star transfer grade.

Isaiah Johnson was in the rotation last year and should move up to the starting lineup with Gibson and one of the other newcomers. Transfers from the FCS or DII may seem to be roulette chips, but Cincinnati has an excellent track record recently.

Joe Royer continued Cincinnati’s tight end legacy – the All-Big 12 end was drafted in the fifth round. Gavin Grover is next in line after getting 250 snaps as a true freshman and he was one yard shy of a touchdown against Kansas.

Finally some returning starters. In December, the trio of star offensive linemen made a joint announcement that they would remain at Cincinnati. They do lose Gavin Gerhardt, but the trio of left tackle Joe Cotton, left guard Evan Tengesdahl, and guard/center Taran Tyo make this one of the strongest Big 12 lines yet again. Last year they ranked #2 nationally in Sack Rate, #3 in my OL Run Push, #5 in yards/carry, and were named a Joe Moore Award semifinalist. Entering fall camp, Nolan Latulippe and Xavier Lozowicki are projected to fill in the two open spots on the starting five.
pick_six_2026.defense:
The offense held up their end of the bargain, ranking #11 in my opponent-adjusted offensive rankings. Tyson Veidt’s defense struggled – #54 of 68 Power 4 – with the pass defense placing in the bottom five.

Satterfield opened up the rolodex and reconnected with Nate Woody, his defensive coordinator from back at Appalachian State. He specifically cited the 2025 unit’s lack of disruption – pressure, sacks, and interceptions – and Woody’s aggressive scheme is the perfect solution. Last year their 3-3-5 base ranked #123 in my Negative Play rate, often due to dropping eight into coverage. Woody is shifting Cincinnati back to a 3-4 but said they’ll always bring a fourth in pass rush.

Woody’s 2024 defense at Army ranked #1 nationally in total defense and helped lead their 12-win season. Here at Cincinnati he is inheriting a new-look roster with nine starters gone.

All-Big 12 linemen Dontay Corleone and Jalen Hunt graduated and starter Mikah Coleman went to Miami Ohio. Marquaze Parker emerged in spring ball as the top pass rusher, and Thomas Johnson (NC Central) had 12 sacks and 18 tackles-for-loss last year at the FCS level.

Tackle-machine Jake Golday was drafted in the second round but Cincinnati gets back a third-year starter in Jonathan Thompson. He has been consistent and should push for all-league honors in the new scheme. Simeon Coleman and Brian Simms move into starting roles with incoming Filip Maciorowski (Northern Illinois) who had 97 tackles last year.

The lone starter back in the secondary is a big one in All-Big 12 Antwan Peek. The do-it-all hybrid was named a Jim Thorpe semifinalist and fits into the nickel corner role here. Satterfield said he wanted more disruption, and Peek will lead the way. The staff signed another round of defensive backs from the portal and as many as four could start. MJ Cannon (Bowling Green) earned All-MAC honors and was a spring standout along with safety Ty Goodwill (South Alabama).

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Kansas suffered plenty of one-score losses with blown fourth-quarter leads but it will only get tougher from here with the worst five-year recruiting average in the Big 12. In the past two transfer cycles they added just one four- star.

The defense has a few proven all-conference candidates to build around but overall they placed third-worst in my opponent-adjusted defense stat last year. There are too many uncertainties to call for a bowl bid.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Lance Leipold fixed a broken program and got them back to consecutive bowl games in 2022-2023 for just the second time in school history. As that core of veteran players has graduated through the program, Kansas has now stacked consecutive 5-7 years since the nine-win peak in 2023.

Many coaches will talk about the tight margins that can make or break a season, but here at Kansas it is far from just coach-speak. Close losses have cursed Kansas.

Last season in the long-awaited return of the Border War, Kansas held a late lead but lost to Missouri by 11. Kansas allowed last-minute touchdown drives that flipped the Cincinnati and Arizona games from wins to losses. And in the season finale, Utah took back a 97-yard Pick Six that likely flipped the result.

Finishing games has been a consistent problem the past two years. In 2024 and 2025, Kansas held fourth-quarter leads in nine of their losses. Yes, nine blown leads in the final frame.

Leipold views the past two years with mixed emotions, noting that “in a very short time, making a bowl has now become the expectation” which is a far cry from when they were the dead last in Power 4 as the punching bag of the 2010s decade.

The Utah loss was an unfortunate way for sixth-year quarterback Jalon Daniels to end his career. Daniels threw three picks including the decisive Pick Six, but should be remembered as a program legend. Through all the injuries, the Daniels Era gave the program memorable moments, led the highs of the Leipold rebuild, brought ESPN’s College Gameday to Lawrence for the first time, and even debuted their state-of-the-art $450 million stadium.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Daniels departs, but Kansas brought back a familiar face in offensive coordinator Andy Kotelnicki. He led consecutive Top 10 offenses here in 2022 and 2023 per my opponent- adjusted rankings. His offenses consistently ranked high in explosiveness, yards/play, pass

protection, and third-down conversions.

In 2024 he took the Penn State coordinator job and boosted their explosiveness, Tyler Warren won the Mackey Award, and the running back pair rewrote the school record book.

It may appear to be the first quarterback battle since 2020, but Kotelnicki is quick to note the staff led position battles here over the Daniels era and are experienced for this 2026 battle. Cole Ballard is a former walk-on who rose up the depth chart and was the backup for Daniels last year. Isaiah Marshall is another contender, and the staff got him game experience with a quarterback-run package last year. They signed Rice’s starting quarterback Chase Jenkins, who rushed for 531 yards (13 carries/game) but placed 12th in AAC QB Rating. Ballard has the slight edge but it will be a fall camp battle.

Leshon Williams and Daniel Hishaw each rushed for 500+ yards but both are gone. The staff signed three veteran transfers and it will be a committee approach here. Yasin Willis was Syracuse’s lead rusher last year with 558 yards, Jalen Dupree led Colorado State with 508, but the real wildcard is the electric former Top200 prospect Dylan Edwards (Kansas State). Edwards has over 1,000 yards combined the past three years at KSU and Colorado, but the Derby, KS native has been held back with injuries. He is a threat to score whenever he touches the ball and will contribute in the pass game and as a return specialist.

Four of the top six receivers are gone, including the speedy All-Big 12 Emmanuel Henderson. Cam Pickett returns in the slot, Keaton Kubecka remains in the rotation, and the staff signed two instant playmakers from the non-AQ level. Nik McMillan (Buffalo) led the entire MAC with 82 yards/game and nearly eclipsed 1,000. He set a school record with seven straight 100-yard games and earned first-team All-MAC. Nahzae Cox was a starter for Middle Tennessee and adds a 6’3 frame with speed as a deep threat.

Tight end Carson Bruhn broke into the starting lineup as a redshirt freshman before an injury, and he is back along with incoming Jailen Butler (Old Dominion).

2025 was Kansas’ fourth-straight Top 20 offense, and the offensive line was a key reason. They ranked #11 in my OL Run Push and three linemen earned All-Big 12 recognition: Bryce Foster, Enrique Cruz, and Kobe Baynes.

Unfortunately all three are gone and the staff hit the portal to reload those three open spots. The three additions all bring starting experience and are rated as three-star transfers. Kasen Carpenter (Oklahoma State) was a former starting center for Tulsa, Nick Morrow (California) started 16 games at tackle, and Connor Stroh (Texas) started five at guard. Amir Herring and Calvin Clements are returning starters though they could use a boost in pass blocking.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Last offseason, Kansas went through a defensive coordinator change, learned a new scheme, and had to replace the entire back seven. As expected, there were growing pains and Kansas fell to the bottom ten of my opponent-adjusted defensive rankings.

This year that flips to a veteran back seven, a second-year coordinator bonus, but the loss of nearly 2,000 snaps along the defensive line.

All-Big 12 defensive end Leroy Harris is back and end Dakyus Brinkley is a rising star on the opposite side. Kansas signed Michigan State starter David Santiago with the hope that this trio can produce a more consistent pass rush. Last year they relied more on blitzing linebackers and cornerbacks.

Blake Herold returns at defensive tackle and he could push for all-league honors, but the other three tackles are gone. The staff signed Tre’Von McAlpine (Tulane) who earned second-team All-AAC last year as a run-stuffing nose tackle.

Kansas retained their top playmaker in Trey Lathan. The middle backer led the team in tackles, and made the two key plays in the 27- 20 win over UCF when he recovered a fumble at the goal-line and later made the game-sealing tackle in the final minute. Bangally Kamara graduated with Big 12 honors but Kansas landed Boston College captain Daveon Crouch and two SEC backers Landyn Watson (Kentucky) and Jaron Willis (South Carolina).

The new-look secondary struggled last year with a bottom ten finish in opponent-adjusted passing, but the hope is that it will pay dividends as veterans in 2026. Three starters are back with safety Taylor Davis and the corner pair of Jalen Todd and Austin Alexander. They signed Louisville’s starting safety Corey Gordon, and Jaden Harris (Miami & Georgia) who was stuck in crowded NFL factories.

pick_six_2026.outlook: Marion was a strong coordinator pick, Colorado signed a fourth straight Top 25 transfer class and restocked the receiver room. But to get to bowl season they have to fix both lines of scrimmage and get better effort from the defense.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Deion Sanders led a program revival season in 2024 with his son Shedeur at quarterback and two-way phenom Travis Hunter packing the highlight reel. Both ended up in New York City as Heisman finalists and Hunter became the first defender to win it in a generation.

For 2025, Colorado went with another full-scale transfer class but the talent drain and loss of star power caught up to them.

The quarterback battle lasted through fall camp and spilled into the season, with Sanders using a rare three-man rotation where each guy got multiple possessions before picking the hot hand. Eventually all three guys started games and all three were benched with mixed results.

After the historic 9-win season, the 2025 team finished 3-9. Sanders called his defense “hot garbage” during an in-game television interview, they blew a pair of 14-0 leads against BYU and TCU, then it collapsed with blowouts losses to Utah 53-7, Arizona 52-17, and Arizona State 42-17.

From a Game Grader perspective, no team had a worse one-year decline. Colorado peaked at #19 in 2024 and fell all the way to the bottom five -- #63 of 68 Power 4 – in 2025. Both sides of the ball finished in the bottom

ten of my opponent-adjusted ranks.

When pressed on his future, Sanders doubled down on himself and his program vision: “I don’t doubt me, let’s get that straight, I don’t doubt me.”

Right away he landed one of the top coordinator hires this cycle with the innovative Brennan Marion bringing his so-called “Go-Go Offense” to Boulder.

Then Colorado signed a top 25 transfer haul – Sanders’ fourth in four years – with a trio of four-stars and multiple all-conference players. Yes, it’s another transfer-heavy roster, but this time with the elimination of the second, post-spring transfer window, there will be no summer Musical Chairs.

His first three seasons averaged 22 new transfers per summer, essentially an entire recruiting class leaving and joining after spring ball. That retention will help with the new scheme installation and Sanders views it positively saying they “really know the hand that you’re dealt” rather than restarting in fall camp.
pick_six_2026.offense:
When asked to describe his Go-Go Offense, Marion said it is a “Friday offense, a Saturday offense, and a Sunday offense” meaning they draw concepts from all three levels of football. While that sounds like typical coach-speak, there is some truth to it here, as this is a super-creative offense that is both run-heavy but takes vertical passing shots more than most.

Over six years as a head coach and coordinator, Marion’s offenses have averaged over 30 points/game, and his Sacramento State unit last year exploded for 34 points and 426 yards per game, with runs on a very high 69% of snaps.

That is quite the contrast to Colorado’s pass-heavy tendency over the Sanders era.

Kaidon Salter started the most games, Ryan Staub had one start and his breakthrough moment in the Delaware win, but both are gone. Top100 recruit Julian Lewis surged late in the season and retained his redshirt, and is set to battle Utah transfer Isaac Wilson in fall camp. Wilson was also a four-star prospect thrown into action as a true freshman, and struggled with more picks than touchdowns as a part-year starter during Utah’s injury-filled 2024 season.

Marion tends to go with a two-back formation and there are four guys in the mix for carries. Micah Welch is back after leading the team with 384 yards last year, DeKalon Taylor is back healthy and has the skillset for this scheme, and Richard Young (Alabama) is a 210-pound power back. Marion brought his thunder/lightning pair with him from Sacramento State with Damian Henderson and speedy JaQuail Smith – they combined for 1,100 yards and 10 touchdowns last year.

All-Big 12 star and team MVP Omarion Miller transferred out to Arizona State as the #3 ranked receiver this cycle. Colorado added a four-star of their own with Texas starter DeAndre Moore, plus first-team All-MAC Kam Perry (Miami Ohio). Then they signed Biletnikoff semifinalist Danny Scudero (San Jose State) who led the entire country with 1,297 yards. Last year’s #2 target Joseph Williams is back, plus

Marion brought another speedster with him from Sacramento State in 4.3 40 burner Ernest Campbell. This room is the clear strength of the roster.

Zach Atkins returns at tight end, and the position will be utilized more since they are moving away from the four-wide formations of the past few seasons.

The offensive line struggled again last year allowing a sack on 11% of pass attempts (#130) and failing to create a consistent run push (#102). Their best lineman Jordan Seaton missed some games due to injury and now transferred out as a five-star to LSU. In the past three years, an insane 27 different linemen have started games.

It will be another reset here in 2026 with just one full-time starter returning in Larry Johnson. Marion wanted to “build a wall of big humans” and did just that with a pair of 6’8 transfers Leon Bell (California) and Bo Hughley (Georgia). Both guys have Power 4 starting experience. So do Taj White (Rutgers) and center Demetrius Hunter (Houston) and Jayven Richardson was Missouri’s sixth man last year.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Colorado completed the three-year boomerang on defense: bottom ten in 2023, a Top 25 surge in 2024, and then all the way back down in 2025. They allowed 223 rushing yards/game – second worst in America.

Coordinator Robert Livingston went to the pros and Sanders promoted Chris Marve from within. Marve was the defensive coordinator on Brent Pry’s Virginia Tech teams 2022-2024 with a three-year average rank of #37 of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted rankings.

The defense is a total reset and could feature new transfers at all eleven spots. The only returning player with more than six starts is safety Ben Finneseth and from there the staff signed impressive groups at linebacker and in the secondary.

Finneseth will battle All-CUSA Naeten Mitchell (New Mexico State) and former four-star prospect Randon Fontenette (Vanderbilt). The top corner pair appears to be Cree Thomas (Notre Dame) and All-Sun Belt Justin Eaglin (James Madison). Boo Carter is a total wildcard – the former Top100 was once a top SEC freshman and is looking for a bounce-back year and may even get snaps on offense.

Three linebacker transfers will battle for the starting spots with former four-star Liona Lefau (Texas), All-MAC Gideon Lampron (Bowling Green), and New Mexico State starter Tyler Martinez.

The defensive line is an area of uncertainty after five guys transferred out to Power 4 rosters. They backfilled with players from the FCS and non-AQ level and all four starters will be transfers. Santana Hopper (Tulane) is the headliner after earning first-team All-AAC honors as a productive tackle. Ezra Christensen (New Mexico State), Toby Anene (North Dakota State), Tyler Moore (Coastal Carolina), and Sedrick Smith (Maryland) all received three-star transfer grades.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Rutgers retained All-Big Ten stars in Raymond and Duff, but now the quarterback spot is an uncertainty.

It was a historically bad defense last year but there was no overnight fix as just two starters return and they went FCS-heavy. Rutgers came up short in the transfer portal by losing five starters and then signing the league’s lowest-ranked class. That talent drain will keep them out of bowl season again in 2026.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Timing is everything in college football, and unfortunately for Rutgers their two sides of the ball have not matched up.

Over the past 10-year window, Rutgers is dead last 68th of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted offense. During most of that time, Greg Schiano’s defense has had to carry the weight and single-handedly get them to bowl eligibility.

But the past two seasons, and especially 2025, the strengths flipped but did not overlap. Offensive coordinator Kirk Ciarrocca finally got Rutgers above average on offense in 2024, and then last year they posted a 3,000-yard passer, 1,000-yard rusher, and 1,000-yard receiver all together for the first time since 2007. They ranked #29 in my opponent-adjusted number – 10th in passing – and set a school record for games scoring 30+ points.

Normally, that offensive output paired with a typical Schiano defense would be enough to get Rutgers to eight or nine wins. Instead, the defense collapsed at the same time the offense clicked.

Rutgers finished dead last in FBS by allowing 7.8 yards/play, and the 7.6 in league-play is the Big Ten’s worst since 2000. My opponent-adjusted numbers agree, and not only did Rutgers finish dead last in 2025, it was the lowest-rated statistical defense I’ve graded since I began tracking in 2010.

Even with the extreme contrasts, Rutgers was in position to return to bowl season and finally snap the losing streak to Penn State. But they blew second-half leads in four losses, fourth- quarter leads in three, and had untimely mistakes that flipped the results. After lighting up the stout Iowa secondary in the first half, Rutgers threw a costly late interception, a botched shotgun snap tacked on 15 more yards to a missed field goal in the three-point Minnesota loss, and Penn State scooped up a play-action fumble for the decisive touchdown.

To flip the script in 2026 there were three requirements this offseason: retain top starters, add high-quality talent from the transfer portal, and fix the defense.

Rutgers lost five proven starters who transferred out to Power 4 programs, signed the lowest- rated transfer class in the Big Ten, and led a 64-day search for the defensive coordinator. That looks like two strikes, and the third, while an unconventional hire, remains up for grabs.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Ciarrocca did a phenomenal job here and it finished as Rutgers best offense of their entire Big Ten era (2014-2025). Athan Kaliakmanis saved his best season for last as he threw for 3,100 yards, 20 touchdowns, and surged up to #7 in QB Rating in the Big Ten.

Rutgers now turns to a pair of former four-star recruits with incumbent backup AJ Surace battling incoming Dylan Lonergan (Boston College). Lonergan was originally at Alabama, then Bill O’Brien handpicked him to lead his BC offense in 2025. He posted a few 300-yard games in September but slowed down once opposing coordinators got some film, and he was eventually benched.

Lonergan has a strong arm but needs more game experience with pocket awareness and decision- making. Surace has a high ceiling but had minimal snaps last year. This battle should go into August.

While they did lose five starters to the portal, the staff was able to retain three important All-Big Ten stars on offense: running back Antwan Raymond, receiver KJ Duff, and guard Kwabena Asamoah.

Raymond took on the workhorse role with four 100-yard games including his huge 41-carry, 240- yard explosion in the Purdue win. That performance ranked third all-time here behind a pair of Ray Rice games. He earned second-team All-Big Ten and was one of ten semifinalists for the Doak Walker.

The 6’6 Duff was a reliable playmaker all season and was the top downfield threat with an average target depth of 17 yards. He excels in jump balls and one-on-ones – the one-handed catch against Penn State is a “catch of the year” candidate. His co-star Ian Strong transferred out with a four- star ranking, and slot receiver DT Sheffield graduated. Veteran backup Ben Black moves up into a starting role on the outside, while Michael Thomas and four-star true freshman Dyzier Carter are in the slot.

Asamoah is the anchor to build the offensive line around again after consecutive All-Big Ten seasons. Tyler Needham returns at tackle, and the two of them have a combined 55 starts. Three starters depart, but Rutgers does get back two original projected starters Ryder Langsdale and Dantae Chin who both missed the season with injuries. Center Gus Zilinskas graduated but his brother Hank transferred in after starting for Colorado. The line remained below-average in OL Run Push (#81) but collapsed in pass protection (#127) allowing a sack on 10% of pass attempts.
pick_six_2026.defense:
After the historically bad season, Schiano made a change on this side of the ball. The search process lasted over two months and he eventually made a surprise hire of South Dakota head coach Travis Johansen. As the defensive coordinator there in 2024 he led a Top 10 FCS defense, and last year as head coach they went 10-5 with an FCS quarterfinals appearance.

His transition unit will feature just two returning starters and as many as four FCS transfer starters.

The entire starting defensive line is gone. Bradley Weaver, Jordan Thompson, and top pass-rusher Eric O’Neill all graduated, and defensive end Jordan Walker transferred out to Georgia Tech. The staff signed three non-AQ linemen to fill out the starting line. There are all rated as three-star transfers though all three earned all-league honors last year: Malachi Davis (Toledo), J’Dan Burnett (Tulsa), Rondo Porter (App State). Zaire Angoy and Keshon Griffin both have game experience at tackle.

In their 4-2-5 scheme, only two linebackers got the vast majority of snaps. Dariel Djabome is gone but Abram Wright returns at one backer spot. Two transfers from lower levels will battle for the other spot: All-AAC Ty Morris (Rice) and Pioneer Conference Player of the Year Sean Allison (Drake).

Like the backers, there was minimal rotation in the secondary, and four of the five starters are gone. Their top two corners left for Power 4 programs with Jacobie Henderson going to Virginia and four-star transfer Bo Mascoe heading to Texas.

Three FCS transfers are projected starters as Mikey Munn (South Dakota), Bradlee Jones (Citadel), Zahmir Dawud (Villanova) all come in with three-star transfer grades. Munn was an FCS All-American, led the nation in interceptions, and followed his coach to Rutgers. Kaj Sanders is the lone returning starter but the secondary needs vast improvements after finishing #131 in opponent QB Rating, #130 in yards/attempt, #123 in explosive passing, and dead last in my opponent-adjusted stat.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Brown is elevating the overall talent profile here and wants to prove that 2024 wasn’t just a one-hit wonder. Angeli is back healthy and though it was a small sample size, the offense looked completely different with him under center.

Both lines of scrimmage are major liabilities for 2026, and it may take another year of experience until the record- setting recruiting classes change the on-field momentum.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
In late September, Syracuse won in Clemson’s “Death Valley” for the first time ever, and the major upset got them to a 3-1 start. It appeared that Fran Brown was backing up his 10-3 breakout debut 2024 season, and that quarterback Steve Angeli was keeping up last year’s pace from Kyle McCord.

They were playing – and coaching – with confidence. A surprise onsides kick and gutsy fourth-down conversions helped them jump out to a 10-0 lead on Clemson, a lead they would not give up.

In the postgame interview an exuberant Brown joked about “eating for free” back in Syracuse. But one injury caused a sudden shift, and exactly one week later he issued a full apology to the Syracuse fan base for a 38-3 meltdown loss to Duke.

Late in the Clemson win, Angeli tore his Achilles’ tendon and the season-ending injury wrecked the entire 2025 season. The quarterback problem cascaded with other position group weaknesses and the end result was an eight-game losing streak to close out a 3-9 season. The final two were quite the pair of gut punches. First, the school’s most points allowed since 1891 in a 70-7 loss to Notre Dame in which the Irish led 21-0 before the offense even took a snap. Then in the finale, they were blown out 34-12 by one-win Boston College, with Syracuse running a high school style wildcat offense. Even eight weeks after the injury, the staff had no solution at quarterback.

The defense was no help. They allowed a Power 4 worst 35 points/game, and finished 66th of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted, per-play metric. Brown fired coordinator Elijah Robinson and hired Broyles Award nominee Vince Kehres from Toledo.

Brown then backed up his recruiting reputation by signing the school’s best recruiting class of the modern era, again. Brown’s three classes are the top three of the online recruiting era, and he’s already signed 23 of the school’s 50 highest-rated commits since 2000. Five-star Calvin Russell (Miami Northwestern) chose Syracuse over late in-state pushes from Florida, Florida State, and Miami and became the school’s highest-rated recruit of all-time.
pick_six_2026.offense:
In Angeli’s 3+ games he threw 10 touchdowns, just 2 picks, 1,317 yards with a high 8.4 per attempt. His QB Rating would have ranked third in the ACC had he met the minimum threshold of games played. Against UConn he led two scoring drives in the final five minutes to force overtime, then hit Justus Ross-Simmons at the pylon for the game-winner. He also had 245 yards and 2 scores against Clemson before the injury.

When the starter goes down a statistical decline is expected, but the drop-off here was a season- ruiner for Syracuse. Angeli had more yards and touchdowns than the rest of the room put up in 8+ games without him. After the injury, Syracuse ranked dead last in my opponent-adjusted passing (68th of 68 Power 4) as they rotated through Rickie Collins, walk-on Joe Filardi, and tight end Dan Villari.

Brown added to the quarterback room with first-team All-CUSA Amari Odom (Kennesaw State).

The offensive line was a total weakness that limited the potential of talented athletes at the skill positions. The line ranked #99 in OL Run Push and #118 in Pass Protection. TJ Ferguson and Da’Metrius Weatherspoon were bright spots but both graduated, along with Austin Collins, meaning Syracuse needs to find three new starters up front. Byron Washington took over the right guard spot as a true freshman and they’ve got experience at the tackle spots with Trevion Mack and Kam Pringle. Brown’s hire of longtime NFL coach Juan Castillo is intriguing and comes at their most critical position.

In 2024 three receivers went over 900+ yards but in 2025 no one even hit 600. The entire receiving core is gone as Ross-Simmons graduated, and Johntay Cook and four-star Darrell Gill both transferred to Ole Miss. Brown added a pair of former four-star recruits who lack college experience

in Elijah Moore (Florida State) and Matt Outten (Penn State), and starters from lower levels Cole Weaver (Miami, OH) and 6’3 Zamondre Merriweather (JUCO). Incoming five-star Calvin Russell should earn a starting spot right away.

No running back had a single 100-yard game all season, and Yasin Willis’ 558 rushing yards were a program-low since 2020. Willis transferred out to Kansas, #2 back Will Nixon graduated, and a pair of transfers will reshape the room. Ahmad Miller (Jackson State) rushed for 1,000+ yards at the FCS level, while Ju’Juan Johnson (LSU) is a do-it-all athlete.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Robinson was fired after consecutive bottom ten defenses and the 2025 unit hit national lows. An already thin defensive line lost its best player Maraad Watson to a late transfer, then lost starter Rashard Perry to injury. Both veteran safeties were injured, too. A struggling unit was weakened further by being on the field more than most, due to the broken offense.

Kehres won DIII titles at Mount Union and then turned around Toledo’s defense from worst to first in the MAC. The 2025 unit was towards the top of the national leaderboards in almost every key stat category.

He’s got some rising stars to build around in the back seven. Chris Peal was one of the top cover corners in the ACC, and he forms a top corner duo with Demetres Samuel, the two-way true freshman phenom. At inside backer, Antoine Deslauriers earned Freshman All-America honors after leading the team with 60 tackles.

All three starting linebackers return with Gary Bryant and Jamie Tremble flanking Deslauriers. Kehres brought Chris D’Appolonia with him from Toledo and he can rotate onto the field on pass downs with a boost to pass coverage.

Both veterans Duce Chestnut and Devin Grant graduated from the secondary, and they need to find two new starters. They signed Western Kentucky starter Nazir Ward to compete with Cornell Perry

and Davien Kerr.

The line is a complete rebuild again. The team mustered just 20 sacks in 12 games, and aside from a 7-sack explosion vs. Pitt, it was basically just one per game. Syracuse loses its top lineman Kevin Jobity along with veterans David Reese and Denis Jaquez. The tackle spots benefit from a second-year bonus for Nissi Ogbebor and Rashard Perry’s injury return. The staff signed four mid-three star transfer linemen: Dillan Fontus (Maryland), Tunmise Adeleye (UNLV), Keyshawn Johnson (Tennessee Tech) and Jartavius Flounoy (Georgia State). Fontus should be a starter after holding his own in the Big Ten, while former five-star Adeleye had eight sacks the past two years.

This is the definition of a rebuilding season.

pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Fresh off their school-record 11-3 season, Iowa State opened up 2025 with a win over Kansas State in the Ireland kickoff, got a 54-yarder from Kyle Konrardy to beat Iowa again, and jumped out to a 5-0 start.

The season flipped due to an injury run that knocked out several starters including both All-Big 12 cornerbacks. The 5-0 start was followed by four straight losses.

Iowa State looked to be headed for a fifth straight loss but Aiden Flora returned a punt 79 yards for a touchdown to flip the TCU game and spark a win streak to close the season out at 8-4.

While there was no return trip to the Big 12 title, this was just another solid coaching job by Matt Campbell – his fifth eight-win season. A decade removed from being a Big 12 punching bag, it’s a testament to what Campbell built here that an eight-win season is now just the expected norm.

The offseason storyline would have been the return of a senior-laden roster that went 8-4 – with three one-score losses – despite some poor injury luck.

That was thrown out the window on December 5th.

Campbell has been a popular candidate every year when the coaching carousel heats up, but year after year, job offer after job offer, he remained committed to Iowa State. The school’s all-time winningest coach shockingly accepted the head coaching spot at Penn State, and within hours Iowa State already hired his successor Jimmy Rogers.

Athletic director Jamie Pollard had this plan on the backburner in case Campbell was ever swayed away from Ames: “Rogers is a rising star, and has been on my short-list ever since I met him… he told me during our first visit years ago that he wanted to be the next head coach at Iowa State.”

The rising star claim is an understatement. In his first season as a head coach Rogers led South Dakota State to a 15-0 national title in 2023, a 12-3 final four run in 2024, and then went 7-6 at Washington State with a completely new roster.

Washington State brought in 70 new players, yet he was able to land a Top 20 defense and take several Playoff contenders to one-score decisions: Ole Miss by 3, Virginia by 2, and James Madison by 4.
pick_six_2026.offense:
That extreme roster turnover is critical experience, because he and his staff will need to do it again here. Campbell brought 20 Cyclones – 15 starters – with him to Penn State. In total, Iowa State welcomes in 60 newcomers, and 16 projected new starters all from lower levels (non-AQ, FCS, DII).

The offense was hit especially hard with all 11 starters transferring or graduating.

Rocco Becht followed Campbell to Penn State and leaves as one of the best Iowa State quarterbacks of all- time. He placed third in career passing yards (9,274), second in touchdowns (64) and led several fourth- quarter comebacks. Backup quarterback Alex Manske joined him, and a pair of transfers battled in spring.

Jaylen Raynor (Arkansas State) was a three-year starter with multiple All-Sun Belt accolades and a productive stat-line: 9,877 yards of offense and 67 total touchdowns. Raynor appeared to win the job over Zane Flores (Oklahoma State) who threw 7 picks and just 3 touchdowns in a tough spot last year.

Then the dominos started following. Leading rusher Carson Hansen to Penn State. Top two receivers Chase Sowell and Brett Eskildsen … top two tight ends Ben Brahmer and Gabe Burkle … starting guard Trevor Buhr … all to Penn State. That’s five All-Big 12 players out the door.

Hansen’s co-star Abu Sama went to Wisconsin so it will be a new duo at running back with MAC Freshman of the Year Cameron Pettaway (Bowling Green) joining the elusive Aiden Flora.

The top four receivers are gone and the staff signed starters off lower-level schools like Omari Hayes (Tulane) and Cody Jackson (FCS Tarleton). Carter Pabst (Washington State) got some time as a freshman and followed the staff here, Evan Boyd (Michigan State) was a Big Ten backup, and Dominic Overby remains in the rotation from last year.

Raynor has a familiar face to throw to with the addition of his Arkansas State tight end Tyler Fortenberry who caught 32 balls last year.

The Iowa State offensive line led a consistent run push down the stretch and they rushed for 150+ in the final seven games – a Top 10 streak to close the season. It is a complete restart here as all five starters are gone including their 50-start ironman Tyler Miller. This will be a full transfer starting five here in 2026. Braden Smith (Tarleton) was an FCS All-American at guard, Jake Taylor (Oklahoma) was a starter in 2024 before an injury, and the other three bring a handful of starts: Gavin Broscious (Michigan State), DeAndre Carter (Auburn), and Maasai King (Akron).

Rogers hired Tyler Roehl at offensive coordinator, and before his stop here in 2024 he was leading the national champion power rushing attack for North Dakota State. Rogers’ South Dakota State faced off against him and must have earned his respect.
pick_six_2026.defense:
The legendary Jon Heacock retired after a decade leading the defense here in Ames. His development and installation of the 3-3 so-called Dime Stack defense puzzled opposing coordinators and was a key reason for the program’s rise. In those ten years, seven defenses ranked in the Big 12’s top three, and he coached 80 All-Big 12 defenders.

Rogers brought his coordinator Jesse Bobbit with him after the successful South Dakota State years and a Top 20 unit last year at Washington State. They will switch back to a four-man front.

Eight starters transferred out and seven followed Campbell to Penn State. The new starting eleven has two Iowa State incumbents, one Power 4 transfer, 3 non-AQ, 4 FCS, and 2 DII.

Domonique Orange was drafted and there was a noticeable difference when he was not on the field. Zaimir Hawk returns at nose tackle and the staff had huge spring reviews of Bryson Lamb (Washington State). Isaac Terrell (Washington State) was a top pass rusher with 7 sacks and 12 tackles-for-loss.

The starting trio – Caleb Bacon, Kooper Ebel, and Cael Brezina – all went to Penn State so Carson Willich elevates into a starting role alongside a rising star Sullivan Schlimgen (Washington State). Montreze Smith is a former FCS All- American, and Tristan Exline (UT Permian Basin) put up an insane 143 tackles, 19.5 for loss, and was a Harlon Hill finalist aka the “Division II Heisman.”

The top six defensive backs are gone. Jaheim Singletary (Arkansas) is a former Top100 prospect but his playing time has decreased each year. Seth Johnson (Montana State) will start opposite him at the other corner spot. Perhaps their top transfer this cycle, the All-AAC safety Braden Awls (Tulane), was injured in spring so the pair will likely be Jacksonville State starter Malcolm Jones and Micah Harper (Montana) who previously was productive at BYU.

pick_six_2026.outlook:
Stanford’s .308 win percentage (24-54 overall) over the past seven seasons is the worst in Power 4. Without the usual coaching change transfer haul to pump the roster with fresh talent, Stanford signed the fewest transfers in Power 4.

Instead, they actually have the #5 five-year recruiting average in the ACC, some proven playmakers on defense, and avoid the last-place projection.

Pritchard has a multi-year rebuilding project on his hands here.
pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Andrew Luck returned to The Farm and took over full control of the football program through the newly created General Manager role. Just before spring practice he fired head coach Troy Taylor and hired his former NFL head coach Frank Reich to take over as a one-year interim.

Despite the late start to 2025, Reich was able to break Stanford out of their three-win cycle, went 4-2 in home games, and won The Big Game over Cal to snap a four-year drought. He noted the importance of that win and the foundation it could lay going forward: “got the Axe back… the chemistry, the brotherhood in the locker room, the way we practice… we made progress.”

The defense led the way in their wins, with a Pick Six and goal-line stand against Boston College, another goal-line stand and three red zone stops against Florida State, and a pair of fumble touchdowns to beat Cal.

In the background, Luck was conducting a full-scale head coaching search and eventually landed on a familiar Stanford name: Tavita Pritchard.

Pritchard threw the game-winning touchdown in the historic upset win over #2 USC in 2007 as 41-point underdogs and then ironically lost the starting quarterback job to Luck himself. The benching actually accelerated Pritchard’s coaching career and he stayed on for a decade including five years as David Shaw’s offensive coordinator.

Since leaving Stanford he spent the last three seasons in the NFL, most recently as the QB coach for the Washington Commanders and helped guide Jayden Daniels to his breakout Offensive Rookie of the Year season in 2024. While Pritchard does not have any head coaching experience, he does have a clear passion for his alma mater – a critical ingredient to recent success stories like Clark Lea (Vanderbilt), Brent Key (Georgia Tech), and Kenny Dillingham (Arizona State).

Pritchard has a multi-year rebuilding project on his hands. While 2025 season was a five-year high, the gap between Stanford and the league contenders is still noticeable.

In their six games against ranked opponents, Stanford lost all six by double-digits and five by 24+ points. Their high academic ratings help attract national talent on the high school recruiting trail, but also act as a barrier to incoming transfers. Usually a coaching change transfer class acts as a spark with 30+ transfer additions. Stanford finished dead last in Power 4 this cycle with just three incoming FBS transfers.
pick_six_2026.offense:
The Stanford offensive line has been the focal point of the program’s highs under Harbaugh and Shaw, and the main catalyst of the decline since. Pritchard understands the importance and specifically mentioned the offensive line in his opening press conference: “I know we’ll be built up front – we will make that the heart and soul of the offense.”

He inherits a veteran unit but one that has struggled statistically for the past several seasons. In 2025 they were the only offensive line in America to finish in the bottom ten of both my OL Run Push and Pass Protection metrics. They allowed a sack on 10% of pass attempts and their 2.5 yards/carry finished dead last in America.

Pritchard hired Virginia’s offensive line coach Terry Heffernan to take over the offensive coordinator role. Heffernan’s UVA line was the most improved from 2024 (#127) to 2025 (#11) in Pass Protection and he’ll attempt to work his magic here.

Niki Prongos is the headliner at left tackle and should get some All-ACC hype this season. 2025 was the third season in a row in which Stanford had a true freshman lineman start 6+ games and all that youth experience pays dividends in 2026. Kahlil House is a third-year starter, Simione Pale

is back from injury, Fisher Anderson is a returning starter at center, and Josh Williams took over a starting spot as a true freshman and held it the final six games.

Both starting quarterbacks are gone and now it’s a complete rebuild. Ben Gulbranson finished dead last in the ACC in QB Rating and graduated, and then backup Elijah Brown transferred out to Washington. Stanford signed Michigan’s 2024 starter Davis Warren who threw 7 touchdowns, 10 picks, and spent 2025 rehabbing an ACL tear. Dylan Rizk (UCF) has a few Power 4 starts on his resume and adds a dual-threat skillset, the 6’6 Charlie Mirer led a touchdown drive to close the season against Notre Dame, and three-star Mike Mitchell made it a four-man race.

Micah Ford rushed for 643 yards – a Stanford high since 2019 – and returns along with Sedrick Irvin who had the game-winning score to beat San Jose State in the final seconds.

Stanford lost some firepower from the pass game with their top two receivers CJ Williams and Bryce Farrell and top tight end Sam Roush all departing. Williams and Roush earned All-ACC honors and leave the room low on experience. Caden High steps into the lead receiver role, a pair of Yale transfers Nico Brown and David Pantelis bring All-Ivy resumes, and Carter Shaw (David’s son) transferred in from UCLA. Roush will be tough to replace after leading ACC tight ends in receptions (49) and yards (545) but Benji Blackburn and Chico Holt are the next men up.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Stanford allowed 408 yards/game, a program best since 2017, and it was their best rushing defense in over a decade. They saved their best work for the red zone with Top 25 finishes in red zone scoring and red zone touchdown percentage, and their performance near the goal-line flipped the Florida State and BC games to wins.

They return their top four tacklers, none more important than second-team All-ACC inside linebacker Matt Rose who finished with the league’s second-most tackles (106). The linebacker core returns intact with Rose and Jahsiah Galvan in the middle, and Tevarua Tafiti and Ernest Cooper on the outsides.

Up front, All-ACC Clay Patterson is gone, but plenty of experience returns with nose tackle Braden Marceau- Olayinka and ends Omar Staples and Zach Rowell.

The secondary was torched all season and allowed a nation-worst 289 passing yards/game along with bottom 25 ranks in all key categories. Two starters depart – safety Mitch Leigber and corner Collin Wright – but All-ACC honorable mention safety Jay Green returns. The safeties were tackle-machines and accounted for four of the team’s top six. Green, Scotty Edwards and Charlie Eckhardt are all back. The staff signed corner Leroy Bryant who started five games for Washington.
