pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
Boston College won their opener by 56 over Fordham, won their finale by 22 over Syracuse – and lost all ten games in between. So much for the second-year coach bonus.

The losses came in all varieties. Costly goal-line turnovers in winnable games (Michigan State, Stanford, California), 30+ point blowouts (Pittsburgh, Clemson, SMU), a walk-off field goal (Georgia Tech), and competitive losses to rivals (UConn and Notre Dame).

Two years in and BC is farther away from head coach Bill O’Brien’s program blueprint he pitched at the opening press conference. He constantly mentioned being tough and physical – a nod to the school’s offensive line NFL pipeline – but the offense finished in the national bottom 10 in rushing yards/carry. Combined with a poor run defense, BC finished second-worst in Power 4 in my “Run the Ball, Stop the Run” metric.

The win over Syracuse helped avoid the school’s first 0-11 (vs. FBS opponents) season in 50 years, but before any positive momentum could be carried into the offseason, Boston College was hit with a mass

exodus to the transfer portal.

30 scholarship players transferred out, which is an abnormally high number in a non-coach change offseason. Most of the proven playmakers from the 2025 team graduated or left The Heights. Then O’Brien went with a double coordinator switch heading into spring ball, hiring journeyman coordinator Ted Roof to call the defense, and naming himself as the offensive coordinator and play-caller.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Alabama transfer Dylan Lonergan impressed in fall camp and won the starting job over incumbent starter Grayson James. Lonergan started fast, threw for 390 yards and four scores in the overtime loss to Michigan State, and actually led the nation in completions/game in late September. In the fifth game, O’Brien benched him for James, and the position remained unsettled the rest of the way.

There was no help from the run game, which finished in the bottom ten of all key categories, and the offensive line also struggled in pass protection with a #100 national rank.

Both the quarterback room and the offensive line are complete restarts heading into 2026. Lonergan transferred out to Rutgers, James graduated, and the staff’s two transfer signees have zero FBS snaps on the resume. Grayson Wilson was a three-star high school recruit who redshirted at Arkansas last year, while Mason McKenzie earned the GLIAC Player of the Year honors from the same DII conference where Ole Miss breakout star Trinidad Chambliss played in.

McKenzie picked Boston College over Northwestern and Temple and posted a gaudy stat-line over his two years at Saginaw Valley State: 4,301 yards passing, 1,773 yards rushing, and 41 total touchdowns. McKenzie appears to be the favorite heading into fall camp and brings more mobility to the position compared to the 2025 room.

Four starters depart from the offensive line, including the young bright spot Eryx Daugherty who transferred out to Louisville. The staff pumped the room with experienced transfers, even if those snaps came at a lower level. The one with Power 4 starting experience, Kristian Phillips (Michigan State) joins returning center Michael Crounse as two projected starters. Robert Smith got game reps as a true freshman at guard, Pape Sy is a returning backup tackle, and the four other transfers bring experience from the non-AQ and FCS levels: Trevon Humphrey (NC Central), Owen Snively (Eastern Michigan), Reggie Jackson (Jacksonville State), and perhaps the biggest upside in 6’7 290- pound Veguer Jean-Jumeau (Tennessee State) who was apparently drawing some SEC interest.

The line rebuild is even more critical than usual, given the lack of FBS experience at quarterback, and the loss of their best skill players. Lewis Bond was named offensive MVP and graduates as one

of the most reliable BC receivers in recent memory. Reed Harris flashed breakout potential and was set to be the next star receiver but he left for Arizona State as the #4 ranked transfer WR this cycle.

Jaedn Skeete steps into the top role and was playing well before injuries derailed his season. The staff added a trio of three-star transfers with speedsters Landon Wright (Washington State) and Javarius Green (UNC) and 6’6 Reed Swanson (Colgate). Johnathan Montague was drawing big reviews before a 2025 season-ending injury and is another potential contributor.

BC also lost their top two running backs, as Turbo Richard transferred to Indiana and Jordan McDonald graduated. They signed a one-two punch from the portal in Evan Dickens (Liberty) and Nolan Ray (Maryland). Dickens posted a 1,339-yard, 16-touchdown season to earn All-CUSA honors while Ray brings short-yardage physicality.

They lose tight end Jeremiah Franklin who placed in the national top ten of receptions, but do bring back a star to build around in Freshman All-American Kaelan Chudzinski who is a pure pass threat.
pick_six_2026.defense:
The defense finished second-worst – 67th of 68 Power 4 – in my opponent-adjusted metric and regressed in all 17 of my stat categories. Injuries were a factor with nine defenders missing significant time.

Missed tackles and a lack of a pass rush were the two worst flaws. BC’s two defensive ends combined for just 3 sacks and 4.5 tackles for loss all season. As a unit they ranked #130 in my Negative Play Rate, #125 in yards/carry, and #121 in opponent QB Rating.

Roof has a complete rebuild here as the top six defensive linemen, top three linebackers, and three defensive backs are all gone.

Nose tackle Owen Stoudmire would have been the lone returner on the line but was a late transfer out to Nebraska. Chris Marable steps up into the starting role after some solid experience down the stretch, while Favor Bate and E’Lla Boykin move up into the end spots.

The staff signed plenty of transfers to compete with them, headlined by a pair of former four-star recruits in KJ Sampson (Florida State) and Christian Hudson (Colorado). Their only two four-star recruits from the 2026 class are both defensive ends with Mason Leak (Avon, CT) and Demeterius Thompson (Clayton, MO) adding some pass rush.

It’s a reset at linebacker, too. Daveon Crouch went to Kansas, Owen McGowan graduated, and a pair of three-star transfers are projected starters with Anthony Palano (Washington State), and athletic cover backers Justin Medlock (SMU) and Bodie Kahoun (Notre Dame).

BC’s cornerback duo was injured early in season which left them over-exposed to explosive passing (#125). This is the most experienced unit on the team with corner Syair Torrence, nickel Cam Martinez, and safeties KP Price and Carter Davis all returning. One key departure was hard-hitting safety Omar Thornton who transferred to Miami with a high four-star transfer grade.

pick_six_2026.recap_2025:
It was shocking to see such an offense-first program hire a defensive minded coach, and especially such a young one with no head coach experience. The Ryan Walters era ended quickly with a 5-19 two-year record.

Even more shocking was that Purdue doubled down and went with another defensive hire. At least this time, Barry Odom came in with decades of experience and was fresh off a full-scale program turnaround at UNLV where he leveraged NIL and the transfer portal to lead them to a Mountain West title game.

Odom went transfer-heavy here in his first year, bringing in 55 new players for 2025. He also hired Josh Henson to bring Purdue back to its pass-heavy, Air Raid roots.

Purdue opened up with wins over Ball State and Southern Illinois but then dropped the final ten games of the season. If you squint you can find some improvement: 2-10 was a one-win improvement over the 1- 11 disaster, there were more competitive finishes, they moved up from dead last in Game Grader to second-to-last.

They outgained Minnesota by 200+ yards but threw a late Pick Six that flipped the game to a loss. Then they blew a 24-21 lead with four minutes left allowing two late Rutgers field goals. Those were competitive, but the season ended with a very uncompetitive 56-3 Bucket Game loss to bring the two-year combined score to Indiana 122, Purdue 3.

For the first time since 1920-21, Purdue went winless in Big Ten play in consecutive seasons.

Odom went transfer-heavy again this cycle and Purdue signed the #10 class in the Big Ten. Combined with the recruiting class, they are pumping another round of 55 new players into the program. To notch some league wins and return to bowl season, they will need a better hit rate than last cycle, find some playmakers, and hope for a significant second-year bonus.
pick_six_2026.offense:
Purdue averaged just 18.8 points per game, and that was somehow an improvement over the 2024 disaster. Injuries made the situation worse, as their top receiver, top tight end, and top

running back played a combined 12 games.

Just two starters return from last year, and while virtually every position is up for grabs in fall camp, Odom made it clear that one is settled. Ryan Browne returns after starting all 12 games – the first Purdue quarterback to accomplish that since David Blough in 2016 – and despite throwing more picks than touchdowns, Odom gave his full endorsement: “I want to say, from as high of a mountain top as I can be on, I believe in Ryan Browne.”

His first six games were noticeably better than his final six, perhaps due to a shoulder injury he took in the seventh game. Browne has flashed his speed and athleticism but posted a low 59% completion rate and ranked dead last on the Big Ten QB Rating leaderboard.

Top receiver De’Nylon Morrissette missed the whole season, All-Big Ten Max Klare transferred to Ohio State, and then tight end George Burhenn only played in four games. This was an ineffective group of pass-catchers that lacked explosiveness and was plagued by dropped balls, and Purdue has lacked a true game-changing receiver since Charlie Jones in 2022.

The four-man rotation is gone, Morrissette is due back from injury, and the staff signed a new group of transfers. Bisi Owens (Penn) earned All-Ivy honors, Asaad Waseem (Florida Atlantic) caught 66 balls for 699 yards last year, and Xavier Townsend was a rotational receiver at Iowa State and UCF. Burhenn is also expected back, and will be joined by Kylan Fox who was UCF’s second tight end last year.

Devin Mockobee graduates after becoming the first Purdue running back to lead the team in rushing four straight seasons. His final year was cut short with an injury but he still finished fourth on the all-time rushing leaderboard here with 2,987 yards. The staff signed a thunder/lightning

duo in Jerrick Gibson (Texas) and return ace Travis Terrell (Jackson State), plus Fame Ijeboi (Minnesota) who got a big freshman workload last year.

The offensive line cut their sack number in half, from a 10% sack rate (#116) to 5% (#31) in 2025. The group struggled to create a consistent run push, and it is a complete rebuild after two starters graduated and another two transferred out to Power 4 programs.

Joey Tanona is the anchor at left tackle that new line coach Zach Crabtree will build around. In spring the starting line featured three incoming Power 4 transfers in center Boaz Stanley (South Carolina), right guard Micah Banuelos (USC), and right tackle Nuku Mafi (Oklahoma State). All three were rated three-star transfers though they all started games last year. Former Top250 recruit and UGA transfer Marques Easley is projected to start at left guard.
pick_six_2026.defense:
Purdue finished 65th of 68 Power 4 in my opponent-adjusted defense stat, and in the national bottom five in yards/play (#133) and yards/pass attempt (#134). Odom fired coordinator Mike Scherer and surprisingly brought back Kevin Kane who was in charge of the Purdue defense during the Ryan Walters era 2023-24.

For as bad as the 2025 defense struggled, Kane’s 2024 unit was statistically worse. They allowed 40 points/game and ranked last in the Big Ten in all major categories. Not exactly a “splash hire” for the fans to get excited about.

Three starters left for other Power 4 programs and just three starters return for 2026.

The interior line was a relative bright spot but starters Demeco Kennedy (Louisville) and big nose tackle Chops Harkless (Kentucky) both transferred out. TJ Lindsey is recovering from an ACL tear and is joined by Big Ten veteran Curt Neal (Illinois).

The ends failed to generate pass rush without bringing extra backers via blitz packages. Their top guy CJ Nunnally graduated and he had more sacks than the rest of the room combined. Breeon Ishmail and CJ Madden are experienced ends and the staff signed Elo Modozie, their lone four-star transfer, who was stuck in a crowded Georgia room after excelling at Army before that.

Mani Powell graduated with Big Ten honors, another starter Alex Sanford left for Pittsburgh, but Charles Correa is a hard-hitter and Tom Dienhart of Gold & Black calls him “an ultimate warrior, the heartbeat of the defense.”

Two more Big Ten transfers round out the projected trio at linebacker with Jojo Hayden (Illinois) and former four-star Anthony Speca (Penn State).

Last cycle, the staff pumped veteran transfers into the secondary and the strategy did not pay off. Not only were the yardage stats bad, this group couldn’t grab takeaways – four interceptions was a Big Ten low. A corner and the top three safeties are gone, but the staff was able to retain starting corner Hudauri Hines and nickel Smiley Bradford. Mister Clark (FIU) was an All-CUSA first-teamer and Don Saunders (Utah) brings a 6’4 frame at corner. Jaden Mangham was an All-Big Ten honorable mention safety at Michigan State in 2023 before a limited role at Michigan the past two years.
